abd.name: Abidjan
abd.text: Abidjan, the bustling commercial hub of Côte d’Ivoire, sits on the Ébrié Lagoon on the Atlantic coast of West Africa. Founded as a small fishing village in the 19th century, it grew rapidly after becoming the colonial capital of French Ivory Coast in the 1930s and later the country’s economic centre. Today the city dazzles visitors with its striking skyline of glass towers, lively markets such as the sprawling Treichville bazaar, and a vibrant nightlife along the lively Rue Princesse. Friendly locals, tasty street food and easy access to nearby beaches make a short stay both lively and memorable.

abj.name: Abuja
abj.text: Abuja, the capital city of Nigeria, sits in the centre of the country on the Aso Rock plateau, roughly 300 km inland from the Atlantic coast. Planned in the 1970s and officially becoming the capital in 1991, it replaced Lagos to provide a more central seat of government. Today the city blends modern architecture with wide, tree-lined avenues; visitors can explore the striking National Mosque, the serene Abuja Arts and Culture Village, and the nearby Zuma Rock, while enjoying a calm, well-maintained urban environment that feels distinctly different from the bustling coastal metropolises.

abq.name: Albuquerque
abq.text: Albuquerque lies in central New Mexico, straddling the Rio Grande between the Sandia and Manzano mountain ranges and bisected by historic Route 66. The settlement was founded in 1706 as Alburquerque, a Spanish colonial outpost that later grew into the state’s largest city. Today visitors can wander the colourful Old Town with its adobe churches and bustling markets, ride the world-famous hot-air balloons that dot the sky each October, explore the nearby mountains by tram or trail, and enjoy a lively mix of Southwestern cuisine, street art and modern museums, all set against a backdrop of striking desert-mountain scenery.

abz.name: Aberdeen
abz.text: Aberdeen, perched on the northeast coast of Scotland, sits where the River Dee meets the North Sea and is framed by the rugged Cairngorms to the west. Founded as a royal burgh in the 12th century, it became a thriving medieval port and later earned the nickname “Granite City” for the sparkling grey stone that lines its streets and gives its buildings a distinctive sparkle in the daylight. Today visitors can wander the bustling waterfront, explore the historic Old Town with its medieval cathedrals, and enjoy a lively arts scene, while the surrounding coastline offers dramatic cliffs, sandy beaches and excellent seafood.

acc.name: Accra
acc.text: Accra, the bustling capital of Ghana, lies on the Atlantic coast of West Africa, nestled between the Gulf of Guinea and the country's hinterland. Founded in the 15th century by the Ga people, it grew into a key trading port and later became the seat of the British Gold Coast administration before Ghana’s independence in 1957. Today the city mixes modern skyscrapers with vibrant markets, colourful street art and historic sites such as the 17th-century Jamestown lighthouse. Visitors can savour spicy street food, hear live highlife music, and feel the warm hospitality of locals as they explore its lively streets and seaside promenade.

add.name: Addis Ababa
add.text: Addis Ababa, Ethiopia’s bustling capital, lies in the central highlands at an altitude of roughly 2,350 metres, giving the city a cool, pleasant climate year-round. It was founded in 1886 by Emperor Menelik II, who chose the site for its fertile plateau and strategic position. Today the city is a lively crossroads of tradition and modernity, with colourful markets such as Merkato, the impressive National Museum housing the famous “Lucy” fossil, and the headquarters of the African Union. Visitors can savour excellent coffee, explore vibrant street art and feel the warm, cosmopolitan spirit that defines this African hub.

adl.name: Adelaide
adl.text: Adelaide, the capital of South Australia, sits on the eastern shore of Gulf St Vincent at the foot of the Mount Lofty Ranges. Founded in 1836 as a planned colony, it was named after Queen Adelaide, consort of William IV, and was laid out with wide streets, a central grid and generous parklands that still define the city. Today visitors enjoy a relaxed atmosphere, strolling through bustling markets, sampling world-class food and wine in the nearby Barossa Valley, and exploring cultural institutions such as the Art Gallery and the historic Adelaide Oval, all set against a backdrop of sunny Mediterranean climate.

adn.name: Aden
adn.text: Aden, a bustling port city on the southern tip of Yemen, sits at the mouth of the Red Sea’s Gulf of Aden and looks out across the strait toward the Horn of Africa. Historically it was a key coaling station for the British Empire in the 19th century and served as a vital gateway for trade between Africa and the Middle East. Today the city offers a vivid mix of old and new: you can wander its lively souks, sample fresh seafood on the waterfront, and explore the historic British colonial buildings that dot the skyline, all while feeling the warm, salty breeze from the sea and the lively rhythm of everyday Yemeni life.

adz.name: Adana
adz.text: Adana, a bustling city in southern Turkey, lies on the banks of the Seyhan River about 30 kilometres inland from the Mediterranean coast. It has been an important centre since antiquity, serving as a key hub in the ancient region of Cilicia and later flourishing under Roman rule. Today the town hums with a lively mix of modern cafés, bustling markets and historic streets, while the scent of its famous kebabs drifts from street stalls. Visitors can stroll along the riverfront promenade, explore the 16th-century stone bridge of Taşköprü and enjoy a warm, sunny climate that makes outdoor cafés particularly pleasant.

aer.name: Sochi
aer.text: Sochi sits on the sunny shores of the Black Sea at the foot of the Caucasus mountains, in Russia’s Krasnodar Krai region, stretching over a narrow strip of coastline that feels both seaside and alpine. It first rose to prominence in the late-19th century as a health resort for the Russian aristocracy, and today it is perhaps best remembered for hosting the 2014 Winter Olympics, which transformed its infrastructure and skyline. Visitors can wander palm-lined promenades, take a cable-car up to the ski slopes of the nearby mountains, and enjoy a blend of modern hotels, lively cafés and historic Soviet-era architecture, all under a mild climate that makes it a year-round destination.

aga.name: Agadir
aga.text: Agadir is a coastal city in southwestern Morocco, set on the Atlantic shoreline at the foot of the Anti-Atlas mountains. It was once a small Berber fishing village before becoming a major port in the 16th century, and after the devastating earthquake of 1960 the town was rebuilt with wide boulevards and modern architecture. Today visitors enjoy a sunny climate, a long sandy beach perfect for strolling or surfing, a lively souk selling spices and crafts, and a promenade lined with cafés where you can watch the sea and the city’s relaxed, contemporary vibe.

ahw.name: Ahvaz
ahw.text: Ahvaz, the bustling capital of Iran’s oil-rich Khuzestan province, sits on the banks of the Karun River, the country’s longest waterway, in the far southwest near the Iraqi border. Historically it was a key settlement of the ancient Elamite civilization and later became an important centre for the Persian Gulf trade routes. Today the city dazzles visitors with its striking bridges spanning the river, lively bazaars where you can haggle for spices and handicrafts, and a surprising mix of modern skyscrapers and traditional mud-brick homes, all set against a backdrop of sweltering summer heat and a warm, welcoming atmosphere.

akl.name: Auckland
akl.text: Auckland, New Zealand, lies on the narrow isthmus between the Hauraki Gulf and the Tasman Sea, surrounded by volcanic cones and two harbours that give the city its nickname “the City of Sails”. It was founded in 1840 as a trading post and quickly grew into the country’s main port, playing a key role in early European settlement. Today the city buzzes with a relaxed, multicultural vibe: cafés spill onto pedestrian streets, waterfront walks offer stunning views of the skyline and islands, and easy access to beaches, vineyards and native bush makes it a lively base for exploring both urban culture and the great outdoors.

akt.name: Aktau
akt.text: Aktau is a striking port city perched on the western shore of the Caspian Sea in far-southern Kazakhstan, where the desert meets the water. Founded in 1964 as a closed settlement for uranium mining, it was known as Shevchenko until Kazakhstan’s independence restored its original name in 1991. Today the town is a blend of Soviet-era concrete and sleek new high-rises, with a palm-lined promenade, clean beaches and a lively fish market overlooking the sea. Visitors can stroll along the waterfront, explore the underground museum of the city’s secret past, and enjoy the stark, beautiful contrast of turquoise water against endless steppe.

aky.name: Akureyri
aky.text: Akureyri, perched on the shores of the deep Eyjafjörður fjord in northern Iceland, is the country’s second-largest town and a charming gateway to the Arctic north. The settlement received its first formal municipal charter in 1786, marking the start of a thriving community that has grown around the surrounding mountains and coastal scenery. Today visitors find a lively town centre lined with colourful houses, cosy cafés and a surprisingly lush botanical garden, while easy bus and road links make it simple to explore nearby waterfalls, volcanic landscapes and whale-watching trips; in winter the streets are often dusted with snow, giving the town a festive, yet relaxed, atmosphere.

alc.name: Algeciras
alc.text: Algeciras sits on the southern tip of Spain’s Costa del Sol, perched on the Bay of Gibraltar where the Mediterranean meets the Atlantic. Historically it grew from a modest Roman settlement into a key Moorish port, later becoming an important naval base after the British captured nearby Gibraltar in the early 18th century. Today the town bustles with a lively waterfront promenade, colourful markets and fresh seafood taverns, while ferries whisk you across to Tangier and the nearby Rock of Gibraltar. With its warm climate, vibrant multicultural atmosphere and easy access to both beaches and mountain trails, Algeciras feels like a gateway to the crossroads of Europe and Africa.

alg.name: Algiers
alg.text: Algiers, the capital of Algeria, sits on the Mediterranean coast where the sea meets the foothills of the Kabylie mountains, offering striking white-washed buildings that climb the cliff-side Casbah. Founded by the Phoenicians and later becoming a key Ottoman port, the city’s historic quarter was declared a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1992 for its blend of Arab, Berber and French colonial architecture. Today visitors wander lively markets smelling of fresh spices, sip coffee in breezy cafés overlooking the harbor, and enjoy a mix of modern art galleries and traditional street music that give Algiers a vibrant, multicultural energy.

alm.name: Almaty
alm.text: Almaty, nestled at the foothills of the Trans-Altaic Mountains in southeastern Kazakhstan, is the country’s former capital and its largest city. Founded as a Russian fort in the mid-19th century, it grew into a cultural hub and was the seat of government until the capital moved to Astana in 1997. Today the city blends modern cafés, vibrant bazaars and leafy parks with stunning mountain backdrops; visitors can stroll along the tree-lined Arbat, sip tea in a Soviet-era tea house, or take a short drive to the nearby ski resort of Shymbulak for breathtaking alpine views.

alp.name: Aleppo
alp.text: Aleppo, in northern Syria, sits on the banks of the Queiq River about 30 kilometres inland from the Mediterranean coast, roughly halfway between Damascus and the Turkish border. It is one of the world’s oldest continuously inhabited cities, famed for its medieval citadel that has stood guard since the Crusades and for being a key stop on the ancient Silk Road. Today the old souks still buzz with traders selling spices, textiles and pistachios, while restored Ottoman houses and the bustling Al-Madina al-Qadima district let visitors feel the layered history, even as the city rebuilds after recent conflict.

alx.name: Alexandria
alx.text: Alexandria, Egypt, sits on the Mediterranean coast about 225 kilometres west of Cairo, where the Nile meets the sea. Founded by Alexander the Great in the 4th century BC, it soon became home to the famous Library of Alexandria, a centre of learning that drew scholars from across the ancient world. Today the city blends its historic charm with a lively waterfront: you can stroll along the corniche, explore the modern Bibliotheca Alexandrinae on the former library site, and savour fresh seafood in bustling souks while the sea breezes carry the scent of history and the hum of contemporary cafés.

amb.name: Ambon
amb.text: Ambon, perched on the eastern side of Ambon Island in the Maluku archipelago, is the provincial capital of Maluku, Indonesia, and sits on a natural harbour that once made the town a key hub in the 16th-century spice trade. The Dutch East India Company established Fort Victoria there in the 1630s, and the town later saw fierce fighting during World War II. Today Ambon feels relaxed yet lively: colourful markets spill onto the waterfront, street vendors serve steaming bowls of sago soup, and the streets echo with the rhythms of Maluku’s folk songs. The surrounding waters are renowned for excellent diving, offering visitors a blend of history, culture and natural beauty in one compact, welcoming town.

amd.name: Ahmedabad
amd.text: Ahmedabad, situated in the western Indian state of Gujarat along the Sabarmati River, is a bustling metropolis famed for its rich heritage and vibrant street life. Founded in the 15th century by Sultan Ahmed Shah, the city’s historic walled centre, the Pol, still houses intricately carved havelis, bustling bazaars and the striking Jama Masjid. Today visitors can wander through the UNESCO-listed old city, savour delicious Gujarati thalis, explore the tranquil Sabarmati Ashram where Mahatma Gandhi once lived, and admire contemporary art at the Calico Museum, all amid a lively mix of modern cafés and colourful festivals.

amm.name: Amman
amm.text: Amman, the capital of Jordan, sits on a series of seven hills in the north-central part of the country, overlooking the Jordan Valley to the east and the desert landscape of the east and south. The city grew from the ancient Greco-Roman settlement of Philadelphia, founded by Ptolemy II in the 3rd century BC and later incorporated into the Roman Empire, leaving ruins such as the spectacular Amphitheatre in the downtown area. Today Amman blends old and new: bustling souks and modern cafés sit side by side, rooftop terraces offer sweeping views of the hills, and the friendly locals are happy to share their rich culinary and cultural heritage with curious visitors.

ams.name: Amsterdam
ams.text: Amsterdam, the lively capital of the Netherlands, sits on the banks of the Amstel River and spreads across a network of historic canals that give the city its famous, picturesque charm. First granted city rights in 1300, it grew into a major trading hub during the Dutch Golden Age, when artists like Rembrandt and Vermeer worked in its bustling workshops. Today the streets are a mix of centuries-old gabled houses and modern cafés, with cyclists weaving between the canals, museums showcasing world-class art, and a relaxed, multicultural atmosphere that makes wandering the city feel both timeless and fresh.

anc.name: Anchorage
anc.text: Anchorage, Alaska’s largest city, lies on the Cook Inlet at the base of the Chugach Mountains, roughly 260 miles north of the Canada-US border. It grew rapidly after the construction of the Alaska Railroad in the early 20th century, becoming a key supply hub during World War II when the nearby military bases were expanded. Today the city feels like a laid-back frontier outpost with modern amenities: you can stroll along the scenic waterfront, explore museums that tell the story of native cultures and gold-rush pioneers, and venture out for spectacular wildlife sightings or mountain hikes just a short drive away.

and.name: Andorra la Vella
and.text: Andorra la Vella, the capital of the tiny Pyrenean principality of Andorra, lies nestled in a high mountain valley between France and Spain, at about 1,023 metres above sea level. The town dates back to at least the 9th century, when it was mentioned in a charter granting the Andorran people a charter of liberties that later became the basis of their unique co-princely system. Today visitors find a charming mix of stone-covered streets, modern boutiques and ski-resort cafés, with easy lifts to the surrounding slopes and a lively promenade lined with restaurants serving hearty mountain fare.

ank.name: Ankara
ank.text: Ankara, the capital of Turkey, sits in the heart of the Anatolian plateau about 450 km east of the Mediterranean coast. Historically it was the centre of the ancient Phrygian kingdom and later became the base of Mustafa Kemal Atatürk’s nationalist movement, leading to its designation as the Republic’s capital in 1923. Today the city blends modern government buildings and bustling cafés with historic sites such as the Roman-era Ankara Castle and the Museum of Anatolian Civilisations. Visitors enjoy strolling through leafy parks, sampling lively street food, and experiencing a cosmopolitan vibe that reflects both its deep past and contemporary Turkish life.

ans.name: Antsiranana
ans.text: Antsiranana, formerly known as Diego Suarez, lies at the northern tip of Madagascar where the Indian Ocean meets the Bay of Antsiranana, a sheltered harbour framed by striking limestone cliffs. The town was founded in the late 19th century as a French naval base and still bears traces of its colonial past in the wide, tree-lined avenues and the historic lighthouse on the peninsula. Today visitors enjoy a laid-back atmosphere, strolling along the promenade, watching colourful fishing boats bob in the calm waters and sampling fresh seafood at bustling market stalls, while the nearby beaches and coral reefs offer excellent opportunities for swimming and snorkeling.

ant.name: Antwerp
ant.text: Antwerp sits on the banks of the Scheldt River in northern Belgium, about 45 kilometres from the Dutch border and a short train ride from Brussels. In the 16th century the city thrived as one of Europe’s leading ports, handling a great share of the continent’s diamond trade—a legacy that still defines the bustling diamond district today. Visitors wander the historic centre with its towering Gothic cathedral, stroll along the lively waterfront, and sample world-class beer and chocolate in cosy cafés, while modern art museums and stylish boutiques give the city a contemporary buzz.

apw.name: Apia
apw.text: Apia, the capital city of Samoa, sits on the central coast of the island of Upolu, nestled between a natural harbour and the verdant hills that rise inland. Founded in the 19th century, it became the focal point of Samoan politics after the signing of the Treaty of Berlin in 1889, which established a joint German, British and American administration. Today the town is a relaxed blend of colonial-era buildings, bustling markets and beachfront promenades; you can sip fresh coconut water while watching colourful outriggers glide past, explore the Robert Louis Stevenson Museum, or savour Samoan cuisine at lively roadside stalls, all under a warm, tropical sun.

aqb.name: Aqaba
aqb.text: Aqaba is Jordan’s only coastal city, perched on the north-east corner of the Red Sea’s Gulf of Aqaba and bordered by Saudi Arabia, Israel and Egypt. It first entered world headlines during the 1917 Battle of Aqaba, when T. E. Lawrence and Arab forces captured the Ottoman port. Today the town is a sunny gateway for snorkellers and divers exploring colourful coral reefs, while its bustling souk offers spices, jewellery and fresh fish. The promenade is lined with cafés and modern hotels, and the surrounding desert mountains provide striking backdrops for sunset walks.

aqp.name: Arequipa
aqp.text: Arequipa, nestled on the high plateau of southern Peru at the foot of the snow-capped volcanoes El Misti, Chachani and Pichu Pichu, is known as the “White City” for its elegant buildings of white volcanic sillar stone. Founded in 1540 by the Spanish, it became an important colonial centre and later a hub for the independence movement. Today the city dazzles visitors with a blend of historic plazas, lively markets and superb restaurants serving regional dishes such as rocoto relleno; the surrounding valleys offer spectacular trekking and the crisp mountain air makes strolling the cobbled streets a delight.

aru.name: Arusha
aru.text: Arusha is a bustling town in northern Tanzania, perched at the foot of Mount Meru and just a short drive from the Serengeti and Ngorongoro Crater. It was the site of the 1961 signing of the Arusha Declaration, which set out Tanzania’s socialist policies under President Julius Nyerere. Today the town feels lively and welcoming, with colourful markets selling fresh produce and crafts, a growing café culture where you can sip coffee while watching traffic of matatus and safari-bound buses, and easy access to wildlife parks that make it a convenient gateway for adventurous travellers.

asb.name: Ashgabat
asb.text: Ashgabat, the capital of Turkmenistan, lies in the south-eastern part of the country near the foothills of the Kopet Dag mountains and close to the Iranian border. Founded in the 19th century as a Russian fortress, it became the centre of Soviet Turkmenistan in the 1920s and was renamed from Poltoratsk after Turkmen independence. Today the city dazzles visitors with its wide marble avenues, glittering fountains and striking white-clad skyscrapers, while the bustling markets offer carpets, spices and traditional tea. Despite its modern, glossy image, Ashgabat retains a warm, hospitable feel and serves as a gateway to the desert and historic Silk-Road sites nearby.

asm.name: Asmara
asm.text: Asmara, perched on the Ethiopian-highland plateau at about 2,300 metres, is the capital city of Eritrea in the Horn of Africa. The town grew from a modest 12th-century settlement and was chosen as the administrative centre of Italian Eritrea in 1897, which left a legacy of elegant Art-Deco and modernist buildings that still line its wide avenues. Today, visitors wander through cafés serving rich coffee, explore the UNESCO-listed “City of Lights” with its blend of colonial architecture and vibrant street markets, and enjoy the cool, dry climate that makes strolling the historic streets a pleasant, almost timeless experience.

asp.name: Alice Springs
asp.text: Alice Springs sits in the heart of the Australian continent, on the edge of the arid Simpson Desert and the MacDonnell Ranges, about 1,500 km south of Darwin. Established in 1872 as a telegraph station linking Adelaide to Darwin, the town grew around this vital communication hub and later became a key supply centre for cattle stations and explorers. Today the streets buzz with a relaxed outback charm: you can wander the vibrant Todd Mall, admire Aboriginal art galleries, and venture on guided walks to spectacular nearby gorges, while the distant red cliffs and the ever-present scent of desert eucalyptus remind you that you are truly in the Red Centre.

ast.name: Astana
ast.text: Astana, the capital of Kazakhstan, sits on the banks of the Ishim River in the north-central part of the country, where the steppe meets the foothills of the Urals. It was renamed the capital in 1997, moving the government from Almaty, and its modern skyline reflects a rapid development programme that began after independence. Today the city feels futuristic yet welcoming, with striking glass-clad buildings such as the Khan Shatyr and the Palace of Peace and Reconciliation, spacious parks along the river, and a lively mix of cafes where you can taste both traditional Kazakh dishes and contemporary cuisine.

asu.name: Asuncion
asu.text: Asunción, the capital of Paraguay, sits on the east bank of the Paraguay River opposite the Argentine city of Clorinda, roughly midway between the tropics and the subtropics. Founded in 1537 by Spanish explorer Juan de Salazar, it is one of South America’s oldest cities and retains a colonial grid that still shapes its streets. Today the city blends historic churches and colourful neighbourhoods with lively cafés, modern museums and a riverside promenade where locals gather for a relaxed stroll. Visitors enjoy the warm hospitality, affordable dining and a surprisingly vibrant arts scene amidst the laid-back atmosphere.

asw.name: Aswan
asw.text: Aswan, perched on the western bank of the Nile in southern Egypt, is a sun-kissed gateway to the ancient world. It grew around a narrow island that was the site of the Temple of Isis at Philae, a sanctuary relocated stone-by-stone after the construction of the Aswan High Dam in the 1960s. Today the town is a relaxed blend of bustling markets, felucca-ridden boat trips on the river and wide, palm-lined promenades. Visitors can wander the cool stone halls of the Nubian Museum, watch the river change colour at sunset, and enjoy tea in a café while the distant call to prayer drifts over the water.

ath.name: Athens
ath.text: Athens, the capital of Greece, sits on the southeastern side of the Attica peninsula, overlooking the Saronic Gulf and framed by the hills of the Acropolis. It is the birthplace of democracy, where the ancient Assembly met in the 5th century BC to discuss civic affairs. Today the city blends its millennia-old ruins with a lively modern scene: you can wander through the marble columns of the Parthenon, sip coffee in bustling neighbourhoods such as Plaka and Monastiraki, and enjoy a vibrant nightlife and thriving food markets, all under a warm Mediterranean sun.

atl.name: Atlanta
atl.text: Atlanta lies in the heart of the state of Georgia, in the southeastern United States, at the foothills of the Appalachian Mountains and alongside the Chattahoochee River. Founded in 1837 as a terminus for a new railway line, the city grew quickly and later served as a crucial hub for the Civil Rights movement, with the 1965 signing of the Voting Rights Act taking place nearby. Today Atlanta blends modern skyscrapers with leafy neighbourhoods, offering a lively food scene, world-class attractions such as the Georgia Aquarium and the Martin Luther King Jr. National Historical Site, and a warm, southern hospitality that welcomes visitors year-round.

atq.name: Amritsar
atq.text: Amritsar, nestled in the north-western part of Punjab, India, lies close to the border with Pakistan and is a major hub on the historic Grand Trunk Road. Founded in the 16th century, the city is best known for the Golden Temple, the spiritual centre of Sikhism, which was completed in the early 1600s and has long attracted pilgrims from around the world. Today Amritsar buzzes with a lively mix of bustling bazaars, fragrant street-food stalls serving dishes such as buttery kulchas and spicy chole, and the poignant reminder of history at the Jallianwala Bagh memorial, making it a vibrant destination for culture lovers and food enthusiasts alike.

auh.name: Abu Dhabi
auh.text: Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, lies on an island in the Persian Gulf, bordering the mainland to the south and west. It grew from a modest fishing and pearl-diving settlement into a modern metropolis after oil was discovered in the 1950s, and the city’s first mosque, the Al Bahrain, dates back to the early 20th century. Today visitors find a striking blend of sleek skyscrapers, such as the iconic Burj Khalifa-style Etihad Towers, and tranquil heritage sites like the Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque, whose marble domes and reflective pools create a serene atmosphere. The waterfront promenade, upscale malls and desert safaris offer a mix of luxury, culture and adventure for any traveller.

avi.name: Avignon
avi.text: Avignon, a charming city in the Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur region of southeastern France, sits on the left bank of the Rhône River about 30 km north of the Mediterranean coast. It is famed for the Palais des Papes, the massive medieval papal palace that served as the residence of the popes during the 14th-century Avignon Papacy, when the seat of the Roman Catholic Church was moved from Rome. Today the city feels relaxed yet lively, with its narrow cobbled streets, bustling markets and vibrant cafés spilling onto the historic squares. The annual Festival d’Avignon brings street performances and theatre to the ancient walls, making a visit both a walk through history and a lively cultural experience.

ayt.name: Antalya
ayt.text: Antalya, a vibrant coastal city on Turkey’s southwestern Mediterranean shoreline, lies at the foot of the Taurus Mountains and enjoys a sunny climate year-round. It grew out of the ancient Roman settlement of Attalia, founded in the second century BC and later fortified with impressive walls that still frame the historic Kaleiçi quarter. Today the city blends old and new: narrow, cobbled streets lead to bustling bazaars, while sleek waterfront promenades offer cafés, yachts and golden beaches; the backdrop of turquoise sea and rugged hills makes a visit both relaxing and full of colourful culture.

bah.name: Manama
bah.text: Manama, the capital of Bahrain, sits on the north coast of the island nation facing the Persian Gulf, just a short ferry ride from Saudi Arabia. Historically it grew from a modest pearl-diving village into a bustling trading port in the 19th century, when merchants from across the Gulf gathered to sell oysters, dates and textiles. Today the city blends sleek skyscrapers with traditional souqs, offering shaded cafés serving fragrant Arabic coffee, the glittering Bahrain World Trade Centre, and a lively waterfront promenade where modern art installations sit beside centuries-old mosques, making it a vibrant place to explore.

bak.name: Baku
bak.text: Baku, the vibrant capital of Azerbaijan, sits on the western coast of the Caspian Sea at the southern tip of the Absheron Peninsula. It has been a key trading hub since at least the 12th-century Silk Road, when merchants from Europe and Asia converged on its bustling ports. Today the city blends ultra-modern skyscrapers such as the Flame Towers with the cobbled streets of the UNESCO-listed Old City, where ancient mosques and caravanserais sit beside lively cafés. Visitors can stroll along the promenade, sample fragrant Azerbaijani cuisine, and enjoy a lively cultural scene that mixes traditional music with contemporary art.

bal.name: Baltimore
bal.text: Baltimore sits on the western shore of the Chesapeake Bay in Maryland, about 40 miles north of Washington, D.C. It grew around the 1729 port that later became a major gateway for immigrants and a key Union supply line during the Civil War. Today the city blends historic charm with modern buzz: you can wander the cobbled streets of Fell’s Point, admire the striking Inner Harbor skyline, sample crab cakes at bustling waterfront restaurants, and explore world-class museums such as the American Visionary Art Museum. Friendly locals, lively music scenes and scenic waterfront walks make a visit both relaxed and memorable.

bar.name: Bari
bar.text: Bari, the bustling port city on the Adriatic coast of southern Italy, is the capital of the Apulia region and a gateway to the heel of the Italian boot. Founded by the Romans, it later became an important medieval trading hub, and its 11th-century Basilica of San Nicola still houses the relics of Saint Nicholas, drawing pilgrims from across Europe. Today the historic centre is a maze of narrow lanes, lively cafés and bustling fish markets, while the sleek waterfront promenade offers striking sea views, modern restaurants and a relaxed, sun-kissed atmosphere that blends ancient charm with contemporary Italian life.

bbd.name: Bobo-Dioulasso
bbd.text: Bobo-Dioulasso lies in the western part of Burkina Faso, perched on the edge of the Mouhoun River and about 350 km from the capital, Ouagadougou. Founded in the 15th century as a small trading outpost, it grew into a vibrant centre of the Marka kingdom and later became the colonial railway hub that linked the region to Ghana and Côte d’Ivoire. Today the town bustles with colour: its bustling markets overflow with woven fabrics, fresh produce and lively music, while the historic Grand Mosque and the well-preserved colonial architecture offer a charming glimpse into its rich past.

bcn.name: Barcelona
bcn.text: Barcelona, perched on the northeastern coast of Spain along the Mediterranean Sea, is the vibrant capital of Catalonia. Founded as a Roman colony, it later became the seat of the Crown of Aragon, a medieval power that shaped much of Mediterranean history. Today the city buzzes with a mix of historic charm and modern flair: you can wander the winding lanes of the Gothic Quarter, admire Antoni Gaudí’s surreal architecture such as the still-unfinished Sagrada Família, and relax on sandy beaches while cafés serve tapas and cava. Its lively streets, sea breezes and cultural festivals make it a memorable stop for any traveller.

bdo.name: Bandung
bdo.text: Bandung, nestled on the volcanic plateau of West Java at about 750 metres above sea-level, is famed for its cool climate and lush surrounding tea fields. In 1955 the city hosted the historic Asian-African Conference, marking a milestone in post-colonial diplomacy, and many elegant Art-Deco buildings from that era still line its streets. Today visitors wander its bustling markets, sip coffee in chic cafés, and explore nearby attractions such as the volcanic crater of Tangkuban Perahu or the colourful streets of the historic Braga neighbourhood, all while enjoying the refreshing mountain air and a vibrant, youthful atmosphere.

bdt.name: Bridgetown
bdt.text: Bridgetown, the capital of Barbados, sits on the southwest coast of the island facing the Caribbean Sea and the busy port of Carlisle Bay. Founded in the early 17th century, it became a key hub of the British Atlantic trade and its historic Garrison, now a UNESCO World Heritage site, still houses well-preserved 18th-century stone buildings and the impressive St Michael’s Cathedral. Today the city blends colourful colonial architecture with modern cafés, bustling markets and a lively waterfront promenade where locals and visitors alike enjoy street food, live music and the warm, breezy atmosphere of a tropical harbour town.

bei.name: Beira
bei.text: Beira is a bustling port city on the east coast of Mozambique, situated at the mouth of the Pungue River where it meets the Indian Ocean. Founded by the Portuguese in the late 19th century, it quickly became a key gateway for trade into the interior of southern Africa and played a vital role during the colonial era as a supply hub for neighbouring territories. Today visitors find a lively waterfront lined with modest cafés and markets, a backdrop of low-rise buildings and the striking Mozambique Channel beyond. The city’s warm climate, friendly locals and easy access to nearby beaches and the historic railway make it a pleasant, off-the-beaten-track stop for curious travellers.

bel.name: Belfast
bel.text: Belfast, the capital of Northern Ireland, sits on the River Lagan where it meets Belfast Lough on the island’s eastern coast. Historically it was the world’s leading ship-building hub, most famously launching the RMS Titanic in 1912. Today the city blends its industrial heritage with a vibrant cultural scene: you can wander the revitalised waterfront, explore museums that recount its past, and enjoy lively pubs, restaurants and street art in the Cathedral Quarter. Friendly locals, green parks and stunning coastal views make Belfast a welcoming place to discover.

ber.name: Berlin
ber.text: Berlin, the vibrant capital of Germany, lies in the northeastern part of the country on the River Spree and is surrounded by the state of Brandenburg. Founded in the 13th century, it became the capital of the Kingdom of Prussia and later the seat of the German Empire, and its historic Brandenburg Gate still marks the former divide between East and West during the Cold War. Today the city buzzes with a mix of modern architecture, world-class museums and leafy parks; cyclists glide along bustling streets, cafés spill onto cobblestones, and the nightlife hums long after the sun sets, making Berlin a lively playground for history lovers and creative explorers alike.

bey.name: Beirut
bey.text: Beirut, perched on the sparkling Mediterranean coast of Lebanon, is the country’s bustling capital and a gateway between East and West. Founded by the ancient Phoenicians, the city was dramatically reshaped after the civil war that ended in 1990, emerging as a modern hub while retaining its historic layers. Today visitors wander lively souks filled with spices and jewellery, sip coffee on the bustling Corniche overlooking the sea, explore museums that trace millennia of civilisation, and enjoy a vibrant nightlife that blends Lebanese tradition with contemporary flair, all set against a backdrop of dramatic mountain vistas.

bfn.name: Bloemfontein
bfn.text: Bloemfontein, situated in the heart of South Africa’s Free State province, sits on the highveld at about 1,400 metres above sea level and serves as the country’s judicial capital. Founded in 1846, the town became the capital of the independent Orange Free State before it was incorporated into the Union of South Africa in 1910. Today visitors find a relaxed, tree-lined city with a mix of colonial architecture and modern amenities; the iconic Naval Hill museum complex, the well-kept Free State National Botanical Garden and a lively café culture make it a pleasant stop for history lovers and nature enthusiasts alike.

bgd.name: Baghdad
bgd.text: Baghdad, the bustling capital of Iraq, sits on the banks of the Tigris River where the river’s wide bends create a natural crossroads between the desert and fertile plains. Founded in the 8th century as the heart of the Abbasid Caliphate, it once housed the legendary House of Wisdom, a centre of learning that attracted scholars from across the medieval world. Today the city blends ancient souks with modern cafés: the aroma of spices drifts from market stalls, while sleek glass towers rise beside historic mosques. Visitors can wander the riverside promenade, sample Iraqi cuisine, and feel the resilient spirit of a city that has endured for more than a thousand years.

bgi.name: Bangui
bgi.text: Bangui, the capital of the Central African Republic, sits on the north bank of the Ubangi River where it meets the Congo, giving the city a riverside charm and a strategic position that once made it a key French colonial trading post founded in 1889. Today the town is a bustling mix of colourful markets, modest French-era buildings and lively riverfront cafés, while the surrounding hills provide scenic views. Visitors can wander the lively streets, sample local cuisine and take a short boat trip on the Ubangi, though they should be aware that infrastructure is modest and basic amenities may be limited.

bgn.name: Bergen
bgn.text: Bergen sits on the western coast of Norway, cradled by seven surrounding mountains and the inlet of Byfjorden, making it a gateway to the dramatic fjords of the region. Founded in 1070, the city grew wealthy as a vital stop on the medieval Hanseatic League’s trade route, a legacy still visible in the colourful wooden wharf of Bryggen, a UNESCO World Heritage site. Today visitors wander its narrow cobbled streets, ride the Fløibanen funicular for panoramic sea-and-mountain views, and enjoy fresh seafood at lively markets, while the ever-present rain adds a fresh sparkle to the city’s lively atmosphere.

bho.name: Bhopal
bho.text: Bhopal, the capital city of Madhya Pradesh in central India, sits on the fertile banks of the Upper Lake and Lower Lake, giving it the nickname “City of Lakes”. It was founded in the early 18th century by the Afghan ruler Dost Mohammad Khan, who established the princely state of Bhopal that later became known for its progressive female rulers in the 20th century. Today the city blends historic charm with modern bustle: you can wander through the elegant Taj-ul-Masjid, explore the well-preserved Bhimbetka rock-shelter caves nearby, and relax by the tranquil lakeside promenades, all while enjoying lively markets, tasty street food and a welcoming atmosphere.

bil.name: Bilbao
bil.text: Bilbao sits on the north-eastern edge of Spain, tucked against the mouth of the Nervión River in the Basque Country and framed by the rolling green hills of the Cantabrian Mountains. The city grew from a medieval trading port and, after the 19th-century industrial boom, became a major centre for steel and shipbuilding. Today, Bilbao is a vibrant mix of old and new: you can stroll along the historic Casco Viejo with its narrow streets and lively pintxos bars, then marvel at the gleaming titanium curves of the Guggenheim Museum, while the riverfront promenades and lush parks offer relaxed, modern ambience perfect for a day of exploration.

bir.name: Birmingham
bir.text: Birmingham sits in the West Midlands of England, about 100 miles north-west of London and 20 miles east of the Welsh border, straddling the River Rea. It grew from a medieval market town into the world’s first industrial city, its factories and canals playing a key role in the Industrial Revolution. Today the city buzzes with a vibrant mix of cultures, from the bustling Bullring shopping centre to the striking modern architecture of the Library of Birmingham, while its historic Jewellery Quarter and lively canalside pubs remind visitors of its rich past.

bis.name: Bissau
bis.text: Bissau, the bustling capital of Guinea-Bissau, sits on the Atlantic coast at the mouth of the Rio Cacheu, where mangrove-lined waterways meet golden beaches. Founded as a Portuguese trading post in the 17th century, it became the centre of the colony’s administration before independence in 1973. Today the city hums with colour: lively markets sell fresh fish, fragrant spices and vibrant fabrics, while colonial-era buildings stand beside modern cafés. Visitors can wander the waterfront promenade, watch sunset over the harbour, and feel the warm, welcoming rhythm of a place where history and contemporary life blend effortlessly.

bjr.name: Bahir Dar
bjr.text: Bahir Dar, perched on the southern shore of Lake Tana in north-west Ethiopia, is a tranquil lakeside town framed by palm-fringed promenades and the mist-capped Blue Nile Falls just a short drive away. It grew around a 13th-century monastery on the lake’s islands, a testament to the region’s long Christian heritage. Today the town buzzes with colourful markets, boat trips to ancient islands dotted with centuries-old churches, and cafés where you can sip coffee while watching gulls glide over the water; the gentle breeze and friendly locals make it a relaxed yet vibrant spot for travellers.

bjs.name: Beijing
bjs.text: Beijing, the sprawling capital of China, sits in the northern part of the country where the ancient plains meet the foothills of the Yan Mountains. It has been the seat of Chinese imperial power for centuries, famously housing the Forbidden City, the grand palace complex constructed in the early 15th century that was the home of successive emperors. Today the city blends that deep heritage with a bustling modern vibe: sleek skyscrapers rise beside historic hutongs, the air hums with the clatter of subway trains, and you can sample everything from sizzling street-food stalls to world-class museums, all within a city that never seems to slow down.

bkg.name: Bangkok
bkg.text: Bangkok, the bustling capital of Thailand, sits on the Chao Phraya River in the country’s central plain, about 40 km from the Gulf of Thailand. Founded in 1782 as the new seat of the Siamese kingdom, the city grew around the Grand Palace and its nearby temples, which still dominate the historic core. Today, visitors find a lively mix of sleek sky-scrapers, colourful street markets and a network of canals that echo its nickname “Venice of the East”. The streets hum with the scent of sizzling street food, the chatter of tuk-tuk drivers and the glow of neon signs, offering a sensory adventure at every turn.

bkh.name: Bukhara
bkh.text: Bukhara, perched in the heart of Uzbekistan’s Kyzylkum Desert, lies about 140 km south-west of Samarkand and is cradled by the fertile Zeravshan River valley. It was a key stop on the Silk Road and, from the 9th to the 12th centuries, flourished as a major centre of Islamic learning and trade under the Samanid dynasty. Today the city feels like an open-air museum: narrow, winding lanes lead past stunning mosques, madrassas and a towering minaret, while bustling bazaars sell fragrant spices and hand-woven textiles, offering visitors a vivid blend of history and lively local life.

bkk.name: Bouake
bkk.text: Bouaké, perched in the heart of Côte d’Ivoire’s Vallée du Bandama, is the country’s second-largest city and a major crossroads where the north-south and east-west highways intersect. It began as a modest railway stop in the 1930s and grew rapidly, later becoming the de-facto capital of the rebel-held north during the civil conflict of the early 2000s. Today the city hums with activity: bustling markets overflow with fresh mangoes, cocoa and handmade textiles, while cafés and music venues showcase lively Ivorian rhythms. Friendly locals greet visitors with warmth, and the streets reflect a city confidently rebuilding and modernising.

bko.name: Bamako
bko.text: Bamako, the bustling capital of Mali, lies on the south-western bank of the Niger River where the river turns sharply eastward, about 250 km inland from the Atlantic. Founded in the 19th century, it became the centre of French colonial administration after the French captured the nearby city of Ségou in 1895, and later the seat of an independent Mali in 1960. Today the city hums with a lively mix of markets, music venues and modern cafés; you can wander the colourful souks, sample street-food tags alongside fresh river fish, and hear the echo of traditional griot songs alongside contemporary Afro-beat rhythms.

bkv.name: Bukavu
bkv.text: Bukavu lies on the southwestern shore of Lake Kivu in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, perched at the foot of the Rwenzori mountains and a short drive from the Rwandan border. The town began as the Belgian colonial outpost Costermansville in 1913 before being renamed Bukavu after independence. Today visitors find a lively market where fresh fish from the lake and locally grown coffee are sold alongside colourful textiles, and cafés offer relaxed views of the lake’s gentle waves against a backdrop of volcanic hills. Though the region has known periods of unrest, Bukavu’s streets are welcoming, its people warm, and the surrounding scenery spectacular for a day of exploration.

blb.name: Belem
blb.text: Belém, the bustling gateway to the Amazon, sits on the northern bank of the Pará River where it meets the mouth of the Amazon in Brazil’s far north-east. Founded in 1616 as a Portuguese colonial outpost, the city became the principal port for the rubber boom of the late 19th century, shaping its grand architecture and lively riverfront. Today visitors wander the historic centre, admire the ornate Ver-o-Pé market’s tropical fruits and spices, and stroll beneath the towering arches of the Basilica of Our Lady of Nazareth, while river ferries offer scenic trips to the lush islands of the bay.

blg.name: Belgrade
blg.text: Belgrade, Serbia’s lively capital, sits at the confluence of the Danube and Sava rivers in the heart of the Balkans. It has been a strategic crossroads for centuries, famously withstanding a siege by the Ottoman Empire in 1521 before later becoming the capital of Yugoslavia. Today the city buzzes with a mix of historic cafés, vibrant street art and spacious riverfront promenades where you can watch ferries glide past the ancient Kalemegdan Fortress. Friendly locals, a thriving nightlife and plenty of museums make Belgrade a welcoming stop for any traveller.

blr.name: Bengaluru
blr.text: Bengaluru, the capital of Karnataka in southern India, lies on the Deccan Plateau at an elevation of about 900 metres, giving it a pleasantly cool climate compared with much of the country. Founded in the 16th century by Kempe Gowda I, the city grew from a modest mud fort into a major centre of the British colonial administration and later the “Silicon Valley of India”, renowned for its tech parks and start-up culture. Today visitors find a vibrant mix of modern glass skyscrapers, bustling street markets and leafy gardens such as Cubbon Park, while historic sites like the 17th-century Tipu Sultan’s Summer Palace offer a glimpse of its rich past.

bna.name: Nashville
bna.text: Nashville, the capital of Tennessee, sits in the heart of the state on the banks of the Cumberland River. The city grew from a frontier settlement founded in 1779 and became the state capital in 1826, later earning its reputation as “Music City” thanks to the establishment of the Grand Ole Opry in 1925 and a thriving recording industry. Today visitors find a lively mix of honky-tonk bars on Broadway, world-class museums such as the Country Music Hall of Fame, and a buzzing food scene ranging from Southern barbecue to inventive farm-to-table eateries, all set against a backdrop of leafy parks and riverfront walkways.

bnd.name: Bandar Abbas
bnd.text: Bandar Abbas is a bustling port city on the southern coast of Iran, tucked along the northern edge of the Strait of Hormuz where the Persian Gulf meets the Gulf of Oman. Historically it served as a key gateway for trade between Persia and the wider Indian Ocean, and its harbour was an important stop for caravans and ships long before modern times. Today the city offers a lively blend of modern waterfront promenades, colourful markets selling fresh seafood and spices, and striking views of the surrounding hills, making it a fascinating stop for anyone exploring Iran’s southern coast.

bne.name: Brisbane
bne.text: Brisbane, Queensland, sits on the banks of the winding Brisbane River where it meets the Pacific coast, about 730 km north of Sydney. The city grew from a penal settlement established in 1824 and became the capital of the new colony of Queensland in 1859. Today it feels relaxed yet vibrant: riverfront promenades are lined with cafés, the leafy South Bank parklands host museums and festivals, and the nearby hills and islands offer easy escapes for hiking, beach-going or wildlife spotting. Warm subtropical weather and a friendly, laid-back vibe make it a welcoming base for exploring the east coast of Australia.

bng.name: Benghazi
bng.text: Benghazi, Libya’s second-largest city, sits on the edge of the Mediterranean in the north-east, where the Green Mountain range meets the sea. Founded by the Greeks as Euesperides, it later became an important port for the Ottoman Empire and played a key role in the 1911 Italo-Turkish War. Today the city blends modern cafés, bustling souks and colourful street art with historic sites such as the Italian-era Al-Berka district and the ancient ruins at Cyrene a short drive away. Visitors find warm hospitality, lively markets selling spices and olives, and a pleasant waterfront promenade perfect for an evening stroll.

bnj.name: Banjul
bnj.text: Banjul, the compact capital of The Gambia, sits on St Mary’s Island at the mouth of the Gambia River where it meets the Atlantic, giving the city a maritime feel and easy views of the surrounding estuary. Founded in 1816 as a British trading post, it later became the administrative centre of the British colony known as the Gambia Protectorate. Today visitors find a relaxed waterfront promenade lined with colourful market stalls, colonial-era buildings and the bustling Albert Market, while the nearby riverbanks provide opportunities for boat trips, bird-watching and sampling fresh West African seafood in laid-back cafés.

bnn.name: Benin City
bnn.text: Benin City lies in southern Nigeria, about 90 km inland from the Atlantic coast and serves as the capital of Edo State. It was the centre of the ancient Benin Kingdom, whose sophisticated bronze casting and massive city walls were already renowned to European traders by the 15th century. Today the city bustles with lively markets, colourful street food stalls and friendly locals who are proud of their heritage; the National Museum displays impressive artefacts, while nearby the historic walls and the royal palace invite you to wander and imagine a once-great empire.

bog.name: Bogota
bog.text: Bogotá, the bustling capital of Colombia, sits high in the Andes at about 2,640 metres (8,660 ft) above sea level, giving it a cool, spring-like climate year-round. Founded by the Spanish in 1538, the city grew around the historic neighbourhood of La Candelaria, where colonial churches and colourful façades stand alongside museums such as the Gold Museum, which houses the world’s largest collection of pre-Columbian gold artefacts. Today, visitors enjoy a lively mix of modern skyscrapers, vibrant street art, and excellent coffee shops, while the surrounding mountains provide easy access to hiking and spectacular views of the sprawling urban landscape.

bom.name: Mumbai
bom.text: Mumbai, perched on the west coast of India in the state of Maharashtra, is the country’s bustling financial and entertainment hub. The city grew around the natural harbour of Bombay Harbour, which the British East India Company captured in 1661 and later developed into a major trading port; the iconic Victoria Terminus (now Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus) still bears witness to that colonial era. Today, visitors find a vibrant mix of soaring skyscrapers, historic bazaars and street-food stalls serving spicy vada pav, while the sea-front promenades, art galleries and lively festivals offer a colourful, energetic glimpse of modern Indian life.

bor.name: Bordeaux
bor.text: Bordeaux, nestled on the banks of the Garonne in southwestern France, lies about 500 km south-west of Paris and is the capital of the Nouvelle-Atlantique region. Founded as a Roman settlement called Burdigala, the city flourished as a major trading port in the 18th century, its wealth famously displayed in the elegant stone façades of the historic centre, a UNESCO World Heritage site. Today visitors can wander the wide riverfront promenades, explore the lively markets of the Chartrons district, and sip world-renowned wines in cosy cafés while the modern tram system glides past centuries-old architecture, offering a seamless blend of past and present.

bos.name: Boston
bos.text: Boston lies on the eastern seaboard of the United States, perched on the northern edge of the Massachusetts Bay and bordered by the Charles River. Founded in 1630, it was a centre of the American Revolution, with the famous Boston Tea Party taking place in its harbour in 1773. Today the city blends historic cobblestone streets with a vibrant, modern atmosphere: you can wander the brick-lined Freedom Trail, savour fresh seafood at the bustling waterfront, explore world-class museums, and enjoy lively neighbourhoods where cafés, street performers and cyclists create a lively, welcoming buzz.

bpn.name: Balikpapan
bpn.text: Balikpapan sits on the eastern coast of Borneo in East Kalimantan, Indonesia, its harbour opening onto the Makassar Strait. The town grew around the oil fields discovered in the early 20th century and was a strategic Japanese base during World War II, when it was occupied from 1942 until the Allies liberated it in 1945. Today Balikpapan is a clean, well-maintained city with a relaxed waterfront promenade, bustling markets and easy access to nearby beaches and rainforest reserves such as the Mangrove Forest Park, making it a comfortable base for exploring both urban life and natural scenery.

brg.name: Bruges
brg.text: Bruges, nestled in the north-west of Belgium near the coast, sits in the province of West-Flanders and is criss-crossed by picturesque canals. Founded in the Middle Ages, the city flourished as a major trading hub for the cloth industry and was a key member of the Hanseatic League, which helped shape its wealth and architecture. Today visitors wander cobbled streets lined with medieval guild houses, admire the towering Belfry and glide along water-lit boat tours, while cafés serve steaming chocolate and locally brewed beer, creating a charming blend of history and lively, relaxed ambience.

bru.name: Brussels
bru.text: Brussels, the capital of Belgium and the de facto capital of the European Union, sits in the centre of the country where the River Senne meets the countryside of Flanders and Wallonia. First mentioned in the 10th-century records as a modest market town, it grew around the 13th-century Grand-Place, a UNESCO World Heritage site renowned for its ornate guildhalls and the stunning Town Hall. Today the city buzzes with a mix of historic charm and modern cosmopolitan life: you can savour world-famous chocolates and waffles, wander past impressive Art Nouveau façades, and soak up the lively atmosphere of cafés and multilingual crowds beneath a sky often brushed with the gentle hue of a summer sunset.

bsa.name: Brasilia
bsa.text: Brasilia, the purpose-built capital of Brazil, lies in the heart of the country on the Planalto Central plateau, about 1,000 km inland from the coast. Planned by the architects Lúcio Costa and Oscar Niemeyer and inaugurated in 1960, it was created to move the nation’s political centre away from the crowded coastal cities. Today the city feels strikingly modern, with its bold, sweeping government buildings, wide avenues lined with palm trees and a vibrant mix of restaurants and cultural venues. Visitors can stroll the lakefront, explore the impressive Cathedral of Brasília and soak up the lively atmosphere of a city designed to embody Brazil’s future.

bsb.name: Bandar Seri Begawan
bsb.text: Bandar Seri Begawan, the capital of Brunei, lies on the north-eastern coast of Borneo where the Brunei River meets Brunei Bay. The city grew around the historic water village of Kampong Ayer, a settlement on stilts that has existed for centuries and was noted by early European explorers in the 16th century. Today the capital blends quiet elegance with modern comforts: sleek government buildings sit beside the ornate Sultan Omar Ali Saifuddien Mosque, bustling markets offer fresh tropical fruit, and river cruises let visitors glide past gleaming skyscrapers and traditional wooden houses, giving a calm yet colourful glimpse of life in this tiny but prosperous sultanate.

bsk.name: Bishkek
bsk.text: Bishkek, the capital of Kyrgyzstan, lies in the north of the country at the edge of the Tien Shan foothills, about 800 metres above sea level. Founded in the 19th century as a Russian military outpost, it was renamed Frunze in honour of Soviet marshal Mikhail Frunze before reclaiming its historic Kyrgyz name after independence in 1991. Today the city greets visitors with tree-lined avenues, wide Soviet-era squares and a lively mix of cafés, art galleries and bustling bazaars; Ala-Too Square hosts concerts and the nearby Oak Park offers a pleasant spot for a relaxed stroll.

bsl.name: Basel
bsl.text: Basel is a vibrant city perched on the banks of the Rhine in north-western Switzerland, right where the borders of Germany and France meet. Founded by the Romans as Augusta Raurica, it later became a key centre of the medieval Holy Roman Empire and was the site of the 1431 Council of Basel, one of the most important church assemblies of the Middle Ages. Today the city blends old and new: its well-preserved medieval Old Town, with the striking Basel Minster and bustling market squares, sits alongside cutting-edge museums such as the Kunstmuseum and Fondation Beyeler, lively cafés, and a lively riverside promenade that comes alive with festivals, making Basel a delightful mix of history, culture and modern Swiss charm.

bsr.name: Basra
bsr.text: Basra, Iraq, sits on the Shatt al-Arab waterway where the Tigris and Euphrates rivers meet the Persian Gulf, making it Iraq’s main port and a historic gateway for trade. Founded in the 7th century as a key hub of the early Islamic empire, it later flourished under the Ottoman and British administrations, serving as a vital oil-export centre. Today the city buzzes with a mix of modern markets, bustling riverfront cafés and the occasional glimpse of traditional wooden dhows on the water. Visitors can explore the lively souk, taste fresh seafood, and enjoy the warm, humid climate while watching the sunset over the Gulf horizon.

bst.name: Basseterre
bst.text: Basseterre, the capital of Saint Kitts and Nevis, sits on the southwestern coast of the larger island of Saint Kitts, nestled between the sheltered harbor of Port Zante and the foothills of the volcanic landscape. Founded by the French in the early 17th century, the town was later taken by the British and retains a blend of colonial architecture, including the striking St George’s Anglican Church from 1844. Today the streets buzz with colourful markets, cafés serving locally roasted coffee and rum, and a lively waterfront promenade where visitors can watch yachts glide past while the warm Caribbean breeze carries the scent of tropical flowers.

bta.name: Bata
bta.text: Bata, the bustling port city on the Atlantic coast of mainland Equatorial Guinea, is the country’s commercial centre and capital of Litoral Province. Situated on a broad, palm-lined bay opposite the island of Bioko, it grew from a modest Portuguese trading post in the 16th century into a key Spanish colonial hub and, after independence, into the gateway for the nation’s oil-driven economy. Today visitors find a lively mix of modern high-rise hotels, bustling markets where fresh seafood is sold, and a relaxed waterfront promenade, all framed by swaying coconut palms and the warm, humid breeze of the Gulf of Guinea.

btm.name: Batumi
btm.text: Batumi, Georgia, lies on the Black Sea coast in the far southwest of the country, near the border with Turkey. Founded as a modest fishing settlement, it grew into a bustling port in the 19th century when the Russian Empire developed the region, and its famous Batumi Boulevard dates back to that era. Today the city dazzles visitors with a sleek, modern skyline of glass towers, palm-lined promenades and vibrant cafés, while the subtropical climate keeps the palm trees lush year-round. Stroll along the seafront, sample fresh seafood, and enjoy the lively mix of historic architecture and contemporary culture.

bts.name: Bratislava
bts.text: Bratislava, the capital of Slovakia, sits on the banks of the Danube River where the country meets Austria and Hungary, giving it a distinctly Central European flavour. Its medieval Old Town winds past the 10th-century Bratislava Castle, which once guarded the kingdom’s western frontier and later served as the seat of Czechoslovakia’s government in 1919. Today the city blends historic charm with a lively café culture, river promenades and modern galleries; you can wander cobbled streets, enjoy panoramic views from the castle hill, and savour both traditional Slovak dishes and contemporary cuisine in a relaxed, welcoming atmosphere.

bty.name: Blantyre
bty.text: Blantyre, nestled in the southern highlands of Malawi, is the country’s second-largest city and a key commercial hub perched about 1,300 metres above sea level. It grew out of a Scottish missionary settlement founded in 1876, named after the town of Blantyre in Scotland, the birthplace of explorer David Livingstone. Today the city bustles with lively markets where vendors sell everything from fresh produce to colourful fabrics, while modern cafés and banks line its busy streets. Visitors can explore the historic St Michael’s Cathedral, enjoy the shade of jacaranda trees, and feel the warm, welcoming rhythm of Malawian city life.

bud.name: Budapest
bud.text: Budapest, the capital of Hungary, straddles the Danube River with the historic Buda hills on the west bank and the lively Pest plain on the east. The city was officially created in 1873 by merging the medieval towns of Buda, Óbuda and Pest, a union that turned it into a major cultural and political centre of the Austro-Hungarian Empire. Today visitors can stroll across the iconic Chain Bridge, explore the grand Parliament building, soak in the thermal baths that draw on centuries-old Roman-era springs, and enjoy a vibrant café scene amid Art Nouveau architecture, all set against the backdrop of river-side parks and bustling markets.

bue.name: Buenos Aires
bue.text: Buenos Aires, the bustling capital of Argentina, sits on the western shore of the Río de la Plata in the country's eastern region. Founded in the 16th century, it grew from a modest Spanish settlement into a major port and cultural hub, famously earning the nickname “Paris of South America” for its grand boulevards and European-style architecture. Today the city thrills visitors with lively neighbourhoods such as San Telmo’s cobbled streets, the colourful houses of La Boca, and the sleek modernity of Puerto Madero, while tango music spills from cafés and the aroma of grilled meat drifts from countless parrillas, offering a vibrant mix of history and contemporary Latin flair.

buf.name: Buffalo
buf.text: Buffalo, New York, sits on the eastern shore of Lake Erie at the head of the Niagara River, about a half-hour’s drive from the world-famous Niagara Falls. Founded in the early 19th century, the city grew rapidly as a key stop on the Erie Canal, which opened in 1825 and linked the Great Lakes with the Atlantic seaboard. Today visitors enjoy a vibrant waterfront with the revitalised Canalside district, a bustling arts scene centred on the Albright-Knox Gallery, and the renowned wings of Buffalo chicken served in lively neighbourhood eateries, all set against a backdrop of historic architecture and leafy parks.

buh.name: Bucharest
buh.text: Bucharest, the capital of Romania, sits in the south of the country on the banks of the Dâmboviţa River, about 70 km north of the Danube. The city first appears in records in 1459 and was declared the national capital in 1862, a status it has retained ever since. Today it blends grand Belle-Époque architecture, such as the massive Palace of the Parliament, with leafy parks, vibrant cafés and a lively nightlife scene. Visitors can wander historic Lipscani streets, sample hearty Romanian dishes and feel the buzz of a modern European metropolis that still cherishes its past.

buj.name: Bujumbura
buj.text: Bujumbura, perched on the northeastern shore of Lake Tanganyika in western Burundi, is the country’s largest city and former capital. The town grew from the German colonial outpost of Usumbura, and its name was changed to Bujumbura when Burundi gained independence in 1962. Today the city blends a laid-back lakeside vibe with bustling markets, colourful waterfront promenades and a mix of French and Swahili signage. Visitors can savour fresh fish at lakeside restaurants, explore the lively central market, and take short trips to nearby wildlife parks or the tranquil islands that dot the lake.

byo.name: Bulawayo
byo.text: Bulawayo, Zimbabwe’s second-largest city, sits in the southwest of the country on the high-veld, close to the border with Botswana and the rugged Matobo Hills. It grew out of the royal kraal of King Lobengula, the last Ndebele monarch, and became a key railway hub when the line from Salisbury (now Harare) reached it in the 1890s. Today the town blends wide, tree-lined avenues of red-brick colonial buildings with lively street markets where traders sell everything from fresh fruit to handmade crafts. Visitors can explore the historic railway museum, savour hearty local cuisine, and use Bulawayo as a gateway to the striking granite peaks and abundant wildlife of Matobo National Park.

bze.name: Belize City
bze.text: Belize City, the former capital of Belize, sits on the eastern coast of the country at the mouth of the Haulover Creek where it meets the Caribbean Sea. Founded in 1638 as a small settlement for timber and trade, it later became the administrative centre of British Honduras before the capital moved inland to Belmopan in 1970. Today the city is a lively blend of colonial architecture and colourful market stalls, with the bustling Swing Bridge, historic wooden houses and a vibrant waterfront promenade offering easy access to museums, eateries and boat trips to nearby islands.

bzv.name: Brazzaville
bzv.text: Brazzaville, the capital of the Republic of Congo, sits on the north bank of the mighty Congo River directly opposite Kinshasa, the capital of the Democratic Republic of Congo, making it one of the world’s few cities that face a twin capital across a river. The town was founded in the 1880s by the Italian-French explorer Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza and became the nation’s administrative centre at independence in 1960. Today the city greets visitors with a bustling riverside promenade, colourful markets where vendors sell everything from fresh fruit to hand-crafted jewellery, a handful of well-preserved colonial buildings, and lively cafés where the rhythm of soukous music mixes with the humid tropical air.

cai.name: Cairo
cai.text: Cairo, the bustling capital of Egypt, sits on the banks of the Nile River just south of the Sahara, at the crossroads of Africa and the Middle East. It grew around the ancient settlement of Fustat, founded in the 7th century after the Arab conquest, and later became the seat of the powerful Mamluk sultans. Today the city teems with life: narrow alleys lead to vibrant souks where the scent of spices mingles with the call to prayer, while modern cafés overlook historic sites such as the nearby Giza pyramids, offering a vivid blend of past and present for any traveller.

cal.name: Calais
cal.text: Calais sits on the northern coast of France, directly opposite Dover on the Strait of Dover, where the English Channel narrows to just 34 kilometres. Historically it was the principal continental gateway for England, most famously the departure point for the Allies’ D-Day landings in June 1944. Today the town greets visitors with a bustling waterfront, the striking modern Musee des Beaux-Arts, and the massive Calais Lighthouse offering views of the busy ferry terminals and the rolling white cliffs across the water. A walk along the promenade gives a lively mix of cafés, shops and the salty sea air, making it a pleasant stop for both history lovers and seaside wanderers.

cam.name: Cambridge
cam.text: Cambridge is a historic city in the east of England, set on the River Cam about 50 miles north-north-west of London. It grew around the University of Cambridge, which was founded in 1209 and has produced countless scholars, scientists and writers over the centuries. Today the city is a lively mix of medieval colleges with their iconic courtyards and modern cafés, boutique shops and tech start-ups, earning it the nickname “Silicon Fen”. Visitors can stroll along the picturesque riverside, punt on the Cam, explore museums and enjoy the vibrant cultural scene.

can.name: Guangzhou
can.text: Guangzhou, situated in southern China on the Pearl River delta, is the capital of Guangdong province and a gateway to the bustling Pearl River Delta megacity. Founded over two thousand years ago, it was a key terminus of the ancient maritime Silk Road, trading silk, tea and ceramics with the wider world. Today the city blends modern skyscrapers such as the Canton Tower with historic neighbourhoods like the Qingping Market, where you can sample dim sum and traditional herbs. The streets buzz with neon lights, river cruises and a lively food scene, offering visitors a vibrant mix of history, culture and contemporary Chinese life.

car.name: Cardiff
car.text: Cardiff, the capital city of Wales, sits on the southern coast of the United Kingdom where the River Taff meets the Bristol Channel. It grew around Cardiff Castle, a Norman fortress that was later expanded by the Marquesses of Bute in the 19th century and now houses a museum of the city’s medieval and Victorian past. Today the city blends historic charm with a lively waterfront: you can explore the revitalised Cardiff Bay, enjoy a match at the iconic Principality Stadium, wander the bustling streets of the Castle Quarter, and sample Welsh cuisine in cosy pubs and modern restaurants, all within a welcoming, compact urban setting.

cas.name: Casablanca
cas.text: Casablanca, Morocco’s largest city, sits on the Atlantic coast about 90 km south-west of the capital Rabat. Founded in the 7th century as a modest settlement, it grew dramatically after the French protectorate began in 1912, when the port was expanded and modern architecture was introduced. Today the city blends sleek skyscrapers with historic neighborhoods, offering a bustling waterfront promenade, lively cafés serving mint tea, and the iconic Hassan II Mosque, whose minaret soars 210 metres above the sea. Visitors feel the energetic mix of commerce, culture and ocean breezes that make Casablanca a contemporary gateway to Morocco.

cba.name: Cordoba
cba.text: Cordoba, Argentina, sits in the heart of the country on the banks of the Suquia River, at the foot of the Sierras de Córdoba and roughly 700 km west of Buenos Aires. The city was founded in 1573 by the Spanish explorer Jerónimo Luis de Cabrera, making it one of the oldest European settlements in the region and home to the UNESCO-listed Jesuit Block and Estancias. Today Cordoba buzzes with a youthful energy thanks to its large university population; its historic centre blends cobbled streets and colonial churches with lively cafés, bustling markets and frequent cultural festivals, offering visitors a warm mix of history and modern Argentine life.

cbq.name: Calabar
cbq.text: Calabar sits in the far south-east of Nigeria, on the banks of the Cross River just a short drive from the Atlantic coast and the border with Cameroon. Historically it was the capital of the British Niger Coast Protectorate in the late 19th century and a bustling hub for the regional slave trade before that era ended. Today the town blends colonial charm with vibrant modern life: colourful markets spill onto the streets, the National Museum showcases artefacts from the ancient Efik kingdom, river cruises offer a glimpse of lush mangroves, and the nearby Tinapa leisure complex adds shopping and entertainment to a warm, welcoming atmosphere.

cbr.name: Canberra
cbr.text: Canberra, the capital city of Australia, sits inland in the Australian Capital Territory, roughly halfway between Sydney and Melbourne on the edge of the Brindabella Ranges. It was selected in 1908 as a purpose-built seat of government and officially named the capital in 1913, a decision that resolved a long rivalry between the two larger colonies. Today the city feels spacious and leafy, with wide avenues, abundant parks and lakes, and striking modern architecture such as the Parliament House and the National Gallery. Visitors enjoy strolling around Lake Burley Griffin, exploring the museums, and tasting the thriving café scene amid a calm, well-planned urban landscape.

ccs.name: Caracas
ccs.text: Caracas, the bustling capital of Venezuela, lies in a valley surrounded by the towering peaks of the Ávila mountain range in the north-central part of the country, about 900 metres above sea level. Founded in 1567 by Spanish settlers, it became the centre of the independence movement when Simón Bolívar declared the Republic of Colombia there in 1811. Today the city offers a lively mix of modern skyscrapers, historic colonial plazas and vibrant street markets; you can stroll through the lively Boulevard Los Santos, enjoy panoramic views from the Teleférico cable car, and sample tasty arepas while the tropical climate keeps the air warm and fresh.

ccu.name: Kolkata
ccu.text: Kolkata, the vibrant capital of West Bengal in eastern India, sits on the banks of the Hooghly River, a distributary of the Ganges. Founded by the British East India Company in 1690, it became the centre of the Indian independence movement and was the seat of the British Raj until 1911. Today the city dazzles visitors with its colonial architecture, bustling markets and a lively cultural scene – from the historic Victoria Memorial and Indian Museum to street food stalls serving fragrant fish curry and sweet rosogolla. The mix of old and new makes Kolkata a truly unforgettable stop.

ceb.name: Cebu
ceb.text: Cebu, the bustling island province at the heart of the Philippines, sits on the eastern side of the Visayan Sea, just south of the larger island of Leyte and north of Mindanao. It is famously where Ferdinand Magellan first set foot in 1521, marking the first recorded European contact with the archipelago. Today the city is a lively mix of modern skyscrapers, historic churches and colourful market stalls; you can wander the lively streets of Colon, sample fresh seafood at the bustling harbor, and relax on the white-sand beaches of Mactan while still being close to vibrant nightlife, shopping malls and convenient transport links.

cgp.name: Chittagong
cgp.text: Chittagong, Bangladesh’s second-largest city, sits on the southeastern coast where the Karnaphuli River meets the Bay of Bengal, framed by rolling hills and the Chittagong Hill Tracts. A key port since the 17th century, it was an important hub for British-East India Company trade and later a focal point of the 1971 liberation war. Today visitors find a vibrant mix of bustling markets, colonial-era architecture and fresh seafood stalls, while the nearby Patenga Beach offers breezy walks and the nearby Foy’s Lake provides a calm escape for paddle-boats and cable-car rides.

chc.name: Christchurch
chc.text: Christchurch is situated on the east coast of New Zealand’s South Island, at the mouth of the Avon River and framed by the Port Hills. Founded by English settlers in 1850, the city earned the nickname “the Garden City” for its plentiful parks and tree-lined streets, a tradition that began with the planting of the Avon River’s iconic willow trees. Today visitors can wander through the revitalised central precinct, explore the innovative art installations at the former earthquake-damaged cathedral site, and enjoy the blend of historic timber buildings with modern cafés, all against a backdrop of stunning mountain scenery.

che.name: Cherbourg
che.text: Cherbourg-en-Normandy sits on the tip of the Cotentin Peninsula in north-western France, overlooking the English Channel and the Bay of the Mont Saint-Michel. Founded in the medieval era, the town gained strategic importance during the Second World War and was a key Allied port after the D-Day landings in 1944. Today visitors stroll along the bustling waterfront, explore the impressive Musée de la Cité de la Mer with its historic submarine, and enjoy fresh seafood in a relaxed harbour atmosphere, while the surrounding cliffs and nearby beaches offer striking coastal scenery.

chg.name: Chicago
