chg.text: Chicago, perched on the southwestern shore of Lake Michigan in the north-central United States, grew from a modest trading post into a bustling metropolis during the 19th century, famously rebuilding after the Great Fire of 1871 and emerging as a centre of architecture and industry. Today the city dazzles visitors with its striking skyline, world-class museums such as the Art Institute, lively neighbourhoods ranging from historic Wicker Park to the modern Loop, and a thriving food scene that celebrates everything from deep-dish pizza to innovative fine dining. Its lakeside parks and vibrant festivals make it a warm, energetic destination for any traveller.

chi.name: Chita
chi.text: Chita, a city in the southeastern part of Siberia, sits on the banks of the Chitinka River near the foothills of the Yablonoi Range, about 6,200 km east of Moscow. Founded in 1653 as a Russian fort on the route to the Chinese border, it later became a key hub on the Trans-Siberian Railway, linking Europe with the Far East. Today the city offers a mix of wide boulevards, Soviet-era architecture and lively riverfront cafés, while museums such as the Decembrist Museum tell its colourful past. In summer the surrounding taiga provides easy access to hiking and wildlife spotting, making Chita a pleasant gateway to Siberian adventure.

chs.name: Chisinau
chs.text: Chişinău, the capital of Moldova, sits in the centre of the country on the gentle banks of the Bâc River and is surrounded by gently rolling plains and vineyards. The settlement was first recorded in 1436 as a modest village and, after the Russian Empire annexed the region in 1812, it was designated the provincial capital – a status it has retained through independence. Today the city greets visitors with tree-lined boulevards, Soviet-era blocks softened by leafy parks, a bustling central market full of fresh produce and craft goods, and a growing scene of wine bars and cafés where locals happily share their famous wines and warm hospitality.

ckg.name: Chongqing
ckg.text: Chongqing sits in southwestern China where the Yangtze and Jialing rivers meet, cradled by steep hills and towering bridges that give the city its dramatic skyline. It was the provisional capital of Nationalist China during the Second World War, housing the wartime government and many refugees after the fall of Nanjing. Today the city buzzes with a mix of ultra-modern skyscrapers and traditional neighbourhoods, famous for its fiery hot-pot cuisine, bustling night markets and the scenic cable-car rides that let you glide over the river’s misty waters, offering a lively yet surprisingly welcoming atmosphere for visitors.

cky.name: Conakry
cky.text: Conakry, the bustling capital of Guinea, sits on the Kaloum Peninsula where the Rio Niger meets the Atlantic Ocean, giving the city a lively waterfront feel. Founded in the 19th century as a French trading post, it grew around the old port of Boké and later became the administrative centre of French Guinea. Today visitors find a vibrant mix of colourful markets, colonial-era architecture and a growing arts scene, with fresh seafood stalls lining the quay and the striking Sandervalia National Museum offering insight into the nation’s heritage. The tropical climate means warm evenings are perfect for strolling along the promenade or sipping a cold bissap drink.

cle.name: Cleveland
cle.text: Cleveland, Ohio, sits on the southern shore of Lake Erie at the mouth of the Cuyahoga River, about 60 miles west of the Pennsylvania border. It was founded in 1796 and named for General Moses Cleaveland, the surveyor who led the expedition that established the settlement. Today the city blends its industrial heritage with a lively cultural scene: the waterfront boasts the iconic Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, the bustling West Side Market offers local produce and ethnic foods, and a revitalised downtown brims with museums, theatres and cafés, making a visit both nostalgic and fresh.

clj.name: Cluj-Napoca
clj.text: Cluj-Napoca lies in the heart of Transylvania, about 300 km north-west of Bucharest, nestled among rolling hills and the Someşul Mic river. First mentioned in a 12th-century charter, it became a prominent medieval centre of trade and learning, later housing the first Romanian university founded in 1879. Today the city buzzes with a youthful energy, thanks to its large student population and a thriving tech scene; its cobbled Old Town is dotted with cafés, street art and lively markets, while nearby natural parks offer easy escapes for hiking and wildlife spotting.

cln.name: Colon
cln.text: Colon sits on the Caribbean coast of Panama, right at the Atlantic entrance to the Panama Canal, and it grew from a small 19th-century settlement into a bustling port city. It was the canal’s Atlantic terminus when the waterway opened in 1914, and the surrounding forts and the old railway station still echo that era. Today the town is a lively mix of colourful markets, duty-free shopping in the free-zone district and a promenade lined with palm trees, while the humid tropical heat and the hum of ships moving through the canal give visitors a vivid sense of both history and modern trade.

clo.name: Cali
clo.text: Cali, officially Santiago de Cali, lies in the fertile Cauca River valley of southwestern Colombia, at the foothills of the Andes and about 100 km from the Pacific coast. Founded in 1536 by Spanish conquistador Sebastián de Belalcázar, it grew into a major centre for the sugar-cane industry in the 19th century. Today the city pulses with a lively mix of modern cafés, colourful street art and the irresistible rhythm of salsa that fills its nightclubs and public squares. Visitors can stroll through the historic San Antonio neighbourhood, sample fresh fruit juices in bustling markets and enjoy nearby parks that frame the surrounding mountains.

clt.name: Charlotte
clt.text: Charlotte, North Carolina, sits in the heart of the American South at the confluence of the Catawba River and Lake Norman, roughly a three-hour drive east of the Appalachian foothills. Founded in 1768 and named for Queen Charlotte, the city grew around a thriving railway hub and later became a centre of the textile industry. Today it buzzes with a mix of sleek skyscrapers and leafy neighbourhoods, offering a lively food scene, museums such as the Levine Center for the Arts, and easy access to outdoor pursuits in the nearby Piedmont countryside, making it a welcoming stop for any traveller.

cmb.name: Colombo
cmb.text: Colombo, the bustling capital on the western coast of Sri Lanka, sits at the mouth of the Kelani River and faces the Indian Ocean. The city grew around a Dutch fort built in the 17th century, later expanded by the British, and it was the centre of administration when the island was known as Ceylon. Today Colombo blends colonial architecture with sleek high-rises, its streets alive with colourful markets, tea houses and street food stalls. Visitors can wander the historic Pettah district, enjoy a sunset at Galle Face Green and sample fresh seafood while the city’s friendly rhythm carries on.

cnf.name: Belo Horizonte
cnf.text: Belo Horizonte, the capital of Brazil’s Minas Gerais state, lies in the southeastern highlands about 340 km north-east of Rio de Janeiro and 600 km south-west of Salvador. Founded in 1897 to replace the colonial town of Ouro Prata, it was one of Brazil’s first planned cities, laid out on a grid of wide avenues and green squares. Today the city buzzes with a vibrant mix of modern cafés, lively music venues and expansive parks; the striking modernist architecture of Oscar Niemeyer’s churches stands alongside bustling markets where you can sample local cheese, cachaça and fresh fruit, offering a warm, energetic glimpse of contemporary Brazilian life.

cns.name: Cairns
cns.text: Cairns sits on the tropical north-east coast of Queensland, Australia, at the edge of the world-renowned Great Barrier Reef and the lush rainforest hinterland. Founded in 1876 as a port for the gold fields of the Hodgkinson River, the town grew around its wharves and railway line that linked inland mines to the sea. Today Cairns is a laid-back gateway for adventure seekers – you can stroll the vibrant waterfront esplanade, sip coffee in eclectic cafés, and set off on day trips to snorkel among colourful coral, explore ancient rainforests or ride the Skyrail cableway, all under a warm, humid climate that feels like permanent summer.

cnx.name: Chiang Mai
cnx.text: Chiang Mai, nestled in the mountainous north-east of Thailand about 700 km north of Bangkok, is the region’s cultural heart. Founded in 1296 as the capital of the Lanna Kingdom, its ancient moat and walls still frame the historic Old City, where temples such as Wat Phra Singh showcase golden Lanna architecture. Today the town bustles with a relaxed yet lively atmosphere: morning markets brim with fresh produce and handicrafts, cafés line the riverbanks, and the surrounding hills invite trekking, cycling and visits to hill-tribe villages, making it a perfect blend of heritage and modern charm.

cok.name: Kochi
cok.text: Kochi, a bustling coastal city in the southwestern Indian state of Kerala, sits on a network of islands and the Arabian Sea, where the historic harbour still echoes its centuries-old role in the spice trade. The Portuguese were the first Europeans to establish a fort here in 1503, later succeeded by the Dutch and the British, leaving a mix of colonial architecture and temples that line the streets of Fort Kochi. Today the city blends the old and the new: you can wander past the iconic Chinese fishing nets, sip coffee in chic cafés, explore lively markets and cruise the serene backwaters, all beneath a warm, tropical climate.

col.name: Cologne
col.text: Cologne lies on the banks of the River Rhine in western Germany, about 70 kilometres north of the Luxembourg border. Founded by the Romans as Colonia Claudia Ara Agrippinensium in the first century AD, it became a major medieval trading hub and the seat of one of the oldest archbishoprics in Europe. Today the city is a lively mix of history and modernity: you can wander beneath the towering spire of the Gothic Cologne Cathedral, explore quirky museums such as the Chocolate Museum, and relax on bustling riverfront terraces while sipping a Kölsch in a traditional brewpub.

cor.name: Cork
cor.text: Cork, situated on the south-west coast of Ireland where the River Lee widens into a bustling harbour, is the country’s second-largest city and a historic trading port that received its charter from King John in 1185. Its medieval streets still echo with the past, while today the city hums with a lively arts scene, cosy cafés and vibrant markets such as the English Market, where you can sample fresh seafood and locally produced cheese. Friendly locals are happy to point you towards colourful pubs, scenic walks along the riverbanks and the striking St Finbarr’s Cathedral, making a visit both charming and contemporary.

cot.name: Cotonou
cot.text: Cotonou, the bustling port city on the southern coast of Benin, lies on the Gulf of Guinea just east of the border with Nigeria. Founded in the late 19th century as a modest fishing village, it grew rapidly after the French made it the administrative centre of the colony of Dahomey in the early 1900s. Today Cotonou greets visitors with a lively mix of markets, where colourful stalls sell everything from fresh seafood to woven fabrics, and a shoreline dotted with palm-shaded cafés; the city’s rhythm is energetic yet relaxed, offering a welcoming glimpse of contemporary West African life.

cph.name: Copenhagen
cph.text: Copenhagen, the capital of Denmark, sits on the eastern shore of the island of Zealand and spreads onto the neighbouring island of Amager, facing the Øresund Strait that separates it from Sweden. First mentioned in medieval records, it grew into an important trading port in the 15th century and later became the seat of the Danish monarchy, with the historic Rosenborg Castle still housing the royal regalia. Today the city blends historic charm with modern design: you can wander colourful Nyhavn harbour, cycle along tree-lined streets, explore cutting-edge cuisine in the food markets and enjoy a relaxed, bike-friendly atmosphere that feels both cosy and cosmopolitan.

cpt.name: Cape Town
cpt.text: Cape Town sits on the southwestern tip of South Africa, where the Atlantic Ocean meets the imposing Table Mountain that dominates the skyline. Founded by the Dutch East India Company in 1652 as a supply station for ships rounding the Cape, the city bears the layers of colonial, maritime and indigenous history in its architecture and museums. Today it is a vibrant, multicultural hub with bustling waterfront markets, world-class restaurants and easy access to stunning beaches, vineyards and the mountain’s hiking trails, offering visitors a lively mix of natural beauty, cultural diversity and contemporary South African charm.

cst.name: Constanta
cst.text: Constanta is a bustling port city on Romania’s Black Sea coast, about 120 km east of Bucharest. Founded by Greek colonists in the 7-th century BC, it later became the Roman city of Tomis, famed as the place where the poet Ovid spent his exile. Today the promenade stretches along a lively seafront lined with cafés, and the historic Old Town reveals Ottoman-era mosques, Art Nouveau buildings and the impressive Casino, now an iconic ruin. Visitors can wander the lively markets, enjoy fresh seafood on the beach, and explore museums that trace the city’s millennia-long maritime heritage.

cstr.name: Castries
cstr.text: Castries, the capital of Saint Lucia, sits on a sheltered harbour on the island’s north-west coast, framed by lush hills and the sparkling Caribbean Sea. Founded by the French in the mid-1650s, it became the island’s administrative centre in the early nineteenth century and still retains a colonial grid of streets centred around the bustling market square. Today visitors find a lively waterfront lined with colourful buildings, lively street vendors selling tropical fruit and crafts, and easy access to historic sites such as Fort Charlotte, while cruise ships regularly dock, giving the town a vibrant, cosmopolitan feel.

csx.name: Changsha
csx.text: Changsha, the capital of Hunan province in south-central China, sits on the banks of the Xiang River about 300 km south of Wuhan. It was the base of the early 20th-century revolutionary leader Mao Zedong, who organised the famous Autumn Harvest Uprising there in 1927. Today the city blends modern skyscrapers with lively historic streets: you can wander the bustling Huangxing Road shopping district, savour spicy Hunan cuisine at night markets, and take a leisurely stroll through the ancient Yuelu Academy and its leafy hill, while the riverfront promenade offers views of illuminated bridges and a vibrant river-cruise scene.

ctg.name: Cartagena
ctg.text: Cartagena, a vibrant coastal city on Colombia’s Caribbean coast, sits on a natural harbour framed by the historic walled enclave of the old town. Founded in 1533, it became a crucial port for Spanish treasure fleets and later a stronghold of the trans-Atlantic slave trade, which left a legacy of impressive fortifications such as the Castillo San Felipe de Barajas. Today the city bustles with colourful colonial architecture, lively plazas, and a lively street-food scene; strolling along the cobbled streets you’ll hear the rhythm of salsa, smell fresh ceviche, and enjoy stunning sunsets over the sea from the historic walls.

ctu.name: Chengdu
ctu.text: Chengdu, the bustling capital of Sichuan province in southwest China, sits on the fertile plain of the Chengdu River and is framed by the towering Longmen Mountains to the north. The city traces its roots back over two thousand years, famously becoming the seat of the Shu Kingdom during the Three Kingdoms period, a time when the legendary strategist Zhuge Liang governed from his thatched-roofed “thatched cottage.” Today Chengdu delights visitors with a relaxed pace of life, fragrant tea houses, and the chance to see giant pandas at the world-renowned research centre, while its vibrant street food scene offers fiery Sichuan peppercorns, and its modern skyline blends seamlessly with ancient temples and leafy parks.

cun.name: Cancun
cun.text: Cancun sits on the northeastern tip of the Yucatán Peninsula, bordering the Caribbean Sea in the state of Quintana Roo, Mexico. The area was a modest fishing village until the Mexican government designated it as a tourism hub in the early 1970s, building the first major hotel zone to showcase the region’s white-sand beaches and crystal-clear waters. Today, visitors find a vibrant mix of modern resorts, lively nightlife and easy access to nearby Mayan ruins such as El Mérida and the underwater museum of submerged sculptures, making it a lively yet relaxing seaside destination.

cuz.name: Cusco
cuz.text: Cusco, nestled in the southeastern Andes of Peru at around 3,400 metres above sea level, was the historic capital of the Inca Empire and today forms the gateway to the famed ruins of Machu Picchu. Its cobbled streets are lined with a striking mix of stone Inca foundations and colourful Spanish colonial façades, many of which are protected as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Visitors can wander bustling markets selling alpaca textiles, savour traditional Peruvian dishes in lively plazas, and enjoy crisp, clear mountain air while exploring museums that bring the city’s rich past vividly to life.

cwb.name: Curitiba
cwb.text: Curitiba, the capital of the Brazilian state of Paraná, lies in the south-central part of the country about 400 km west of the coastal city of Florianópolis. The town began as a modest settlement in 1693 and was designated the state capital in 1853, later becoming renowned for its pioneering urban planning and extensive green spaces. Today visitors find a clean, well-organised city with an efficient bus network, striking modernist architecture, and a network of parks and tree-lined avenues; highlights include the glass-capped Botanical Garden, the bustling farmers’ market at Rua das Flores, and a vibrant culinary scene that blends traditional Brazilian flavours with European influences.

dac.name: Dhaka
dac.text: Dhaka, the bustling capital of Bangladesh, sits on the banks of the Buriganga River in the heart of the country’s low-lying delta. First established as the Mughal provincial capital in the early 1600s, it later became the centre of the 1971 struggle for independence. Today the city is a vibrant mix of old and new: crowded streets buzz with rickshaws and street-food stalls, historic sites such as the 17th-century Lalbagh Fort stand beside gleaming glass towers, and the warm, lively hospitality of its residents makes exploring its markets, mosques and riverside cafés an unforgettable experience.

dad.name: Da Nang
dad.text: Da Nang sits on Vietnam’s central coast, nestled between the sparkling East Sea and the marble-capped Hai Van Pass, with the ancient town of Hoi An a short drive to the south and the former imperial capital Hue to the north. It was a key French naval base in the 19th century and later a strategic airfield during the Vietnam War. Today the city buzzes with a relaxed yet modern feel: sun-soaked beaches stretch alongside sleek riverside promenades, street-food stalls serve fresh seafood, and the iconic Dragon Bridge lights up the night sky, making Da Nang a lively gateway to both history and coastal charm.

dak.name: Dakar
dak.text: Dakar, the bustling capital of Senegal, sits on the tip of the Cape Verde Peninsula, jutting into the Atlantic Ocean on West Africa’s westernmost point. Founded by the French in the 19th century, it later became the centre of the independence movement that freed Senegal in 1960, and its vibrant markets still echo that spirit of self-determination. Today the city blends colourful colonial architecture with modern cafés, lively music venues and the striking African Renaissance Monument. Visitors can wander the lively souks of Sandaga, enjoy fresh seafood by the waterfront, and soak up the warm, friendly atmosphere of a place where history and contemporary life dance together.

dal.name: Dallas
dal.text: Dallas, Texas, sits in the north-central part of the state, about 250 miles west of the Mississippi River and roughly 250 miles east of the Texas Panhandle. Founded in 1841, it grew rapidly after the arrival of the railroads and became a key centre for the cotton and oil industries in the late-19th century. Today the city blends modern skyscrapers with wide, tree-lined boulevards, offering visitors a lively mix of world-class museums, vibrant food markets and expansive parks. You’ll hear a friendly buzz of commerce, catch a glimpse of the famous skyline from Reunion Tower, and feel the warm hospitality that Texas is renowned for.

dam.name: Damascus
dam.text: Damascus, the capital of Syria, lies in the south-west of the country on the Barada River, about 80 km inland from the Mediterranean coast. It is widely regarded as one of the world’s oldest continuously inhabited cities, with evidence of settlement dating back to the third millennium BC and a rich legacy as a centre of early Islamic culture. Today the city blends ancient stone souks, the impressive Umayyad Mosque and narrow alleyways with bustling cafés and modern shops; visitors can wander through historic quarters, sample fragrant local dishes and feel the lively rhythm of a metropolis that still carries the echo of its millennia-old past.

dar.name: Dar es Salaam
dar.text: Dar es Salaam sits on the eastern coast of Tanzania, hugging the Indian Ocean at the mouth of the Msimbazi River and serving as the country’s main port and commercial hub. Founded in the mid-19th century, it became the capital of German East Africa and later of independent Tanzania until the government moved to Dodoma in the 1970s. Today the city bursts with colourful markets, bustling waterfront promenades and artful Swahili architecture, while the nearby beaches and the historic Askari Monument offer a relaxed contrast to the lively traffic and fragrant street food stalls.

dav.name: Davao
dav.text: Davao, a bustling city on the southeastern tip of Mindanao in the Philippines, sits at the mouth of the Davao River and is framed by the towering Mount Apo, the country’s highest peak. It was founded as a Spanish outpost in the mid-19th century and later became an important centre for the export of bananas and other tropical fruits. Today the city blends modern malls and lively night markets with spacious parks and river cruises, offering cool evenings, friendly locals and easy access to both pristine beaches and rugged highland trails.

dbn.name: Durban
dbn.text: Durban sits on the east coast of South Africa, tucked against the warm Indian Ocean in the province of KwaZulu-Natal. It was founded in 1835 as a trading post by the British and later became an important port for sugar, cotton and other commodities. Today the city bustles with a lively promenade known as the Golden Mile, where palm-fringed beaches, bustling markets and a blend of Indian, Zulu and colonial influences create a colourful, relaxed atmosphere; visitors can savour fragrant curries, explore the vibrant harbour and enjoy year-round sunshine in a friendly, multicultural setting.

dca.name: Washington DC
dca.text: Washington DC, the capital of the United States, lies on the Potomac River between Maryland and Virginia. Designed by Pierre L’Enfant in the late 18th century, it was the site where the Constitution was first ratified and where the nation’s most important institutions were built. Today the city is a compact, walkable blend of grand monuments, world-class museums and lively neighbourhoods; you can stand beneath the towering Washington Monument, explore the Smithsonian galleries for free, and enjoy diverse food stalls or a relaxed coffee on a tree-lined street, all under a backdrop of historic brick façades and modern glass towers.

dda.name: Dire Dawa
dda.text: Dire Dawa lies in eastern Ethiopia, about 500 km east of Addis Ababa and close to the border with Djibouti, perched on the banks of the Harar River. Founded in 1902 as a railway hub for the new line linking Addis Ababa with the port of Djibouti, it quickly became the country’s first modern, planned town and a key centre for trade. Today the city buzzes with a lively market where Somali, Oromo and Ethiopian merchants sell spices, textiles and fresh coffee, while colonial-era buildings sit beside sleek new cafés; the surrounding hills offer easy day trips to wildlife reserves, making a visit both culturally rich and pleasantly relaxed.

del.name: Delhi
del.text: Delhi, the bustling capital of India, lies in the northern part of the sub-continent on the banks of the Yamuna River. It has been the seat of power for several empires, most famously serving as the Mughal capital in the 17th century and later becoming the centre of British administration before independence in 1947. Today the city blends ancient monuments such as the red-sandstone Red Fort and the towering Qutub Minar with modern high-rise districts, lively street markets, and a thriving food scene, offering visitors a vivid mix of history, culture and contemporary energy.

den.name: Denpasar
den.text: Denpasar, the bustling capital of Bali in Indonesia, lies on the southern coast of the island facing the Indian Ocean. It grew from a modest fishing village into an administrative centre, becoming the island’s official capital in the early 20th century after Dutch colonial authorities moved the seat from Singaraja. Today the city mixes modern high-rise buildings with traditional markets, where you can sample fresh tropical fruit and fragrant spices. Visitors can explore the lively waterfront promenade, sample Balinese cuisine at street stalls, and dip into cultural sites such as the historic Pura Jagatnatha temple, all while feeling the warm, relaxed rhythm of island life.

die.name: Dieppe
die.text: Dieppe is a charming coastal town in the Normandy region of north-western France, set on the English Channel about 170 km north of Paris. It grew famous in 1942 when Allied forces launched a daring raid on its harbour, an event that helped shape the later D-Day landings. Today the town is a relaxed seaside destination with a bustling fishing port, a long pebble beach perfect for strolling, and a lively promenade lined with cafés and shops. Visitors can wander the historic Château de Dieppe, explore maritime museums, and enjoy fresh seafood while watching the Atlantic breeze roll in.

dil.name: Dili
dil.text: Dili, the bustling capital of Timor-Leste, sits on the north-eastern coast of the island of Timor, tucked against the Bay of Dili and the Ombai Strait. Founded as the administrative centre of Portuguese Timor, it later endured Japanese occupation during World War II before becoming the heart of an independent nation in 2002. Today the town is a lively mix of pastel-coloured colonial buildings, colourful markets selling fresh fruit and hand-woven textiles, and a waterfront promenade perfect for sunset walks. Friendly locals welcome visitors with coffee, music and stories of their resilient heritage.

djb.name: Djibouti City
djb.text: Djibouti City, the capital of the tiny Horn of Africa nation of Djibouti, sits on the Gulf of Tadjoura at the entrance to the Red Sea, where the African continent meets the Arabian Peninsula. Founded in the late 19th century as a French colonial port, the city grew around the strategic harbour that still serves as a key refuelling stop for ships transiting the Suez Canal. Today the streets buzz with a blend of French, Arab and Somali influences: colourful markets sell incense and fresh seafood, the waterfront promenade offers sweeping views of turquoise water and nearby volcanic islands, and the warm, dry climate makes it easy to explore the lively cafés, modern mosques and the striking blend of colonial architecture and sleek new developments.

dkh.name: Dakhla
dkh.text: Dakhla, a coastal town perched on the Atlantic at the tip of Morocco’s disputed Western Sahara region, is famous for its striking lagoon that stretches inland behind a long sandy spit. Historically it was a key Spanish outpost in the early 20th century, serving as a naval base before being handed back to Morocco in the 1970s. Today the town feels relaxed yet adventurous: wind-surfers and kite-boarders flock to its breezy waters, while cafés line the promenade offering fresh seafood and sunset views over the endless blue, making Dakhla a laid-back haven for nature lovers and water-sport enthusiasts alike.

dla.name: Douala
dla.text: Douala, Cameroon’s bustling economic hub, sits on the banks of the Wouri River where it meets the Atlantic coast in the country’s Littoral Region. Founded as a German trading post in the late 19th century, the city grew into the main port of French Cameroon after World War I and remains the nation’s busiest harbour. Today visitors find a lively mix of modern skyscrapers, colourful markets such as Marché des Fleurs, and historic colonial architecture, all framed by a humid, tropical climate. Street food stalls serve grilled fish and spicy sauces, while the lively waterfront offers a glimpse of everyday Cameroonian life.

dmm.name: Dammam
dmm.text: Dammam, a coastal city on the Arabian Gulf in the Eastern Province of Saudi Arabia, lies about 400 km east of Riyadh and neighbours the twin ports of Al-Khobar and Dhahran. Historically it grew from a modest fishing village into a key trading hub after oil was discovered in the 1930s, prompting rapid development and the establishment of the Saudi Arabian National Guard’s headquarters. Today Dammam offers a blend of modern skyscrapers, spacious corniche promenades and bustling souks, where visitors can stroll along the waterfront, sample fresh seafood, and enjoy the warm hospitality of a city that balances tradition with contemporary Arab life.

dnd.name: Dundee
dnd.text: Dundee sits on the north-eastern coast of Scotland, perched on the north bank of the Firth of Tay opposite the city of Perth. In the nineteenth century it became the world’s centre of the jute industry, earning the nickname “Juteopolis” as its factories and warehouses stretched along the waterfront. Today the city blends its industrial heritage with a lively cultural scene: the striking V&A Dundee museum draws design lovers, the revitalised waterfront offers cafés and riverside walks, and the historic streets around The Howff host quirky shops and friendly pubs, making a visit both interesting and welcoming.

dnv.name: Denver
dnv.text: Denver, the capital of Colorado, sits at the foot of the Rocky Mountains on the high plains of the western United States, about 1,600 metres above sea level. Founded in 1858 during the gold-rush era, it quickly grew into a major rail hub and was nicknamed the “Gateway to the Rockies”. Today the city blends a lively downtown skyline with historic brick streets in LoDo, a thriving craft-brew scene and easy access to mountain trails and ski resorts. Visitors enjoy a walk along the vibrant 16th Street Mall, explore museums such as the Denver Art Museum, and soak up the sunny, dry climate that makes outdoor activities pleasant year-round.

doh.name: Doha
doh.text: Doha, the capital of Qatar, sits on the east coast of the Arabian Peninsula where the shimmering Persian Gulf meets a flat desert plain. The city grew from a modest pearling settlement in the early 20th century and became the centre of Qatar’s rapid modernisation after oil was discovered in the 1940s. Today, visitors find a striking blend of soaring skyscrapers, such as the iconic Museum of Islamic Art, and traditional souqs where spices and textiles are bartered. The waterfront promenade offers cool sea breezes, and the city’s cafés and restaurants serve a lively mix of Gulf and international flavours.

dov.name: Dover
dov.text: Dover sits on the southeastern tip of England, facing the narrow Strait of Dover that separates Britain from France, and its white chalk cliffs dominate the coastline. The town has been a key gateway for centuries; Roman and later medieval forts were built here, and the famous Dover Castle has guarded the coast since the 12th century. Today the promenade is bustling with cafés, souvenir stalls and the iconic white-cliff walk, while ferries whisk visitors across to Calais in under two hours. With its dramatic sea views, historic sites and lively harbour, Dover feels both a living port and a reminder of Britain’s maritime heritage.

dre.name: Dresden
dre.text: Dresden, nestled on the banks of the Elbe River in eastern Germany, lies about 200 km south-west of Berlin and close to the Czech border. The city was once the capital of the Electorate of Saxony and is famed for its Baroque architecture, most notably the Frauenkirche, which was rebuilt after being destroyed in World War II. Today Dresden blends its rich heritage with a lively cultural scene: you can wander along the historic Altstadt, admire world-class collections in the Zwinger Palace, and enjoy riverside cafés where locals and visitors alike soak up the relaxed, yet vibrant atmosphere.

drw.name: Darwin
drw.text: Darwin, the capital of Australia’s Northern Territory, sits on the edge of the Timor Sea at the mouth of the Darwin River, where the tropical savannah meets mangrove-lined waterways. Established as the settlement of Palmerston in 1869, it was renamed Darwin in honour of the naturalist Charles Darwin and later became a key Allied base before suffering heavy Japanese bombing in 1942. Today the city is a laid-back gateway to Kakadu and Litchfield National Parks, famed for its vibrant waterfront, lively night markets, abundant wildlife parks and a multicultural food scene that reflects its rich Indigenous and Asian heritage.

dtt.name: Detroit
dtt.text: Detroit, Michigan, lies on the banks of the Detroit River directly opposite Windsor, Ontario, in the heart of the American Midwest. The city earned its fame as the cradle of the automobile industry, with Henry Ford establishing the Ford Motor Company in 1903 and introducing the moving assembly line a decade later. Today, visitors find a vibrant mix of historic art deco theatres, bustling street art districts and revitalised waterfront parks, while the legacy of motor-car manufacturing is celebrated in museums such as the Henry Ford and the Detroit Institute of Arts, offering a lively blend of culture and innovation.

dub.name: Dublin
dub.text: Dublin, the capital of Ireland, sits on the east coast where the River Liffey meets the Irish Sea, spreading over the low-lying plains of the province of Leinster. Founded by the Vikings in the 9th century, it later became the seat of English rule and the birthplace of many literary giants, including James Joyce. Today the city buzzes with a warm, welcoming atmosphere: you can wander past Georgian townhouses, sip a coffee in a bustling café, explore lively markets, and enjoy traditional music spilling from cosy pubs, all while the modern skyline rises behind the historic streets.

dud.name: Dunedin
dud.text: Dunedin lies on the southeast coast of New Zealand’s South Island, perched on the narrow coastal plain where the Water of Leith meets the Pacific Ocean. Founded in 1848 by Scottish settlers, it quickly earned the nickname “the Edinburgh of the South” and retains many Victorian and Edwardian buildings, including the historic railway station and the grand First Church of Otago. Today visitors can stroll through the leafy Botanic Garden, explore the vibrant street art of Baldwin Street—the world’s steepest residential road—and take a short drive to the spectacular wildlife-rich Otago Peninsula, where albatrosses, seals and penguins gather.

dus.name: Dushanbe
dus.text: Dushanbe, the capital of Tajikistan, lies in the western part of the country at the foot of the Hissar Mountains, on the banks of the Varzob River. The name means “Monday market” and the settlement grew around a bustling weekly bazaar before being declared the republic’s capital in 1929, replacing Khujand. Today the city blends wide Soviet-era avenues with colourful gardens, modern cafés and lively tea houses; Rudaki Avenue is lined with museums, shops and restaurants serving hearty plov and fresh fruit. Visitors find the people warm and welcoming, and the surrounding mountains provide striking backdrops for leisurely strolls.

dxb.name: Dubai
dxb.text: Dubai, United Arab Emirates, sits on the southeastern coast of the Persian Gulf, bordering the emirate of Abu Dhabi to the south and Sharjah to the northeast. Historically it grew from a modest fishing and pearling settlement, becoming a key trading port in the early 20th century before the discovery of oil transformed its fortunes. Today the city dazzles visitors with its skyline of towering skyscrapers, luxury hotels and world-class shopping, while the historic Al Fahidi district and bustling souks offer a glimpse of its traditional roots, making Dubai a striking blend of past and present.

dzo.name: Mayotte (Dzaoudzi)
dzo.text: Dzaoudzi, perched on the tiny island of Petite-Terre in the French overseas department of Mayotte, lies in the heart of the Mozambique Channel between Madagascar and the African mainland. Historically it served as the capital of the colony of Mayotte until the administrative centre moved to Mamoudzou in 1977, and its harbour was a key stop for French naval ships navigating the Indian Ocean. Today the town feels relaxed yet lively, with colourful market stalls selling fresh fish and tropical fruit, a pleasant promenade along the azure sea, and easy access to nearby beaches and coral reefs that invite snorkelling and gentle walks in a warm, friendly atmosphere.

edi.name: Edinburgh
edi.text: Edinburgh, perched on the east coast of Scotland where the River Forth meets the North Sea, is a compact city of striking contrasts. Its most famous historic landmark, the medieval castle that dominates the skyline, has guarded the city since the 12th century and was the site where the Scottish Crown Jewels are kept. Today the streets are alive with a mix of cobbled Old Town alleys and sleek New Town squares, bustling cafés, and world-class museums; the annual festivals fill the air with music, theatre and a lively, welcoming buzz for visitors of all ages.

eil.name: Eilat
eil.text: Eilat is Israel’s southernmost city, perched on the Red Sea coast at the tip of the Gulf of Aqaba, directly opposite the Egyptian resort of Taba and close to Jordan’s Aqaba. It grew from a small fishing village into a modern port after the 1949 armistice line established Israel’s access to the sea, and it later became a key base for the Israeli navy. Today the town is a sun-splashed playground of coral reefs, desert-backed beaches and bustling promenades, where visitors can snorkel among colourful fish, shop in lively markets and enjoy a relaxed, cosmopolitan atmosphere against a striking mountain backdrop.

ein.name: Eindhoven
ein.text: Eindhoven, situated in the southern province of North Brabant in the Netherlands, lies about 120 kilometres southeast of Amsterdam and is threaded by the River Dommel. It grew from a modest 13th-century settlement into a thriving market town, receiving its city charter in 1232, and later became the birthplace of the Philips electronics empire in 1891, which shaped its modern identity. Today the city buzzes with a lively mix of sleek modern architecture, creative design studios and bustling cafés, while its compact centre invites easy strolling past the lively Stratumseind nightlife strip and the verdant parks that surround the historic St Catharina’s Church.

enu.name: Enugu
enu.text: Enugu, the bustling capital of Enugu State in southeastern Nigeria, sits on the scenic hills of the Udi Plateau about 200 km north-east of the coast. The city earned its nickname “Coal City” after rich coal seams were discovered in the area in 1909, prompting the establishment of Nigeria’s first major coal mine and a railway line that opened in 1915. Today Enugu blends lively markets, vibrant music venues and leafy parks such as the popular Freedom Square, while the surrounding hills offer pleasant walks and views of lush countryside, making it a welcoming stop for curious travellers.

erb.name: Erbil
erb.text: Erbil, the capital of Iraq’s Kurdistan Region, sits on a plateau in the north-east of the country, about 80 kilometres from the Iranian border and a short drive from the ancient Zagros mountains. Archaeologists know the city’s famous citadel has been occupied since at least the 5th millennium BC, making it one of the world’s oldest continuously inhabited settlements. Today the city blends modern cafés, bustling souks and sleek skyscrapers with the stone-walled citadel that towers above the skyline, offering visitors a lively mix of history, culture and warm Kurdish hospitality.

evn.name: Yerevan
evn.text: Yerevan, the capital of Armenia, sits in the Ararat plain about 20 km south of the towering Mount Ararat and just a short drive from the Turkish border. Founded in 782 BC as the fortress of Erebuni, it is one of the world’s oldest continuously inhabited cities and boasts a rich tapestry of churches, Soviet-era architecture and bustling markets. Today the city feels lively yet relaxed, with tree-lined avenues, colourful cafés spilling onto sidewalks and the iconic Cascade steps offering panoramic views of the pink-hued rooftops and distant mountains, making every wander a pleasant surprise.

fbm.name: Kisangani
fbm.text: Kisangani sits on the north-bank of the mighty Congo River, where it widens into the vast Tshopo River, in the eastern part of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. It grew from a small colonial outpost into the country’s third-largest city and was the terminus of the historic Congo-Ocean Railway, linking the interior to the Atlantic coast. Today the town hums with a lively riverfront market, colourful wooden canoes bobbing beside modern cafés, and the surrounding rainforest offers opportunities for guided boat trips and wildlife spotting, giving visitors a blend of bustling urban life and untamed nature.

fez.name: Fez
fez.text: Fez, nestled in northern Morocco about 200 kilometres east of Casablanca, is one of the country’s oldest imperial cities and the best-preserved medieval urban centre in the Arab world. It was founded in the early 9th century and became a thriving hub of scholarship, famously home to the University of al-Qarawiyyin, recognised as the world’s oldest continuously operating university. Today the labyrinthine medina of Fes el-Baladi is a UNESCO World Heritage site, where narrow alleys lead past bustling souks, centuries-old madrasas and fragrant spice stalls, offering visitors a vivid glimpse of history alive amidst lively cafés and artisan workshops.

fln.name: Florianopolis
fln.text: Florianópolis, the capital of Brazil’s southern state of Santa Catarina, sits on the island of Santa Catarina and a thin strip of the mainland opposite the mainland city of São José. The town was founded by the Portuguese in 1673 as Nossa Senhora do Desterro and later renamed after the explorer Floriano Pereira. Today the city is a laid-back seaside haven, famed for its more than forty beaches that range from lively surf spots to tranquil coves, a bustling market of fresh seafood, colourful colonial streets and a vibrant nightlife that spills onto the sand at sunset.

flo.name: Florence
flo.text: Florence, nestled in the heart of Tuscany in central Italy, sits on the banks of the Arno River and is surrounded by gently rolling hills dotted with vineyards and olive groves. The city was the cradle of the Renaissance, a period when artists such as Michelangelo and Leonardo da Vinci were patronised by the powerful Medici family, and it was in Florence that the iconic dome of the Cathedral of Santa Maria del Fiore was completed in the 15th century. Today the streets buzz with a blend of historic charm and modern vibrancy: you can wander past world-renowned museums, sip coffee in lively piazzas, and enjoy the scent of fresh pizza drifting from bustling trattorias, all while the city’s timeless architecture provides a stunning backdrop to everyday life.

fnc.name: Funchal
fnc.text: Funchal, the capital of the Portuguese island of Madeira, sits on a sheltered bay on the island’s southern coast, framed by steep hills and the Atlantic Ocean. Founded in the early 15th century, it quickly became an important port for the sugar trade and later for Madeira wine, a legacy still celebrated in its historic cellars. Today the town is a colourful blend of cobbled streets, lively market stalls and terraced gardens, with cable-car rides offering panoramic views, pastel-coloured buildings lining the promenade, and a pleasant climate that makes strolling through its cafés and seafront terraces a year-round pleasure.

fnt.name: Freetown
fnt.text: Freetown, the capital of Sierra Leone, sits on a sheltered harbour on the Atlantic coast at the western edge of the country, framed by verdant hills and mangrove-lined beaches. Founded in 1792 as a settlement for freed enslaved people returning from Britain and North America, it became a symbol of liberty and the starting point of the historic “Back to Africa” movement. Today the city offers a lively blend of colonial architecture, bustling markets and vibrant music, while the nearby Tacugama Chimpanzee Sanctuary and the sweeping views from Sugar Loaf Mountain provide plenty of reasons to explore its warm, welcoming streets.

fra.name: Frankfurt
fra.text: Frankfurt, situated on the River Main in the state of Hesse in central Germany, is a bustling financial hub often nicknamed “Mainhattan” for its skyline of glass-clad towers. Historically it was the site of the first Frankfurt Parliament in 1848, Germany’s first freely elected national assembly. Today the city blends modernity with charm: you can wander the historic Römer square, explore museums along the Museumsufer, and enjoy the fragrant apple-wine taverns of the Alt-Sachsenhausen district, all while the lively streets buzz with shoppers, commuters and international visitors.

ftz.name: Fortaleza
ftz.text: Fortaleza, the bustling coastal capital of Brazil’s Ceará state, sits on a wide, sandy bay on the Atlantic Ocean. Founded in the early 17th century as a Portuguese fort to protect the region from French incursions, the city still bears the imprint of its colonial past in the historic centre and the nearby Forte de Nossa Senhora da Assunção. Today visitors are greeted by a lively promenade lined with palm-fringed beaches, vibrant markets selling tropical fruit and handcrafted jewellery, and a thriving nightlife that spills from beach bars into colourful street festivals, all under a warm, sunny sky.

fuk.name: Fukuoka
fuk.text: Fukuoka, located on the northern shore of Kyushu’s largest island, greets visitors with a blend of modern energy and relaxed coastal charm. Historically, it was the landing point for the Mongol invasions of 1274 and 1281, events that led to the famous “kamikaze” winds that repelled the fleets. Today the city hums with bustling shopping streets such as Tenjin, tranquil riverside parks, and a lively yatai food-stall scene where you can sample Hakata ramen straight from the broth-rich stalls. With its efficient subway, friendly locals and easy access to nearby beaches, Fukuoka feels both comfortably urban and refreshingly laid-back.

fun.name: Funafuti
fun.text: Funafuti, the capital atoll of Tuvalu, lies in the central Pacific about 1,300 km north-north-west of Fiji and just south of the equator. During the Second World War the island hosted a United States airstrip and supply base, remnants of which can still be seen in the landscape. Today the atoll feels like a tranquil, low-lying slice of tropical paradise, with a shallow lagoon dotted with palm-fringed beaches, a handful of modest guesthouses and a close-knit community that welcomes visitors with warm smiles. The pace is relaxed, the sea is crystal clear, and the island’s gentle charm is offset by an ever-present awareness of rising sea levels.

gau.name: Guwahati
gau.text: Guwahati, the bustling gateway to Northeast India, sits on the south bank of the Brahmaputra River in the state of Assam. It grew around the ancient Kamakhya Temple, a revered Shakti shrine that has attracted pilgrims for centuries and was mentioned in early medieval texts. Today the city blends modern cafés, colourful markets and leafy riverfront promenades, offering river cruises, wildlife parks and easy trips to nearby tea-plantation hills. Visitors enjoy the lively blend of Assamese culture, the aroma of fresh tea, and the backdrop of mist-shrouded hills rising beyond the flowing Brahmaputra.

gaz.name: Gaza City
gaz.text: Gaza City sits on the Mediterranean coast of the Gaza Strip in Palestine, at the northern edge of the historic Philistine plain. It is one of the world’s oldest continually inhabited settlements, mentioned in Egyptian records as far back as the 15th century BC and later flourishing as a bustling Ottoman port. Today the city is a compact, lively place where crowded souks sell fresh fish, spices and textiles, and the seafront promenade offers views of the sea against a backdrop of modern apartment blocks. While movement is limited by the political situation, visitors experience a resilient community, rich street food, and the warm hospitality of its residents.

gbe.name: Gaborone
gbe.text: Gaborone, the capital of Botswana, sits on the southeastern edge of the Kalahari Desert, straddling the border with South Africa and close to the Limpopo River. It grew from a modest colonial administrative centre established in the early 20th century into an independent nation's capital when Botswana gained self-government in 1965. Today the city offers a relaxed, modern vibe: wide streets lined with leafy trees, a bustling downtown market where you can sample fresh fruit and traditional crafts, and nearby wildlife reserves such as the Mokolodi Nature Reserve, making it a pleasant base for exploring both urban culture and the surrounding savanna.

gdl.name: Guadalajara
gdl.text: Guadalajara, the capital of the Mexican state of Jalisco, sits in the western highlands about 500 km northwest of Mexico City and 300 km east of the Pacific coast. Founded in 1542, it became an important centre of Spanish colonial administration and later the birthplace of maria maria’s lively music and the iconic tequila industry. Today the city buzzes with a mix of colonial charm and modern energy: colourful markets such as Mercado San Juan de Dios spill onto cobbled streets, historic plazas host street performers, and a thriving food scene offers everything from tacos al pastor to gourmet restaurants, all set against the backdrop of grand churches and bustling cafés.

gdr.name: Gondar
gdr.text: Gondar, perched on the high plateau of northern Ethiopia near the Simien Mountains, was founded in the early 17th century as the capital of the Ethiopian Empire and is famed for its impressive collection of stone castles and palaces that earned it the nickname “the Camelot of Africa”. Today the town buzzes with a lively blend of history and modern life: colourful markets spill onto cobbled streets, friendly cafés serve freshly roasted coffee, and the UNESCO-listed Royal Enclosure invites visitors to wander among ancient towers while the surrounding hills provide spectacular sunrise vistas and a cool, pleasant climate year-round.

gen.name: Genoa
gen.text: Genoa sits on the north-west coast of Italy, cradled by the Ligurian Sea and backed by the Apennine hills, making it a natural gateway to the Mediterranean. Founded by the ancient Greeks and later flourishing as a powerful Republic, it was the birthplace of explorer Christopher Columbus in the 15th century. Today the city is a lively mix of winding medieval lanes, bustling waterfront promenades and colourful market stalls; you can wander the UNESCO-listed old town, admire the sleek aquarium on the harbour, and savour fresh pesto on a terrace overlooking the sea.

geo.name: Georgetown
geo.text: Georgetown, the capital of Guyana, sits on the Atlantic coast at the mouth of the Demerara River, its streets laid out in a distinctive grid pattern that dates back to the early 19th-century colonial plan. Founded by the Dutch in the 18th century and later taken over by the British, the city retains many colourful wooden buildings, the iconic St George’s Cathedral with its towering wooden dome, and a bustling waterfront market where vendors sell fresh fish, tropical fruits and handmade crafts. Today visitors enjoy strolling along the historic promenades, sampling Creole cuisine in lively cafés, and feeling the gentle river breeze as the city blends its rich heritage with a relaxed, tropical rhythm.

gla.name: Glasgow
gla.text: Glasgow sits on the River Clyde in western Scotland, about 45 miles northwest of Edinburgh and a short train ride from the Irish Sea coast. Once a booming hub of shipbuilding and industry in the 19th century, the city’s historic legacy is visible in its grand Victorian architecture and the famous Riverside Museum, which celebrates its maritime past. Today Glasgow thrives as a vibrant cultural centre, famous for its lively music scene, world-class galleries such as the Gallery of Modern Art, and a friendly, laid-back atmosphere that welcomes visitors to explore its bustling cafés, leafy parks and striking street art.

gnj.name: Ganja
gnj.text: Ganja, Azerbaijan’s second-largest city, sits in the western foothills of the Lesser Caucasus, about 375 km west of Baku and near the Ganja River. It was the birthplace of the 12th-century poet and statesman Nizami Ganjavi, whose house is now a museum. Today the city blends Soviet-era avenues with lively bazaars, tree-lined parks and a revitalised riverfront where cafés spill onto stone terraces. Visitors can wander past the historic Javad Khan Street, admire the colourful mosaics of the Nizami Museum, and enjoy the backdrop of the nearby Goygol Lake on clear days.

goi.name: Goiania
goi.text: Goiania, the vibrant capital of the Brazilian state of Goiás, lies in the heart of the country’s interior, about 200 km south-west of Brasília. Planned from scratch in the early 1930s, it officially became the state capital in 1937, replacing the historic town of Goiás Velho and sparking rapid growth. Today the city dazzles visitors with its wide, tree-lined avenues, striking modernist buildings such as the colourful Praça Cívica designed by Oscar Niemeyer, and a lively cultural scene that includes bustling markets, lively cafés and the nearby Parque Vaca Brava, a favourite spot for picnics and bird-watching.

gom.name: Goma
gom.text: Goma, perched on the northeastern shore of Lake Kivu and shadowed by the active volcano Nyiragongo, is the bustling gateway to the eastern DRC’s mountainous frontier. The town grew dramatically after the 1994 Rwandan refugee crisis, when tens of thousands crossed the border and reshaped its markets and culture. Today visitors find a lively mix of colourful street stalls, warm cafés and energetic crowds, while the nearby volcano’s lava lake offers unforgettable sunrise hikes; the lake itself provides gentle boat trips and fishing, making Goma a vibrant base for exploring both natural wonders and the resilient spirit of its people.

got.name: Gothenburg
got.text: Gothenburg sits on Sweden’s west coast, at the mouth of the Göta älv river where it meets the North Sea, about 300 km north-west of Copenhagen. Founded in 1621 by King Gustav II Adolf as a fortified trading port, it grew into the country’s main gateway for maritime commerce. Today the city feels relaxed yet vibrant, with leafy boulevards lined by cafés, the bustling fish market at Feskekôrka, and a thriving arts scene centred on the historic Haga district. Its archipelago of islands is easily reached by a short ferry ride, offering seaside walks and fresh seafood in a laid-back atmosphere.

gra.name: Granada
gra.text: Granada is a vibrant city tucked on the foothills of the Sierra Nevada in southern Spain, just a short drive from the Mediterranean coast. It rose to fame as the capital of the last Muslim kingdom in Iberia, and its most iconic legacy is the Alhambra, a 14th-century palace-citadel whose intricate Moorish architecture still dominates the skyline. Today the narrow winding streets of the Albaicín neighbourhood echo with the scent of orange blossoms, while bustling tapas bars and lively flamenco venues invite visitors to soak up a mix of historic grandeur and lively, contemporary Andalusian culture.

gua.name: Guatemala City
gua.text: Guatemala City, the bustling capital of Guatemala, sits in the high-land valley of the Central Plateau at about 1,650 metres above sea level, surrounded by volcanoes such as Pacaya and Agua. The city was founded in 1776 when a series of earthquakes devastated the former colonial capital of Antigua, prompting the Spanish authorities to move the administrative centre to this more secure location. Today the metropolis blends modern skyscrapers with historic plazas, lively markets and museums like the National Museum of Archaeology; its streets hum with traffic, colourful street food stalls and a friendly, cosmopolitan vibe that offers visitors a vivid glimpse of contemporary Central American life.

gur.name: Guiria
gur.text: Guiria, the modest capital of Sucre state on Venezuela’s Caribbean coast, sits at the foot of the Paria Peninsula where the sea meets the foothills of the Sierra de Turimiquire. The town was formally founded in 1764 as a harbour serving the cocoa-growing hinterland, and its historic square still echoes the colonial trading days. Today visitors find a laid-back seaside settlement with colourful wooden houses, a bustling market and a promenade lined with palm trees, while easy boat trips launch from its harbour to the nearby islands and the pristine beaches of the Paria Peninsula.

gva.name: Geneva
gva.text: Geneva sits on the southwestern tip of Switzerland, cradled by the lake that bears its name and backed by the towering Alps. The city’s history stretches back to Roman times, and it later became the seat of the Protestant Reformation under John Calvin in the 16th century, shaping its reputation for religious tolerance. Today, strolling along the Quai du Mont-Blanc you’ll find sleek museums, elegant cafés and the iconic Jet d’Eau spouting water high over the lake, while the multilingual crowd reflects Geneva’s role as a hub for international diplomacy and finance, making it both cosmopolitan and surprisingly relaxed.

gye.name: Guayaquil
gye.text: Guayaquil, Ecuador’s bustling port city, sits on the banks of the Guayas River near the country’s Pacific coast, about 400 km south-west of Quito. Founded in the 16th century, it grew into a key hub for the export of cacao and bananas during the early 20th century, shaping its reputation as the “Pearl of the Pacific.” Today the city blends modern high-rises with colourful riverfront promenades, lively markets and the historic Parque Seminario, where you can admire towering Ceiba trees. Friendly locals, abundant seafood and a vibrant nightlife make a visit feel both energetic and welcoming.

gyu.name: Gyumri
gyu.text: Gyumri, Armenia’s second-largest city, sits in the north-west of the country about 120 kilometres north-east of Yerevan, close to the Turkish border and the foothills of the Lesser Caucasus. It was long known as Kumayri and later Alexandropol, and in 1926 it became the capital of the Armenian Soviet Socialist Republic’s north-west region. Today the town charms visitors with its colourful Soviet-era architecture, bustling cafés and a lively arts scene; the restored historic centre invites relaxed strolls among cobbled streets, while the warm hospitality of locals makes a short break feel like a welcoming homecoming.

hab.name: Havana
hab.text: Havana, the bustling capital of Cuba, sits on the north-west coast of the island along the Gulf of Mexico, its harbour guarded by the iconic Malecón seawall. Founded by the Spanish in the early 1500s, the city became a vital port of the Atlantic slave trade and later a key stronghold in the Caribbean during the age of sail. Today visitors wander its colourful, pastel-coloured streets lined with well-preserved colonial architecture, sip coffee in lively plazas, and hear the rhythm of live son and salsa spilling from cafés, while the warm tropical air carries the scent of sea and history.

ham.name: Hamburg
ham.text: Hamburg, Germany’s second-largest city, sits on the River Elbe where it widens into the North Sea, giving it a bustling port that has been a key gateway for trade since the 14th century. The historic Speicherstadt, the world’s largest warehouse district built on timber piles, still houses museums, cafés and the famous Miniatur Wunderland model railway. Today the city blends maritime heritage with modern flair: you can stroll along the lively waterfront of the HafenCity, enjoy a coffee in the leafy Planten un Blomen park, and soak up the vibrant music scene in St Pauli, all while marveling at sleek glass skyscrapers beside centuries-old brick buildings.

han.name: Hanoi
han.text: Hanoi, the capital of Vietnam, lies in the north of the country on the banks of the Red River. The city was founded in 1010 as Thăng Long and served as the historic seat of power for the Đại Việt kingdom, a fact that still colours its many ancient temples and citadels. Today Hanoi is a lively mix of old and new: narrow streets of the Old Quarter buzz with motorbikes, street-food stalls and colonial-era French buildings, while tranquil lakes such as Hoàn Kiếm offer a peaceful retreat amid the urban bustle. Visitors love the blend of history, culture and modern energy that makes the city so distinctive.

har.name: Harwich
har.text: Harwich is a bustling little port town in the county of Essex, perched on the estuary where the River Stour meets the North Sea, just a short train ride from London. Historically it was an important naval base and commercial harbour, with the Harwich Redoubt built in the early 1800s to protect the coast during the Napoleonic wars. Today the town feels relaxed yet lively: you can stroll along the historic waterfront, watch ferries set out for the Netherlands and Denmark, explore the maritime museum, and enjoy fresh seafood in cosy cafés while the sea breeze carries the scent of sails and salt.

hba.name: Hobart
hba.text: Hobart, the capital of Tasmania, sits on the southern shore of the Derwent River where it meets the scenic harbour and is framed by the snow-capped slopes of Mount Wellington. The city began as a British penal colony in 1804, making it one of Australia’s earliest European settlements. Today it blends historic charm with a lively arts and food scene: you can stroll along the bustling waterfront, browse the Saturday Salamanca Market, enjoy fresh seafood in the historic precinct, and take short trips up the mountain for panoramic views of the city and surrounding wilderness.

hel.name: Helsinki
hel.text: Helsinki, the capital of Finland, sits on the southern coast of the country, straddling the Gulf of Finland and a cluster of islands that give the city its breezy, maritime feel. Founded in 1550 by King Gustav Vasa as a trading port, it grew into a vibrant centre of design and technology after becoming Finland’s capital in 1812. Today visitors wander a compact, walkable centre where historic wooden houses sit beside sleek modernist architecture; you can savour fresh seafood at market stalls, relax in seaside saunas, and explore museums, parks and cafés that blend Nordic calm with a lively, contemporary spirit.

het.name: Hohhot
het.text: Hohhot, the capital of Inner Mongolia in northern China, sits on the gentle slopes of the Yulong Grasslands about 150 km south of the Great Wall’s Badaling section. Historically it was a key trading hub on the ancient caravan routes between China and Mongolia, flourishing under the Qing dynasty when it became the regional administrative centre. Today the city blends wide boulevards with traditional Mongolian yurts, offering bustling markets where you can sample roasted lamb and milk tea, modern museums that showcase nomadic culture, and leafy parks perfect for a leisurely stroll.

hfa.name: Haifa
hfa.text: Haifa, perched on the slopes of Mount Carmel overlooking the Mediterranean, sits in northern Israel about 90 km south of Tel Aviv. It grew around the ancient port of Akko and was expanded in the 19th century when the Baháʼí Faith established its World Centre on the mountain, a landmark that still dominates the skyline. Today the city blends modern high-rise apartments with lively bazaars, a bustling waterfront promenade and verdant gardens that climb the hills. Visitors can ride the historic Carmelit funicular, explore the vibrant German Colony, and savour fresh seafood while watching the sun set over the sea.

hfx.name: Halifax
hfx.text: Halifax sits on the Atlantic coast of Nova Scotia, Canada, where the harbour is protected by the Halifax Peninsula and the Chebucto and Bedford peninsulas, making it one of the world’s largest natural deep-water ports. The city was established in 1749 as a British military outpost, and it later endured the Halifax Explosion of 1917, a devastating blast that reshaped the waterfront. Today visitors find a lively blend of maritime heritage and modern culture: historic waterfront boardwalks, bustling seafood markets, colourful row houses, and a thriving arts scene, all set against striking sea-swept scenery and friendly locals.

hgh.name: Hangzhou
hgh.text: Hangzhou, a city in eastern China’s Zhejiang province, lies on the banks of the Qiantang River at the foot of the famous West Lake. It has been celebrated since the Tang dynasty as a capital of the Southern Song, when emperors built the picturesque gardens and temples that still inspire poets today. Modern visitors find a blend of ancient charm and sleek development: you can stroll among lotus-filled waters, sip longjing tea in historic teahouses, and then hop on a high-speed train or explore vibrant tech parks and bustling night markets, all within a city famed for its natural beauty and hospitality.

hiu.name: Honiara
hiu.text: Honiara, the capital city of the Solomon Islands, lies on the northern coast of Guadalcanal Island, nestled between the sparkling waters of Iron Bottom Sound and lush tropical hills. The town grew around the World War II airfield built by the United States, a reminder of the fierce battles that took place on the island in 1942-43. Today Honiara is a laid-back, colourful port where you can wander the bustling central market, taste fresh seafood on the waterfront promenade, and enjoy the warm hospitality of locals, all set against a backdrop of verdant mountains and coral-fringed beaches.

hkg.name: Hong Kong
hkg.text: Hong Kong, a bustling Special Administrative Region on the southern coast of China, sits at the mouth of the Pearl River and comprises Hong Kong Island, the Kowloon Peninsula and over 200 outlying islands. It began as a small fishing village before becoming a British colony after the First Opium War in 1842, a status that shaped its distinctive blend of Eastern and Western architecture. Today the city dazzles visitors with its dramatic skyline, vibrant street markets, world-class dining and efficient public transport; you can hike scenic trails in the New Territories, ride the historic Star Ferry across Victoria Harbour, or simply soak up the energetic atmosphere of its neon-lit streets.

hkt.name: Phuket
hkt.text: Phuket, an island province off Thailand’s southwestern coast, lies on the Andaman Sea opposite the Malay Peninsula and is linked to the mainland by the Sarasin Bridge. The town of Phuket City grew around a 16th-century tin-mining settlement that attracted Chinese traders, and its historic Old Town still displays colourful Sino-Portuguese shophouses. Today the island is a bustling mix of white-sand beaches, lively night markets and modern resorts, while the surrounding waters offer excellent snorkeling and boat trips to nearby islands such as Phi Phi and Similan. Visitors enjoy a relaxed yet vibrant atmosphere, with easy access to Thai cuisine, cultural festivals and the stunning coastal scenery.

hly.name: Holyhead
hly.text: Holyhead sits on the western tip of Holy Island, off the coast of Anglesey in North Wales, and serves as the United Kingdom’s busiest ferry gateway to Dublin. The town grew around a Roman fort known as Caer y Ffos, evidence of its strategic importance for centuries, and later expanded with the 19th-century Admiralty Pier that still frames the harbour. Today Holyhead blends a bustling port atmosphere with rugged coastal scenery: you can stroll along the promenade, watch ferries swing in and out, explore the maritime museum, and enjoy fresh seafood while the sea breezes carry the scent of salt and history.

hmn.name: Hamilton, Bermuda
hmn.text: Hamilton, the capital of Bermuda, sits on the island’s north-central coast at the head of Hamilton Harbour, a natural inlet framed by gentle hills and pastel-coloured houses. Founded in the early 17th century, the town was formally laid out in 1790 and quickly became the administrative heart of the colony, a role it still fulfils today. Visitors stroll along Front Street to discover boutique shops, lively cafés and the striking pink-brick façade of the historic City Hall, while the nearby waterfront promenade offers sweeping views of yachts bobbing in the harbour and the distant Atlantic horizon.

hnl.name: Honolulu
hnl.text: Honolulu, the vibrant capital of the Hawaiian Islands, sits on the southeastern coast of Oʻahu where the Pacific Ocean meets the island’s volcanic mountains. Founded in the early 19th century, it became the seat of the Hawaiian monarchy and later the first American territorial capital after annexation in 1898. Today the city blends tropical scenery with modern comforts: you can stroll along Waikiki Beach, explore historic Iolani Palace, savour fresh poke at a bustling market, and enjoy a lively arts scene framed by palm-lined streets and spectacular sunsets over the harbour.

hoh.name: Hook of Holland
hoh.text: Hook of Holland is a seaside town at the western tip of South Holland, where the Nieuwe Waterweg canal meets the North Sea, just a short drive west of Rotterdam. It was the departure point for the first regular passenger ferry service to Harwich, England, which began in 1893 and helped cement its role as a gateway between the Netherlands and Britain. Today the promenade is lined with colourful beach huts, modern cafés and a bustling ferry terminal, while the wide sandy beach and the iconic windmills on the dunes offer relaxed strolls and striking sunset views over the busy shipping lane.

hou.name: Houston
hou.text: Houston, Texas, lies in the southeastern part of the state near the Gulf Coast, at the intersection of Interstates 10, 45 and 69. Founded in 1836 and named for General Sam Houston, the city grew rapidly after the arrival of the Houston Ship Channel in the early 20th century, which turned it into a major port and industrial hub. Today visitors find a vibrant mix of world-class museums, a lively restaurant scene showcasing Tex-Mex and barbecue, and spacious green spaces such as Hermann Park. The skyline is dominated by modern skyscrapers, yet the warm, welcoming spirit of the city makes it easy to explore its diverse neighbourhoods and cultural attractions.

hrb.name: Harbin
hrb.text: Harbin, the capital of Heilongjiang province in far-eastern China, sits on the banks of the Songhua River close to the Russian border. It grew from a modest Russian railway outpost in the late 1800s, and the city’s wide boulevards and European-style architecture still echo that early influence. Today Harbin is famed for its spectacular ice and snow festival, where massive illuminated sculptures transform the frozen river and streets into a winter wonderland, while its bustling markets, cosy tea houses and lively night scene offer a warm, welcoming contrast to the crisp northern climate.

hre.name: Harare
hre.text: Harare, the capital of Zimbabwe, lies in the north-central part of the country on a plateau about 1,500 metres above sea level, giving it a mild, subtropical climate. Founded in 1890 as the colonial settlement of Salisbury, it became the capital of the self-governing British South Africa Company and later the independent nation’s centre of administration after 1980. Today the city bustles with a mix of modern malls, lively markets and leafy suburbs, while green spaces such as Harare Gardens and the National Botanic Garden offer peaceful retreats; friendly locals are happy to share stories over a cup of rooibos tea.

hrg.name: Hurghada
hrg.text: Hurghada is a bustling seaside town on Egypt’s Red Sea coast, about 500 km southeast of Cairo. Originally a small fishing village, it grew rapidly after the 1970s when the government promoted tourism along the Red Sea, and today it is a major gateway for diving and beach holidays. The town’s promenade is lined with cafés, souvenir stalls and modern hotels, while the crystal-clear waters host vibrant coral reefs teeming with marine life. Visitors can spend the day lounging on golden sands, exploring nearby desert dunes on a quad bike, or hopping on a boat to snorkel among colourful fish and ancient shipwrecks.

hrt.name: Herat
hrt.text: Herat, perched on the western edge of Afghanistan near the Iranian border, lies on the historic Silk Road where caravans once linked the Persian Gulf with Central Asia. Founded centuries ago, the city is famed for the 13th-century Friday Mosque, whose intricate tilework and massive minarets still dominate the skyline and testify to Herat’s past as a centre of art and learning under the Timurid Empire. Today the bustling bazaar offers fragrant spices, hand-woven carpets and lively tea houses, while the renovated citadel and nearby gardens provide quiet spots to soak up the warm, dry climate and the friendly hospitality of its residents.

hyd.name: Hyderabad
hyd.text: Hyderabad, the bustling capital of Telangana in south-central India, sits on the banks of the Musi River between the Deccan plateau and the coastal plains. Founded in 1591 by Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah, it soon became famed for the magnificent Charminar, a four-arched monument that still dominates the old city’s skyline. Today the city blends historic bazaars selling fragrant biryani and pearls with sleek glass towers and tech parks, offering visitors a lively mix of heritage and modernity; you can wander through centuries-old forts, sip chai in leafy cafés, and explore vibrant street art and contemporary museums all within a warm, welcoming atmosphere.

ibd.name: Ibadan
ibd.text: Ibadan, the sprawling capital of Oyo State in south-west Nigeria, sits on a high plateau about 120 kilometres north of Lagos. It grew from a 19th-century Yoruba settlement into a key colonial administrative centre and later became home to the University of Ibadan, founded in 1948 as the country’s first university. Today the city blends hectic markets, leafy avenues and striking colonial architecture; the bustling Bodija Market offers a sensory feast of fabrics and street food, while the historic Cocoa House—Nigeria’s first skyscraper—provides a glimpse of its pioneering past, making a visit both lively and culturally rich.

iks.name: Irkutsk
iks.text: Irkutsk, perched on the western bank of the mighty Lena River in southeastern Siberia, serves as the gateway to Lake Baikal and the surrounding taiga. Founded in 1661 as a wooden fort to protect the expanding Russian trade route to China, the city grew into a bustling centre of Siberian administration and culture. Today the streets are lined with colourful wooden houses, lively cafés and well-preserved 19th-century architecture, while museums showcase the region’s indigenous heritage and its role in the Trans-Siberian Railway. Visitors enjoy crisp river walks, vibrant markets and easy day trips to the crystal-clear waters of Baikal.

ind.name: Indianapolis
ind.text: Indianapolis sits in the heart of Indiana, midway between Chicago and Cincinnati, and serves as the state’s capital and largest city. Established in 1821 as a planned centre for the new state, it quickly grew around the crossroads of the National Road and the Wabash and Erie Canal. Today the city blends modern skyscrapers with wide, tree-lined streets and a vibrant cultural scene; visitors can stroll along the Canal Walk, explore the expansive Indianapolis Museum of Art, and feel the buzz of the famous motor-sport atmosphere at the Indianapolis Motor Speedway, all within a friendly, Midwestern setting.

isf.name: Isfahan
isf.text: Isfahan, perched on the Zayandeh River in central Iran, is often called “Half of the World” for its striking architecture and historic charm. Founded over a thousand years ago, it rose to prominence under the Safavid dynasty in the 17th century, when Shah Abbas I commissioned the grand Imam Reza Square and the iconic Si-o-se Pol bridge. Today the city buzzes with a lively mix of bustling bazaars, fragrant tea houses and serene gardens; the blue-tiled mosques gleam against a backdrop of modern cafés, inviting visitors to stroll along the riverbank and savour the blend of past and present.

isl.name: Islamabad
isl.text: Islamabad, the capital of Pakistan, sits in the Pothohar Plateau at the foothills of the Margalla range, about 30 km north of the ancient city of Rawalpindi. Planned in the 1960s, it replaced Karachi as the nation’s administrative centre and was designed to combine modernity with natural scenery. Today the city feels spacious and green, with wide avenues shaded by pine-laden hills, clean parks and the striking Faisal Mosque dominating the skyline. Visitors can stroll along the serene Rawal Lake, explore the modest museums, and enjoy cafés that serve everything from traditional chai to international fare, all set against a backdrop of crisp, fresh air.

ist.name: Istanbul
ist.text: Istanbul, straddling the Bosphorus where Europe meets Asia, is Turkey’s largest city and a vibrant crossroads of cultures. Once known as Constantinople, it was the capital of the Byzantine Empire and later the Ottoman Empire, and its historic peninsula still holds the awe-inspiring Hagia Sophia, a 6th-century cathedral-mosque-museum that dominates the skyline. Today the city buzzes with bustling bazaars, rooftop cafés overlooking glittering waterways, and a lively street art scene, while ancient stone walls and Ottoman palaces sit side by side with modern skyscrapers, offering visitors a seamless blend of past and present.

ixc.name: Chandigarh
ixc.text: Chandigarh, perched at the foothills of the Shivalik range in north-western India, is the joint capital of the states of Punjab and Haryana. Designed by the Swiss-French architect Le Corbusier after India’s independence, it was one of the first planned cities in the country and was formally inaugurated in 1966. Today the city feels spacious and modern, with tree-lined avenues, wide boulevards and striking concrete buildings punctuated by colourful gardens. Visitors can stroll through the beautifully laid-out Rock Garden, relax by Sukhna Lake, or sip tea at a bustling café while watching locals go about their day.

izm.name: Izmir
