izm.text: Izmir, perched on the sparkling Aegean coast of western Turkey, is the country’s third-largest city and has been a bustling port since ancient times when it was known as Smyrna, a key centre of Greek trade and culture. Today the city blends its rich past with a lively, contemporary vibe: the promenade along the sea is lined with cafés and palm trees, the bustling Kemeralti market offers spices, textiles and street food, and the modern waterfront hosts museums, art galleries and lively festivals. Visitors enjoy a relaxed Mediterranean climate, friendly locals and a seamless mix of historic sites and modern amenities.

jai.name: Jaipur
jai.text: Jaipur, the capital of Rajasthan in north-western India, sits about 260 km south of Delhi on the edge of the Aravalli Range. Founded in 1727 by Maharaja Sawai Jaipal, it was one of the first planned cities in India, laid out on a grid of broad streets and adorned with pink-hued stone buildings, which earned it the nickname “The Pink City”. Today the bustling metropolis blends historic forts, palaces and vibrant bazaars with modern cafés, hotels and a lively arts scene, offering visitors a colourful mix of heritage and contemporary Indian life.

jed.name: Jeddah
jed.text: Jeddah, a bustling port city on the Red Sea coast of western Saudi Arabia, lies about 80 kilometres south of the holy city of Mecca. It was the main gateway for Muslim pilgrims travelling to the Kaaba for centuries, and its historic coral-stone houses form the UNESCO-listed Al-Balad district, the oldest settled area in the Kingdom. Today the city blends tradition with modernity: sleek skyscrapers rise beside bustling souks, the corniche offers a seaside promenade lined with cafés and art installations, and the warm, welcoming locals make wandering its markets and waterfront a genuinely pleasant experience.

jhb.name: Johor Bahru
jhb.text: Johor Bahru, the bustling capital of the southern Malaysian state of Johor, sits on the tip of the Malay Peninsula just across the Johor-Singapore Causeway, offering easy views of Singapore’s skyline. The town grew from a modest fishing village in the mid-19th century and was developed into the sultanate’s centre by Sultan Abu Bakar, who built the impressive Istana Besar in the 1860s. Today it is a lively mix of modern malls, colourful street markets and colonial-era architecture; visitors can savour diverse street food, explore museums and temples, and enjoy a relaxed riverfront promenade while feeling the city’s friendly, multicultural spirit.

jkt.name: Jakarta
jkt.text: Jakarta, Indonesia’s bustling capital, sits on the north-west coast of the island of Java, straddling the Java Sea. Founded by the Dutch in the early 17th century as Batavia, it served as the administrative centre of the Dutch East Indies and retains historic colonial architecture in the old town of Kota Tua. Today the city is a vibrant mix of towering skyscrapers, colourful markets and modern cafés, where you can savour street-food satay beside sleek shopping malls, and explore museums that trace the nation’s rich past while the lively traffic and warm, humid air remind you you’re in a truly dynamic metropolis.

jnb.name: Johannesburg
jnb.text: Johannesburg, South Africa’s largest city, sits on the highveld of Gauteng province at about 1 750 metres above sea-level, roughly 55 km south of the historic gold-mining town of Kimberley. Founded in 1886 after gold was discovered on the Witwatersrand, it quickly grew into the country’s economic engine and played a central role in the anti-apartheid struggle, with sites such as the former Soweto police station now forming part of the Apartheid Museum. Today the city blends sleek skyscrapers with vibrant street art, bustling markets and green spaces like the Johannesburg Botanical Gardens, offering visitors a lively mix of culture, history and modern South African hospitality.

jog.name: Yogyakarta
jog.text: Yogyakarta, often simply called Yogyakarta, lies on the island of Java in central Indonesia, perched between the volcanic peaks of Merapi and Merbabu. It was the capital of the Mataram Sultanate and later the seat of Indonesia’s revolutionary government in 1945, giving it a rich blend of Javanese heritage and modern nation-building history. Today the city buzzes with lively streets lined with batik workshops, street food stalls and the sprawling campus of Gadjah Mada University, while the nearby Sultan’s Palace (Kraton) offers tranquil gardens and traditional performances, making a visit feel both cultural and comfortably contemporary.

jos.name: Jos
jos.text: Jos, perched on the Jos Plateau in the heart of Nigeria’s middle belt, sits at about 1,200 metres above sea-level, giving it a noticeably cooler climate than much of the country. The town grew in the early 1900s as a British colonial hill station and soon became the centre of the country’s tin-mining boom, a legacy still hinted at in the old mines and the colourful displays at the National Museum. Today visitors find a pleasant mix of bustling markets, craft shops and relaxed cafés, with easy trips to nearby wildlife parks and scenic high-land walks that showcase the region’s distinctive pine-covered hills.

jrs.name: Jerusalem
jrs.text: Jerusalem, Israel – nestled in the hills of the Judean Mountains between the Mediterranean Sea and the Dead Sea, this ancient city sits at the crossroads of three continents and three major religions. It has been continuously inhabited for millennia and was the capital of the Kingdom of Israel under King David, a fact recorded in biblical and archaeological sources. Today the Old City’s stone walls enclose bustling markets, sacred sites such as the Western Wall and the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, and winding alleyways where the scent of spices mingles with the hum of tourists and locals alike, offering a vivid blend of history, culture and modern Middle-Eastern life.

jub.name: Juba
jub.text: Juba, the bustling capital of South Sudan, sits on the banks of the White Nile in the country’s southern region, roughly 300 km from the Ugandan border. Founded as a colonial outpost in the early 20th century, it became the seat of the Sudanese government after independence in 1956 and later the capital of the new nation in 2011. Today the city is a lively mix of colourful markets, modern office blocks and riverfront promenades, where the warm climate and friendly locals make a visit feel both energetic and welcoming, despite occasional traffic and ongoing development.

jyp.name: Jayapura
jyp.text: Jayapura, perched on the north-eastern tip of the island of New Guinea, is the bustling capital of Indonesia’s Papua province and the easternmost city of the country. It grew from a modest Dutch outpost called Hollandia, which served as a key Allied base during World War II before the town was renamed after Indonesian independence. Today the city greets visitors with a tropical climate, colourful markets selling fresh tropical fruit and handicrafts, and sweeping views of the Pacific Ocean and the towering Cyclops Mount. A short drive takes you to pristine beaches, traditional villages and the remarkable biodiversity of the nearby rainforest, making Jayapura a lively gateway to the cultural and natural wonders of Papua.

kan.name: Kano
kan.text: Kano, in northern Nigeria, sits on the northern edge of the Sudanian savanna about 150 km south of the Sahel, roughly 500 km inland from the coast. It grew from the ancient Kano Kingdom, which was already a thriving commercial centre by the 10th century and later became one of the most important emirates of the Sokoto Caliphate in the early 19th century. Today the city buzzes with a mix of old and new: the bustling Kurmi market spills onto the streets, historic walls and the grand Emir’s Palace sit alongside modern malls and lively cafés, offering visitors a vivid taste of Nigeria’s heritage and contemporary life.

kbl.name: Kabul
kbl.text: Kabul, the capital of Afghanistan, sits in a high valley where the Kabul River cuts through the Hindu Kush mountains at roughly 1,800 metres above sea level. The city has been a key crossroads on the ancient Silk Road for centuries, and it was the seat of the Afghan empire under Emir Abd al-Rahman Khan in the late 19th century. Today visitors find a bustling mix of modern cafés, colourful bazaars and restored historic sites such as the 16th-century Gardens of Babur, while the surrounding hills offer striking views and a reminder of the city's resilient spirit.

kch.name: Kuching
kch.text: Kuching, the capital of Sarawak on the island of Borneo, sits on the banks of the Sarawak River and is surrounded by lush rain-forests and mangroves. The town’s name, meaning “cat” in Malay, reflects a long-standing local legend, and it was an important trading post during the era of the White Rajahs, when the Brooke family governed Sarawak from the mid-19th century. Today Kuching is a laid-back yet lively city, famous for its colourful waterfront, vibrant night markets and a mix of colonial shophouses, modern cafés and easy access to wildlife sanctuaries, making it a welcoming base for exploring both culture and nature.

kgf.name: Karaganda
kgf.text: Karaganda, a sprawling city in central Kazakhstan about 230 kilometres south of Nur-Sultan, sits on the steppe at the foot of the Kazakh Uplands. It grew rapidly after the discovery of rich coal seams in the 1930s, and was granted official city status in 1938, becoming a key centre of the Soviet Union’s mining industry. Today the city mixes Soviet-era architecture with vibrant street life: wide avenues are lined with cafés serving hearty Kazakh fare, museums showcase the region’s industrial heritage, and the surrounding steppe offers easy day-trips to historic memorials and scenic nature reserves.

kgl.name: Kigali
kgl.text: Kigali, the capital of Rwanda, sits in the country’s central plateau at an altitude of around 1,500 metres, surrounded by rolling hills and lush greenery. The city grew around the site of a colonial railway station and became the capital of the newly independent nation in 1962, later surviving the 1994 tragedy that reshaped Rwanda’s modern history. Today Kigali is clean, safe and remarkably vibrant: its markets brim with colourful crafts, coffee shops serve world-renowned beans, and well-maintained parks offer sweeping views of the surrounding hills, making it a welcoming base for exploring both urban life and nearby wildlife reserves.

kgn.name: Kingston
kgn.text: Kingston, the bustling capital of Jamaica, sits on the southeastern coast where the harbour meets the island’s north-south ridge of hills. Founded in 1692 after an earthquake destroyed Port Royal, it quickly became the island’s commercial and political centre. Today the city blends vibrant street markets, reggae rhythms and historic sites such as the 18th-century Devon House; the waterfront promenade offers striking views of the blue Caribbean Sea, while the lively downtown buzzes with cafés, art galleries and the occasional scent of jerk spice drifting from nearby stalls. It feels both lively and welcoming, a gateway to Jamaica’s culture and natural beauty.

kgs.name: Kingstown
kgs.text: Kingstown, the bustling capital of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, sits on a sheltered harbour on the island’s southwest coast, framed by lush hills and the sea’s turquoise edge. Founded by the French in the early 1720s and later taken by the British, the town retains a colonial charm with colourful wooden houses, a historic market and the impressive St George’s Anglican Cathedral. Today visitors wander the waterfront promenade, sip locally-grown coffee in cosy cafés, explore craft stalls selling jewellery and spices, and can easily set off for the island’s volcanic trails or nearby sailing spots, all within a friendly, relaxed atmosphere.

kha.name: Kashgar
kha.text: Kashgar, perched on the edge of the Taklamakan Desert in Xinjiang’s far west, sits at the crossroads of the historic Silk Road where Chinese, Central Asian and Middle Eastern cultures have mingled for centuries. The town’s ancient Id Kah Mosque, still in use today, testifies to its long-standing role as a Muslim trading hub. Modern visitors wander narrow, bustling bazaars packed with colourful carpets, spices and dried fruits, while the surrounding mountain passes offer stark desert vistas and the occasional glimpse of traditional Uyghur music drifting from tea houses. Despite rapid development, Kashgar retains a timeless, almost otherworldly atmosphere that feels like stepping back into a living caravan city.

khh.name: Kaohsiung
khh.text: Kaohsiung, Taiwan’s bustling southern port city, sits on the island’s southwest coast where the Love River meets the Taiwan Strait. Founded as a trading harbour in the Qing era, it grew dramatically after the Japanese opened the modern railway network in the early 20th century, cementing its role as a commercial hub. Today the city blends sleek skyscrapers such as the 85 metre-tall Landmark Tower with lively night markets, a thriving arts scene around the Pier-2 Creative Park, and easy access to scenic spots like Cijin Island and the nearby Lotus Pond, making it a vibrant place to explore.

khi.name: Karachi
khi.text: Karachi, Pakistan’s bustling coastal metropolis, sits on the Arabian Sea at the southern tip of the country, serving as the capital of Sindh province. Founded as a fishing village, it grew rapidly after the British established the Port of Karachi in the 19th century, becoming a key gateway for trade and the capital of Pakistan until 1960. Today the city offers a lively blend of historic sites such as the 19th-century Frere Hall, colourful markets like Empress Market, and a vibrant food scene famous for its street-side biryani and seafood. Visitors can explore the lively Clifton waterfront, soak up the cosmopolitan atmosphere, and enjoy warm, humid evenings beside the sea.

khk.name: Kharkiv
khk.text: Kharkiv lies in the north-eastern part of Ukraine, about 480 km east of Kyiv and close to the Russian border, nestled on the banks of the Lopan and Kharkiv rivers. Founded in the 17th century, it grew into a major centre of education and industry and was the first city in the country to host a university, the University of Kharkiv, opened in 1805. Today the city buzzes with a lively mix of wide avenues, leafy parks and bustling cafés; its impressive Soviet-era architecture sits alongside modern art galleries, while the vibrant student population gives Kharkiv a youthful, welcoming atmosphere for visitors.

khr.name: Khartoum
khr.text: Khartoum, the capital of Sudan, sits where the Blue and White Niles merge, creating a striking riverfront that defines the city’s layout. Founded in 1821 as a trading post under the Egyptian-Ottoman rule, it later became the seat of the Mahdist State before British-Egyptian administration took over in the late 19th century. Today visitors find a bustling mix of modern cafés, lively markets and wide avenues lined with palm-shaded parks; the National Museum offers a glimpse of ancient Nubian artefacts, while a short ferry ride across the Nile provides striking views of the city’s skyline and the historic confluence that has shaped its character for centuries.

khv.name: Khabarovsk
khv.text: Khabarovsk sits on the banks of the Amur River in Russia’s far-east, close to the border with China, and serves as the administrative centre of Khabarovsk Krai. Founded in 1858 as the fort of Khabarovka and later renamed after the 17th-century explorer Yerofey Khabarov, the city grew into a key trading and military hub on the trans-Siberian route. Today visitors find a lively riverfront promenade lined with cafés, the striking Khabarovsk Regional Museum, and a mix of Soviet-era architecture and modern parks; summer brings river cruises and outdoor festivals, while winter offers crisp air, snow-covered streets and cosy tea houses to warm up in.

kin.name: Kinshasa
kin.text: Kinshasa, the bustling capital of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, sits on the southern bank of the Congo River opposite Brazzaville, the capital of the Republic of the Congo. Founded in the late 19th century as a trading post called Léopoldville, it became the administrative centre of the Belgian Congo and was renamed Kinshasa after independence in 1960. Today the city teems with vibrant markets, lively music venues and riverfront promenades where you can watch ferries glide across the water; the mix of colonial architecture, modern skyscrapers and colourful street art gives visitors a vivid sense of its energetic, rapidly evolving character.

kis.name: Kisumu
kis.text: Kisumu sits on the eastern shore of Lake Victoria in western Kenya, roughly 350 km northwest of Nairobi and close to the borders of Uganda and Tanzania. Founded in the late 19th century as a railway depot, it grew into an important port for the lake’s steam-ship trade and was a key stop on the Uganda Railway. Today the city blends bustling markets, lively waterfront cafés and the vibrant Dunga Hill Camp arts scene; you can stroll along the lake promenade, sample fresh tilapia, and enjoy colourful sunsets over Africa’s largest lake while feeling the warm, relaxed pace of lakeside life.

kjd.name: Khujand
kjd.text: Khujand, Tajikistan’s fourth-largest city, sits on the northern edge of the Fergana Valley beside the Syr-Darya River, close to the borders with Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan. Founded as the ancient Persian settlement of Cyropolis, it became a key Silk Road hub and later a fortified stronghold of the Emirate of Bukhara. Today the town blends historic bazaars with Soviet-era architecture; you can wander past the towering Lenin statue, sample fresh fruit in the bustling market, and enjoy riverside cafés that offer views of the surrounding mountains, giving a relaxed yet vibrant feel to any visit.

kkb.name: Kota Kinabalu
kkb.text: Kota Kinabalu, the capital of Sabah on the north-west coast of Borneo, sits on a sheltered bay backed by the foothills of Mount Kinabalu and fringed with palm-lined beaches. The town was known as Jesselton during the British colonial era and was renamed Kota Kinabalu in 1968 after the nearby mountain. Today it feels relaxed yet vibrant: colourful night markets spill onto the streets, fresh seafood stalls line the waterfront, and easy boat trips launch from the harbour to explore nearby islands such as Manukan and the stunning coral reefs of Tunku Abdul Rahman Park.

kkn.name: Kankan
kkn.text: Kankan, Guinea’s second-largest city, lies in the eastern part of the country on the Milo River, a few hundred kilometres from the border with Mali. It was founded in the 1600s by Malinke traders and later grew into a vital stronghold for Samory Touré’s empire in the late 19th century, playing a key role in resistance to French colonisation. Today the town buzzes with lively markets where colourful fabrics, fresh produce and locally roasted peanuts are sold, while modest colonial-era buildings sit beside bustling cafés; the warm, welcoming atmosphere makes a short stop feel like a genuine glimpse of everyday life in Guinea.

kmg.name: Kunming
kmg.text: Kunming, the capital of Yunnan province in southwest China, sits at the edge of the fertile Yunnan-Guizhou Plateau, about 1,900 metres above sea level and surrounded by mountains and lakes. Historically it was a key stop on the ancient Tea Horse Road, the trade route that linked Chinese tea regions with Tibet and beyond. Today the city is known for its pleasant “spring-like” climate year-round, bustling markets where you can sample exotic fruits and spicy cuisine, and vibrant parks such as Green Lake, where locals practise tai-chi and the streets are lined with colourful tea houses and modern art galleries.

kmn.name: Kerman
kmn.text: Kerman, a sprawling city in south-central Iran, sits at the foot of the Zagros mountains about 1,600 km southeast of Tehran. It has long been a key stop on historic trade routes, famously serving as a caravan hub for the Silk Road and home to the 12th-century Jameh Mosque, one of the region’s oldest surviving religious sites. Today the city blends ancient charm with modern bustle: narrow bazaars spill colourful spices and pistachios, rooftop cafés offer views of the stark desert beyond, and the nearby Lut Desert, a UNESCO World Heritage site, draws adventurers seeking surreal, sun-scorched landscapes.

kmp.name: Kampala
kmp.text: Kampala, the bustling capital of Uganda, lies on the northern shore of Lake Victoria at the foot of several hills that give the city its rolling, leafy character. Founded in 1890 as a trading post for the British Uganda Protectorate, it became the administrative centre and later the nation’s capital after independence. Today the city teems with colour and energy: you can wander through vibrant markets selling fresh produce and crafts, sip coffee at rooftop cafés overlooking the skyline, and explore museums and parks that showcase Uganda’s rich cultural heritage amidst a friendly, cosmopolitan atmosphere.

kns.name: Kaunas
kns.text: Kaunas lies in the heart of Lithuania, where the Nemunas and Neris rivers meet, about 100 km west of the capital Vilnius. First mentioned in 1361, the city later became the temporary capital of Lithuania during the interwar years, a period that left a rich mix of Art Deco and modernist architecture. Today Kaunas feels vibrant and relaxed: its historic Old Town is easy to wander, the lively riverside cafés spill onto cobbled streets, and cultural hubs such as the M. K. Čiurlionis National Museum showcase music, art and history. Visitors enjoy a blend of lively student energy, green parks and a welcoming, laid-back atmosphere.

kpg.name: Kupang
kpg.text: Kupang, the capital of Indonesia’s East Nusa Tenggara province, sits on the western tip of Timor Island where the Timor and Savu seas meet. In the colonial era it served as a Dutch administrative outpost and a key stop for ships travelling between Europe and the East Indies. Today the town buzzes with a lively waterfront promenade, colourful markets selling fresh fish and woven crafts, and well-preserved Dutch-era buildings that overlook a busy harbour. From Kupang you can catch ferries to the famous islands of Komodo and Rinca, making it a handy and pleasant base for exploring this rugged part of Indonesia.

krk.name: Krakow
krk.text: Krakow lies in southern Poland, on the banks of the Vistula River, about 300 km west of the Ukrainian border and roughly 250 km south-east of Warsaw. Founded in the early medieval period, it served as the capital of the Polish kingdom until the late 16th century and was the coronation site for many Polish kings, a tradition that links the city to its historic Wawel Castle. Today the Old Town dazzles with its beautifully restored market square, countless cafés and lively street musicians, while the surrounding museums, vibrant nightlife and nearby salt mines make a visit feel both richly cultural and effortlessly modern.

krr.name: Krasnoyarsk
krr.text: Krasnoyarsk sits on the banks of the mighty Yenisei River in the heart of Siberia, framed by the rugged Sayan Mountains to the south and the vast taiga to the north. The town began as a Russian fort in 1628, guarding the eastern frontier and later developing into a key trading post on the Siberian route. Today visitors find a lively riverfront promenade, impressive Soviet-era architecture, and easy access to the striking Stolby Nature Reserve, where towering granite pillars rise from the forest. The city’s modern cafés, museums and the massive Krasnoyarsk Dam make it a fascinating blend of history and contemporary Siberian life.

ktm.name: Kathmandu
ktm.text: Kathmandu, the bustling capital of Nepal, lies in a valley surrounded by the foothills of the Himalayas, about 1,400 metres above sea level. It has been a centre of trade and culture for centuries, and the city’s Durbar Square still displays the splendid Newar architecture that dates back to the medieval Malla dynasty. Today visitors find a lively mix of ancient temples, colourful markets and modern cafés, with the scent of incense drifting from prayer flags and the hum of traffic sharing the narrow streets. The friendly locals are happy to share stories over a cup of steaming masala tea, making Kathmandu feel both historic and warmly contemporary.

kuf.name: Samara
kuf.text: Samara, Russia, sits on the right bank of the Volga River where it meets the Samara River, about 900 km southeast of Moscow. Founded in the late 16th century, the city grew into a key ship-building centre and later became an important industrial hub during the Soviet era. Today it feels spacious and modern, with wide boulevards lined by leafy parks and striking Soviet-era architecture alongside trendy cafés and riverfront promenades. Visitors can stroll along the embankment for panoramic views of the Volga, explore the lively waterfront market, and enjoy the blend of historic museums and vibrant cultural life that gives Samara its friendly, contemporary vibe.

kul.name: Kuala Lumpur
kul.text: Kuala Lumpur, the bustling capital of Malaysia, sits in the central western part of the peninsula, nestled between the Klang and Gombak rivers. Founded in the mid-19th century as a tin-mining settlement, it quickly grew into a vibrant trading hub and was declared the federal capital in 1957. Today the city dazzles visitors with its striking skyline, where the iconic Petronas Twin Towers loom above a maze of modern malls, street-food stalls and colonial-era shophouses. Efficient public transport, a multicultural atmosphere and a lively night market scene make exploring Kuala Lumpur a lively, unforgettable experience.

kum.name: Kumasi
kum.text: Kumasi, the bustling capital of Ghana’s Ashanti Region, lies in the south-central part of the country about 250 km north of the coast. Historically it was the seat of the powerful Ashanti Kingdom and home to the famous Golden Stool, the symbol of Ashanti sovereignty. Today the city blends tradition and modernity: you can wander through lively markets such as the Kejetia Trading Centre, the largest open-air market in West Africa, explore the tranquil grounds of the Manhyia Palace Museum, and savour street food while hearing the rhythmic beats of highlife music drifting from nearby bars. The friendly locals and rich heritage make Kumasi a warm, vibrant stop for any traveller.

kut.name: Kutaisi
kut.text: Kutaisi, nestled on the banks of the Rioni River in western Georgia, is the historic capital of the Imereti region and one of the country’s oldest settlements. It once served as a royal seat in the medieval Kingdom of Georgia and is famed for the 12th-century Bagrati Cathedral and the nearby Gelati Monastery, both UNESCO World Heritage sites. Today the city buzzes with lively markets, cosy coffee houses and vibrant street art, while easy bus routes whisk visitors to striking natural attractions such as the Sataplia and Prometheus caves, making Kutaisi a charming blend of history and modern Georgian hospitality.

kwi.name: Kuwait City
kwi.text: Kuwait City, the capital of the small Gulf nation of Kuwait, lies on the north-eastern tip of the Arabian Peninsula, hugging the Persian Gulf coast. Founded in the early 18th century, the city grew around a modest fishing village and later became a major trading port under the Al-Sabah dynasty, with the original fort of Kuwait—Al Kout—still standing as a reminder of its maritime heritage. Today the skyline mixes sleek glass towers with traditional souks; visitors can wander the bustling market of Souk Al Juma, admire the modern art at the Kuwait National Museum, and relax along the palm-lined Corniche, where the sea breeze softens the desert heat.

kyi.name: Kyiv
kyi.text: Kyiv, the capital of Ukraine, sits on the banks of the Dnieper River in the north-central part of the country, surrounded by gently rolling hills and lush forested parks. First mentioned in the 5th-century chronicles of the East Slavic state of Kievan Rus’, the city grew around the iconic Saint Sophia’s Cathedral and the golden-domed Motherland Monument that watches over the skyline. Today Kyiv blends its grand historic architecture with a vibrant café culture, lively markets and bustling riverfront promenades, making it a friendly place to wander, sample hearty Ukrainian dishes and enjoy a lively arts scene.

kyr.name: Kyrenia
kyr.text: Kyrenia, perched on the north-eastern coast of Cyprus, looks out over the sparkling Mediterranean and is framed by the dramatic cliffs of the Kyrenia Range. The town’s most iconic landmark is the 16th-century Venetian harbour fort, built by the Republic of Venice to protect its maritime trade routes. Today the harbour is a lively promenade of pastel-coloured cafés, boutique shops and yachting clubs, while the historic old town winds up narrow cobblestone lanes lined with Ottoman houses and fragrant lemon trees. Visitors can stroll along the waterfront, enjoy fresh seafood on the sea-front terraces, and feel the blend of ancient history and relaxed seaside charm that makes Kyrenia a favourite stop for travellers.

kzn.name: Kazan
kzn.text: Kazan, the capital of the Republic of Tatarstan in western Russia, sits where the Volga and Kazanka rivers meet, about 800 km east of Moscow. It was the site of the 1552 siege when Ivan the Terrible captured the Kazan Kremlin, marking the town’s incorporation into the Russian state. Today the city blends the old and the new: the beautifully restored Kazan Kremlin, a UNESCO World Heritage site, stands beside sleek glass towers, bustling cafés and a lively university atmosphere. Visitors can wander historic streets, sample Tatar cuisine such as echpochmak, and enjoy riverfront parks that buzz with locals and tourists alike.

lae.name: Lae
lae.text: Lae, perched on the coastal plain where the Markham River meets the Bismarck Sea, is the bustling capital of Papua New Guinea’s Morobe Province and the country’s second-largest city. Founded in the 1920s as a colonial administrative centre, it grew rapidly during World War II when Allied forces used it as a major supply base after the 1943 liberation. Today the town hums with a lively mix of market stalls, motorbike traffic and cafés spilling onto the streets, while nearby waterfalls and the scenic highlands offer easy day-trip escapes for curious travellers.

lag.name: Lagos
lag.text: Lagos, Nigeria, sits on the southwestern coast where the Atlantic Ocean meets the Niger River delta, spreading over islands and mainland. Founded in the 15th century by Yoruba settlers, it became a major trading hub under Portuguese influence before later serving as the capital of the British colony of Nigeria until 1991. Today the city bustles with colourful markets, vibrant music venues and a lively waterfront promenade; you can explore the historic National Museum, sample fresh seafood at the fish market, and soak up the energetic rhythm of street art and Afrobeat that fills the streets from dawn till dusk.

las.name: Las Vegas
las.text: Las Vegas, nestled in the arid desert of southern Nevada, sits about 270 miles west of Salt Lake City and 30 miles east of the Colorado River. The town sprang up in 1905 when a railway line was built through the area, and it transformed dramatically after Nevada legalised gambling in 1931, turning the fledgling settlement into a playground for risk-takers and entertainers. Today the city is famous for its dazzling Strip of neon-lit casinos, world-class shows and bustling nightlife, while just a short drive away the impressive Hoover Dam offers a striking contrast of natural desert beauty and engineering marvel.

lax.name: Los Angeles
lax.text: Los Angeles, perched on the southern coast of California between the Pacific Ocean and the San Gabriel Mountains, is a sprawling city of sunshine and contrast. Founded in 1781 as a small Spanish pueblo, it grew into the epicentre of the American film industry, earning the nickname “Hollywood” for its world-famous studios. Today visitors wander from the glitter of the Hollywood Walk of Fame to the breezy promenades of Santa Monica Pier, explore the multicultural flavours of Koreatown and Little Ethiopia, and hike the rugged trails of Griffith Park for panoramic city views; all amidst a lively mix of art, cuisine and endless summer weather.

lbs.name: Lubumbashi
lbs.text: Lubumbashi, the second-largest city in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, sits on the southeastern plateau near the border with Zambia, at the foot of the Katanga copper belt. Founded in the early 20th century as a mining outpost, it grew rapidly after the discovery of vast copper deposits that made the region one of the world’s major mineral producers. Today the city blends colonial-era architecture with bustling markets, lively cafés and a growing arts scene; visitors can stroll along its tree-lined avenues, sample hearty Congolese cuisine, and feel the vibrant energy of a place that is both a commercial hub and a gateway to the country’s mineral heartland.

lbv.name: Libreville
lbv.text: Libreville, the capital of Gabon, sits on the Atlantic coast at the mouth of the Komo River in central West Africa. It began in 1849 as a settlement for freed slaves returning from Brazil, giving the town its name – “free city” – and grew into the country’s main port. Today the city blends modern high-rise offices with colourful markets where vendors sell fresh fish, tropical fruit and woven crafts. The waterfront promenade offers views of palm-lined beaches and the occasional sailboat, while cafés serve Congolese-style coffee and the nightlife buzzes around the lively neighbourhoods of the former French quarter.

lda.name: Luanda
lda.text: Luanda, the bustling capital of Angola, sits on a sweeping bay of the Atlantic Ocean at the mouth of the Cuanza River. Founded by the Portuguese in 1575, the city grew around a fortified harbour that later became a key point in the trans-Atlantic slave trade before evolving into a modern oil-driven economy. Today visitors find a lively mix of sleek skyscrapers and colourful colonial architecture, lively fish markets where the day's catch is grilled on the spot, and a vibrant nightlife along the waterfront promenade, all set against warm, tropical breezes.

lhe.name: Lahore
lhe.text: Lahore, the bustling capital of Pakistan’s Punjab province, sits on the banks of the River Ravi in the country’s northeast, roughly 300 km east of Islamabad. It was the historic seat of the Mughal Empire, where Emperor Akbar commissioned the magnificent Lahore Fort in the 16th century, a UNESCO World Heritage site that still dominates the skyline. Today the city is a lively blend of old and new: you can wander through fragrant bazaars selling colourful textiles, sample world-famous street food such as spicy naan and kebabs, and then relax in leafy parks or sip chai beside sleek, modern cafés, all while the echo of centuries-old minarets watches over the vibrant streets.

lhv.name: Le Havre
lhv.text: Le Havre sits on the northern coast of Normandy, at the mouth of the Seine where it meets the English Channel, about 200 km west of Paris. The town was founded in 1517 by King Henri IV to create a new port for France, and its harbour later became one of the country’s busiest. Much of the city was rebuilt after heavy bombing in World War II, and the post-war architecture designed by Auguste Perret earned UNESCO World Heritage status in 2005. Today you’ll find a lively waterfront, wide sandy beaches, modern art museums and a bustling fishing market, all set against striking concrete façades and a vibrant maritime atmosphere.

lhw.name: Lanzhou
lhw.text: Lanzhou, the capital of Gansu Province in north-western China, sits on the banks of the mighty Yellow River where the Loess Plateau meets the desert fringe. Founded over two thousand years ago, it became a key hub on the ancient Silk Road, linking Chinese heartlands with Central Asia. Today the city blends modern high-rise towers with bustling night markets; you can sip freshly-made Lanzhou beef noodle soup beside the river promenade, explore the colourful Zhongshan Bridge, or take a short bus ride to the striking Bingling Grottoes perched on the cliffs of the nearby Liujiaxia Reservoir. The mix of history, culture and striking scenery makes a visit both lively and memorable.

lil.name: Lille
lil.text: Lille sits in the far north of France, just a short train ride from the Belgian border and a stone’s throw from the coast of the North Sea. Founded as a Roman settlement, it later became the capital of French Flanders and was a key stronghold during the Wars of Religion, when the city’s famous citadel was constructed by Vauban in the 17th century. Today Lille buzzes with a lively mix of historic cobbled streets, sleek modern boutiques and bustling markets; its cafés spill onto the Grand Place, and the vibrant cultural scene – from museums to street art – makes wandering its neighbourhoods a delight for any traveller.

lim.name: Limon
lim.text: Limon, perched on Costa Rica’s Caribbean coast, is the bustling capital of the province that bears its name and the country’s main gateway to the Atlantic seaboard. Founded in the 1760s, the town grew into a vital banana-export hub in the early 20th century, shaping the region’s economy and culture. In 1991 a powerful earthquake badly damaged the centre, prompting a modern reconstruction that now blends colourful colonial façades with fresh, low-rise buildings. Today visitors enjoy a laid-back rhythm, lively Afro-Caribbean music, fragrant street food stalls selling arroz con pollo and plantains, and easy access to nearby rainforests, beaches and the famous Tortuguero National Park.

lis.name: Lisbon
lis.text: Lisbon, Portugal’s capital, sits on the western edge of the country where the Tagus River meets the Atlantic Ocean. Founded by the Romans and later rebuilt after the great 1755 earthquake, the city retains a mix of historic narrow streets, colourful tiled façades and grand plazas. Today visitors can wander the hilly neighbourhoods of Alfama and Bairro Alto, enjoy sweeping river views from the São Jorge Castle, and savour fresh seafood in bustling markets, while trams clatter up steep streets and cafés spill onto sun-lit squares, giving the city a lively yet relaxed vibe.

liv.name: Liverpool
liv.text: Liverpool sits on the western edge of the Mersey Estuary in north-west England, its waterfront stretching along the River Mersey. Historically it grew into a major global port in the 18th and 19th centuries, famously serving as the gateway for many emigrants to the New World and for the trans-Atlantic trade that shaped the city’s wealth. Today the city buzzes with music, sport and culture: you can wander the historic Albert Dock, admire the impressive waterfront UNESCO World Heritage sites, enjoy lively pubs and cafés, and catch the vibrant street art and festivals that give Liverpool its warm, welcoming character.

ljb.name: Ljubljana
ljb.text: Ljubljana, the capital of Slovenia, sits in the centre of the country where the Ljubljanica River winds through a compact, tree-lined old town. First mentioned in written sources in the 13th century, it grew around a medieval castle that still crowns the hill above the city centre. Today the streets are a lively blend of pastel façades, bustling cafés and pedestrian zones, and the riverbanks are perfect for a relaxed stroll or a coffee on a sunny terrace. With its mix of historic charm, green spaces and a vibrant cultural scene, Ljubljana feels both intimate and cosmopolitan.

lko.name: Lucknow
lko.text: Lucknow, the capital city of Uttar Pra Pradesh in northern India, rests on the banks of the gently flowing Gomti River and lies about 500 kilometres east of New Delhi. Historically it was the centre of the 1857 Indian Rebellion and later became renowned for its Nawabi culture, evident in the elegant architecture of the Bara Imambara and the bustling markets of Aminabad. Today, visitors find a lively mix of old and new: colonial-era streets lined with chic cafés, fragrant street-food stalls serving kebabs and biryani, and tranquil gardens where you can watch locals go about their day against a backdrop of grand monuments and modern malls.

lln.name: Lilongwe
lln.text: Lilongwe, the bustling capital of Malawi, sits in the central plateau of the country where the Lilongwe River meets the expansive, gently rolling landscape of the Central Region. Established as a colonial administrative centre in the early 1900s, it became the official capital after independence, replacing Zomba in 1975. Today the city offers a relaxed yet lively atmosphere: modern cafés line the colourful streets of the Old Town, the bustling Saturday market overflows with fresh produce and crafts, and the nearby Lilongwe Wildlife Centre provides close encounters with rescued native animals. Visitors enjoy a blend of Malawian hospitality, urban growth, and easy access to surrounding wildlife reserves.

lma.name: Lima
lma.text: Lima, the bustling capital of Peru, lies on the central western coast where the desert meets the Pacific Ocean, its skyline framed by the towering Andes to the east. Founded by Spanish conquistador Francisco Pizarro in 1535, the city became the centre of the Viceroyalty of Peru and retains a rich colonial heritage evident in the stone façades of its historic centre, a UNESCO World Heritage site. Today Lima teems with contrast: colourful neighbourhoods such as Barranco offer bohemian cafés and street art, while sleek skyscrapers house modern offices, and the nearby cliffs provide spectacular sunset views over the sea.

lms.name: Limassol
lms.text: Limassol is a bustling seaside city on the southern coast of Cyprus, nestled between the Troodos mountains and the Mediterranean. Founded by the Romans in the 1st century AD, it later became an important medieval port and the site where King Richard the Lion-heart is said to have married Queen Berengaria in 1191. Today the city blends old and new: palm-lined promenades, lively cafés and a vibrant nightlife sit alongside the historic Limassol Castle and a lively waterfront market, making it a warm, welcoming spot for explorers who enjoy both culture and sunshine.

lom.name: Lome
lom.text: Lomé, the bustling capital of Togo, sits on the Atlantic coast at the country’s southern tip, nestled between Ghana and Benin. Founded in the late 19th century as a modest fishing settlement, it grew rapidly after becoming the administrative centre of French Togoland in 1914, a role that still shapes its colonial-era architecture. Today the city is a lively mix of colourful markets, palm-fringed boulevards and lively cafés where you can savour grilled fish, sample vibrant fabrics and watch traffic hum along the waterfront, all under a warm, sunny sky.

lon.name: London
lon.text: London, the capital of the United Kingdom, sits on the River Thames in southeastern England, straddling both banks of the waterway. Founded by the Romans as Londinium around AD 43, the city grew into a bustling medieval port and later the heart of the British Empire. Today, London feels like a vibrant mosaic of history and modernity: you can stand beneath the towering glass of the Shard, wander the historic cobbles of Covent Garden, and hear the chime of Big Ben while sipping a coffee in a bustling café. Museums, parks, theatres and diverse neighbourhoods make every visit feel fresh and exciting.

lpb.name: La Paz
lpb.text: La Paz, Bolivia’s high-altitude capital, lies in a bowl surrounded by the snow-capped Andes at about 3 600 metres above sea level, making it one of the world’s highest major cities. Founded in 1548 as a modest colonial outpost, it grew into a centre of silver mining and later became the seat of the Republic after independence. Today the city bustles with colourful markets, cable-car lifts that glide over steep streets, and a mix of historic churches and modern cafés, offering visitors striking mountain views, vibrant street life and a warm, welcoming atmosphere.

lpg.name: Las Palmas
lpg.text: Las Palmas de Gran Canaria lies on the north-eastern coast of the island of Gran Canaria in the Canary archipelago, off the coast of north-western Africa but politically part of Spain. Founded in the late 15th century, it grew into a key port for trade between Europe, the Americas and West Africa, and its historic quarter, Vegueta, still displays the 1492 Casa de Colón where Christopher Columbus is believed to have stayed. Today the city mixes bustling waterfront promenades, golden beaches and lively tapas bars with a relaxed, Mediterranean ambience, making it a pleasant base for exploring volcanic landscapes, cultural museums and vibrant nightlife.

lpq.name: Luang Prabang
lpq.text: Luang Prabang sits on the banks of the Mekong River in northern Laos, cradled by lush mountains and a network of smaller streams. Founded as a royal capital in the 14th century, it became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1995 because of its well-preserved blend of traditional Lao wooden houses and French colonial architecture. Today the town feels relaxed and colourful: monks in saffron robes collect alms at sunrise, night markets bustle with handicrafts, and river-front cafés serve fragrant Lao coffee while the ancient temples and French villas provide a charming backdrop for wandering walkers.

lrt.name: Lorient
lrt.text: Lorient, a bustling port town in the far-west of Brittany, lies on the mouth of the river Blavet where it meets the Atlantic. It began as a base for the French East India Company in the 17th century and grew into a major shipbuilding centre, later suffering extensive damage during the Allied bombings of 1943. Today the town is lively and maritime-spirit-filled, with a charming waterfront promenade, the impressive Cité de la Voile sailing museum, and a calendar of festivals that celebrate its seafaring heritage and Breton culture.

lrw.name: Lerwick
lrw.text: Lerwick, the capital of the Shetland Islands, sits on the east coast of Mainland, the largest of the archipelago, and looks out across the North Sea towards Norway. It grew from a modest fishing settlement into an important trading hub in the 17th century, when the Dutch and Scottish merchants established regular commerce that still echoes in its historic harbor. Today the town feels both lively and relaxed: colourful harbourside cafés serve fresh seafood, the narrow streets are lined with stone cottages and museums, and the surrounding cliffs and beaches invite gentle walks while seabirds wheel overhead, offering a uniquely northern charm.

lsk.name: Lusaka
lsk.text: Lusaka, the bustling capital of Zambia, sits in the south-central part of the country on a plateau about 1,300 metres above sea level. Founded in 1905 as a modest railway depot, it became the capital of the British protectorate of Northern Rhodesia in 1911 and later of independent Zambia in 1964. Today the city blends modern skyscrapers with colourful markets, and a walk through the lively downtown reveals street food stalls, the National Museum’s exhibits on Zambian heritage, and the leafy expanse of the Lusaka National Park on the city’s edge, offering a warm, welcoming atmosphere for visitors.

ltk.name: Latakia
ltk.text: Latakia, a bustling coastal city on Syria’s western shoreline, sits on the eastern shore of the Mediterranean Sea just north of the Syrian-Turkish border. Founded in the Hellenistic period as a Seleucid port, it later became an important Roman harbour known as Laodicea ad Mare. Today the city blends its historic charm with a lively promenade, fresh-sea-food restaurants and colourful markets where locals sell citrus and spices; the nearby beaches are popular for swimming and sunset walks, while the old town’s stone alleys and the 12th-century Crusader-era mosque give visitors a taste of its layered past.

lux.name: Luxembourg
lux.text: Luxembourg City lies in the heart of the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg, perched on a rocky outcrop where the Alzette and Pétrusse rivers meet, just a short train ride from Belgium, France and Germany. Founded in the early 10th century, it became a crucial fortification for the Holy Roman Empire and later earned the nickname “Gibraltar of the North” because of its formidable defenses. Today the capital blends cobbled old quarters, such as the UNESCO-listed Grund and the elegant Casemates du Bock, with sleek modern architecture, lively cafés and a bustling mix of cultures, making it a charming base for exploring both history and contemporary European life.

lvg.name: Livingstone
lvg.text: Livingstone sits on the north-western edge of Zambia, right on the banks of the mighty Zambezi River and just a short drive from the spectacular Victoria Falls, one of the world’s largest waterfalls. The town was founded in 1905 and named after the famed explorer David Livingstone, whose grave lies a few kilometres downstream at the Old Drift. Today, Livingstone is a lively hub for tourists: the streets buzz with markets selling handmade crafts, riverside cafés offer views of the river’s mist, and a range of lodges and activity operators make it easy to experience safaris, white-water rafting and sunset cruises on the Zambezi.

lvv.name: Lviv
lvv.text: Lviv, in western Ukraine, sits on the gentle hills near the Polish border, a crossroads of Central and Eastern Europe. Founded in the mid-13th century, the city flourished as a major centre of trade and culture under the Kingdom of Poland, and its historic centre is now a UNESCO World Heritage site. Today Lviv feels like a lively open-air museum: cobbled streets are lined with ornate baroque and art-nouveau facades, cosy cafés serve strong coffee and pastries, and the air hums with music festivals, street performers and the warm chatter of locals and visitors alike.

lxa.name: Lhasa
lxa.text: Lhasa, perched on the Tibetan plateau at around 3,650 metres, is the capital of the autonomous region of Tibet in western China. The city has been the spiritual heart of Tibetan Buddhism for centuries, centred on the Potala Palace which was the winter residence of the Dalai Lamas from the 17th century until the 1950s. Today visitors find a blend of ancient charm and modern development: narrow, prayer-filled lanes lead to bustling markets selling yak butter tea and hand-woven scarves, while wide boulevards showcase sleek hotels and cafés. The thin, crisp air and the ever-present scent of incense give Lhasa a uniquely serene yet lively atmosphere.

lxr.name: Luxor
lxr.text: Luxor, perched on the east bank of the Nile in southern Egypt, is the modern name for the ancient city of Thebes, once the capital of the New Kingdom and home to the grand temples of Karnak and Luxor. It boasts the world-famous Valley of the Kings across the river, where pharaohs such as Tutankhamun were laid to rest. Today the town hums with a lively mix of bustling souks, rooftop cafés and river ferries, while the stone monuments glow in the desert light, offering visitors a striking blend of ancient wonder and contemporary Egyptian hospitality.

lyo.name: Lyon
lyo.text: Lyon, nestled at the confluence of the Rhône and Saône rivers in east-central France, is the country’s third-largest city and a historic crossroads of trade. Founded by the Romans as Lugdunum in 43 BC, it later became a key centre of the silk industry in the 19th century, a heritage still visible in its traboules—hidden passageways linking the old neighbourhoods. Today the city buzzes with a vibrant culinary scene, from bustling bouchons serving traditional Lyonnaise dishes to Michelin-starred restaurants, while its UNESCO-listed old town offers cobbled streets, Renaissance architecture and stunning views from the hilltop Basilica of Notre-Dam de Fourvière.

maa.name: Chennai
maa.text: Chennai, the bustling capital of Tamil Nadu on India’s southeastern coast, lies on the Bay of Bengal just north of the historic port of Madras. Founded by the British East India Company in 1639, the city grew around Fort St George, which still stands as a well-preserved reminder of its colonial past. Today, Chennai offers a lively mix of tradition and modernity: you can wander the vibrant Marina Beach, explore colourful temples such as Kapaleeshwarar, savour fragrant South Indian cuisine in bustling markets, and enjoy a thriving arts scene with music, dance and contemporary galleries, all set against a warm, humid climate.

mad.name: Madrid
mad.text: Madrid, the vibrant capital of Spain, sits in the heart of the Iberian Peninsula on the Manzanares River, surrounded by the rolling Castilian plains. Founded as a modest fortress in the ninth-century, it became the royal seat when King Philip II moved his court there in 1561, establishing the city as the centre of the Spanish Empire. Today the city buzzes with a mix of historic grandeur and modern energy: you can stroll through the leafy Retiro Park, admire world-class art in the Prado, savour tapas in lively plazas, and feel the warm, cosmopolitan rhythm that makes Madrid a favourite stop for travellers.

maj.name: Majuro
maj.text: Majuro, the capital of the Marshall Islands, sits on a narrow atoll of coral islands stretching about 40 km across the central Pacific, just north of the equator and roughly 2 500 km east of the Philippines. It became the administrative centre of the United Nations-mandated Trust Territory after World War II, when the United States established a significant naval base there. Today the town is a laid-back gateway to crystal-clear lagoons and colourful reefs, with simple wooden shops, a bustling fish market and friendly locals offering fresh seafood and a glimpse of island life amidst gently swaying palm trees.

mal.name: Malmo
mal.text: Malmö sits on Sweden’s southern tip, directly across the Øresund Strait from Copenhagen, and is linked to Denmark by the iconic Øresund Bridge. Founded in the 13th century, the city grew around a medieval market town and later became an important hub for shipbuilding and trade, notably producing the world-renowned Malmö Castle in the 16th century. Today Malmö feels refreshingly cosmopolitan: its compact centre is dotted with leafy parks, sleek modern apartments, and a lively waterfront promenade where you can sample Swedish-French cuisine, browse independent boutiques, and soak up a vibrant cultural scene that blends historic charm with contemporary design.

man.name: Manchester
man.text: Manchester, nestled in the north-west of England on the River Irwell, grew from a modest medieval market town into a powerhouse of the Industrial Revolution, famously pioneering cotton spinning and railway engineering in the 19th century. Today the city buzzes with a vibrant mix of culture and sport: you can explore world-class museums such as the Science and Industry Museum, savour street food in the bustling Curry Mile, and feel the electric atmosphere of a match at the iconic Old Trafford. Its leafy canals, modern architecture and lively music scene make Manchester a friendly, energetic stop for any traveller.

mao.name: Manaus
mao.text: Manaus, the vibrant gateway to the Amazon, sits at the confluence of the Rio Negro and the Rio Solimões in north-western Brazil. Founded in the 17th century as a modest Portuguese trading post, it boomed in the late 19th century during the rubber boom, when fortunes were made and grand theatres and mansions sprang up along its riverfront. Today the city blends modern bustle with jungle mystery: colourful market stalls sell exotic fruit, river tours whisk you past towering kapok trees, and the famed Amazon Theatre hosts concerts beneath its ornate façade, while the surrounding rainforest offers unforgettable wildlife excursions just a short boat ride away.

mar.name: Marseille
mar.text: Marseille, perched on the southeastern coast of France where the Mediterranean meets the Rhône-Alpes region, is France’s oldest city, founded by Greek sailors from Phocaea around 600 BC. Its historic Vieux-Port still bustles with fishing boats and cafés, while the striking basilica of Notre-Dame de la Garde watches over the harbor from its hilltop perch. Today the city mixes vibrant street art, lively markets selling olives and bouillabaisse, and a lively waterfront promenade that leads to modern museums and sandy beaches. The blend of ancient stone streets, multicultural flavours and stunning sea views makes a visit feel both timeless and refreshingly contemporary.

mau.name: Maun
mau.text: Maun, situated on the banks of the Thamalakane River in north-west Botswana, is the principal gateway to the Okavango Delta and a short drive from the sprawling Makgadikgadi salt pans. The town began as a modest settlement in the early 20th century, serving as a trading post and later a colonial administrative centre before evolving into a tourism hub. Today, Maun hums with colourful market stalls, river-front cafés and a bustling airstrip that dispatches mokoro-sailing trips and game-viewing safaris into the delta’s winding waterways, offering a warm, laid-back base for adventurers.

mba.name: Mombasa
mba.text: Mombasa, Kenya’s second-largest city, sits on a low-lying peninsula jutting into the Indian Ocean on the country’s southeast coast, just a short distance north of the equator. The town grew around the historic Swahili trading settlements and was fortified by the Portuguese in 1593 when they built Fort Jesus, a UNESCO World Heritage site that still dominates the waterfront. Today visitors can wander the narrow lanes of Old Town with its Arab-influenced architecture, relax on white-sand beaches such as Diani and Nyali, enjoy fresh seafood in bustling markets, and take boat trips to the nearby marine park, where colourful coral reefs teem with life.

mbe.name: Mbabane
mbe.text: Mbabane, the capital of Eswatini, sits high in the Mdimba Mountains of the country’s western region, at an altitude of around 1,200 metres, giving it a cool, mist-laden climate. The town grew from a modest trading post established in the late 19th century and became the administrative centre when the British Protectorate moved its capital from Manzini in the 1960s. Today Mbabane blends colonial-era architecture with colourful market stalls, and visitors can wander its leafy streets, sample traditional Swazi dishes at bustling eateries, and enjoy sweeping views of the surrounding valleys from nearby hillsides.

mbm.name: Mbuji-Mayi
mbm.text: Mbuji-Mayi sits in the heart of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, about 300 km south-east of Kananga, on the banks of the Luilu River and surrounded by the rugged hills of the Kasai region. Historically it grew from a modest mining settlement into the centre of the world’s largest known kimberlite pipe, making it a crucial hub for diamond extraction since the mid-20th century. Today the city bustles with colourful markets where traders display locally-cut diamonds alongside fresh produce, while the streets pulse with the sounds of soukous music; visitors can explore lively cafés, sample Congolese cuisine, and feel the warm hospitality of a community proud of its rich cultural heritage.

mcb.name: Maracaibo
mcb.text: Maracaibo is a bustling city in northwestern Venezuela, perched on the western shore of Lake Maracaibo and framed by the Sierra de Perijá mountains. Founded in 1529, it became an early centre of the Spanish colonial oil trade, and its historic Plaza Bolívar still bears the name of the liberator who visited the town. Today visitors find a lively mix of modern skyscrapers and colourful colonial buildings, bustling markets selling fresh fish and arepas, and the famous “Cerro de la Cruz” viewpoint that offers sweeping sunsets over the lake. The warm, humid climate and friendly locals make it a vibrant gateway to the region’s natural and cultural attractions.

mci.name: Kansas City
mci.text: Kansas City, straddling the border between Missouri and Kansas in the American Midwest, sits on the confluence of the Missouri and Kansas rivers. Founded in the early 19th century, the city grew around the historic Santa Fe Trail, which made it a key gateway for westward expansion. Today visitors enjoy a vibrant mix of jazz clubs, world-class barbecue joints and impressive art installations such as the towering “Lion” sculpture in the downtown plaza. The River Market district offers bustling farmers’ markets and historic warehouses converted into cafés, while the nearby Country Club Plaza delights shoppers with its Spanish-style architecture and lively street ambience.

mco.name: Orlando
mco.text: Orlando lies in the heart of central Florida, roughly midway between the Atlantic coast and the Gulf of Mexico and about an hour’s drive north of the bustling city of Tampa. Founded in the late 19th century, the town grew around the citrus industry and was officially incorporated in 1875; its name honours a soldier who fought in the Second Seminole War. Today the city is synonymous with world-class theme parks such as Walt Disney World and Universal Studios, but it also offers vibrant dining precincts, leafy lakeside parks and a lively arts scene, making it a colourful and welcoming destination for visitors of all ages.

mdan.name: Medan
mdan.text: Medan, the bustling capital of North Sumatra, lies on the island’s northeastern plain, flanked by the lush Bukit Lawang hills and the coast of the Strait of Malacca. Founded in the late 19th century as a key outpost of the Dutch East Indies, the city grew around the historic Great Mosque of Medan, completed in 1906, which still dominates the skyline. Today Medan offers a vibrant mix of colonial architecture, bustling markets brimming with spices and coffee, and easy access to nearby attractions such as the volcanic lake of Toba, making it a lively gateway for curious travellers.

mde.name: Medellin
mde.text: Medellín sits in a lush valley in the Andes of north-west Colombia, about 150 km south of the Caribbean coast and surrounded by towering mountains that give the city its nickname, the “City of Eternal Spring.” Founded in 1616, it later became the centre of a famous flower-growing region and, in the mid-20th century, was the stronghold of notorious drug cartels before undergoing a remarkable urban transformation. Today visitors find a vibrant mix of modern tramways, colourful street art, bustling markets and excellent coffee shops, all set against a backdrop of verdant hills and a pleasantly mild climate.

mdn.name: Medina
mdn.text: Medina, in the western part of Saudi Arabia, sits about 340 km north-east of Mecca on the fertile plain of the Hejaz. It is revered as the city of the Prophet Muhammad, whose mosque—the Prophet’s Mosque—has been a centre of Islamic worship since the 7th century and was expanded many times over the centuries. Today the city blends the sacred and the modern: the vast courtyard of the mosque welcomes millions of pilgrims, while quiet side streets offer traditional markets, palm-groved parks and cafés where visitors can sample local dates and coffee, all under a backdrop of gently rolling desert hills.

mdy.name: Mandalay
mdy.text: Mandalay, the former royal capital of Myanmar, sits on the east bank of the Irrawaddy River about 70 kilometres north of the bustling city of Yangon. Founded in 1857 by King Mindon, it was the last seat of the Burmese monarchy before the British annexation in 1885, and its grand palace ruins still dominate the skyline. Today the city blends history with modern life: monks in saffron robes glide past bustling markets, the golden shimmer of Shwedagon Pagoda’s distant spire is visible on clear days, and visitors can wander the teak-wood streets, sample fragrant tea leaves and watch sunset over the river’s tranquil waters.

mdz.name: Mendoza
mdz.text: Mendoza, nestled on the eastern side of the Andes in western Argentina, sits at the foothills of the towering mountain range and is framed by the sparkling waters of the Tunuyán River. Founded in 1561 by Spanish colonists, the city grew into the heart of the country’s wine country, renowned for its Malbec vineyards that spread across sun-baked valleys. Today visitors wander through spacious plazas shaded by olive trees, sip world-class wines at boutique bodegas, and ride cable cars up to breathtaking high-altitude trails, while the backdrop of snow-capped peaks makes every stroll feel like a picture-postcard adventure.

mec.name: Mecca
mec.text: Mecca, Saudi Arabia, sits on the western edge of the Arabian Peninsula, about 80 kilometres inland from the Red Sea coast and roughly 340 kilometres south-south-west of Riyadh. It is the holiest city in Islam, famed for the Kaaba – a cuboid stone structure built by the Prophet Ibrahim and his son Ismail that has been the focus of Muslim prayer for over a millennium. Today, Mecca is a bustling modern city with towering hotels, expansive shopping malls and well-maintained transport links, but access is strictly limited to Muslims; non-believers can admire its striking skyline and surrounding desert from a distance, appreciating the profound spiritual atmosphere that draws millions of pilgrims each year.

mel.name: Melbourne
mel.text: Melbourne, the vibrant capital of Victoria in southeastern Australia, sits on the banks of the Yarra River and stretches out toward Port Phillip Bay. Founded in 1835, the city grew rapidly after the gold rush of the 1850s, becoming a major commercial hub. Today visitors find a lively mix of tram-filled streets, world-class museums, leafy gardens and a celebrated coffee culture, while the laneway art and bustling markets showcase its creative spirit. Whether you’re exploring the historic arcades or watching the sunset over the bay, Melbourne feels both cosmopolitan and relaxed.

mem.name: Memphis
mem.text: Memphis, Tennessee, lies on the mighty Mississippi River in the southwestern corner of the state, bordering Arkansas. Founded in 1819 and named after the ancient Egyptian city, it quickly became a crucial river port and a crossroads of American culture. Today the city buzzes with the legacy of blues and rock ’n’ roll: you can stroll down historic Beale Street, visit the iconic Graceland home of Elvis Presley, and explore the National Civil Rights Museum at the former Lorraine Motel. With its lively music venues, riverfront parks and famous barbecue, Memphis feels both steeped in history and unmistakably vibrant.

mex.name: Mexico City
mex.text: Mexico City, the bustling capital of Mexico, lies in the high basin of the Valley of Mexico at an altitude of about 2,240 metres, surrounded by volcanoes and mountains. Founded by the Aztecs in 1325 as Tenochtitlán, it became the centre of a powerful empire before the Spanish conquest in 1521. Today the city blends ancient ruins such as the Templo Mayor with modern museums, vibrant street markets and a thriving culinary scene; you can wander historic plazas, ride the extensive metro system and enjoy a mix of colonial architecture and contemporary art, all set against a backdrop of bustling cafés and green parks.

mfm.name: Macau
mfm.text: Macau sits on the western edge of the Pearl River Delta, a short ferry ride from Hong Kong and bordering the Chinese city of Zhuhai. It was established as a Portuguese trading outpost in the 16th century and remained a European colony for over four hundred years before being handed back to China in 1999. Today the city dazzles visitors with its striking mix of colonial stone facades, colourful temples and towering casino resorts, while narrow alleyways offer bustling markets and aromatic street food. The blend of East and West, old and new, makes a stroll through Macau feel like stepping into a living museum with a lively, modern pulse.

mga.name: Managua
mga.text: Managua, the bustling capital of Nicaragua, sits on the southwestern shore of Lake Xolotlán where the Tipitapa and Tuma rivers meet the Pacific-ward plain. Founded in the 16th century, it became the country’s political centre after the 1855 earthquake destroyed the old city of León Viejo, and it has since grown into a vibrant metropolis. Today visitors find a mix of modern cafés, colourful markets and expansive waterfront promenades, with the historic Palacio Nacional and the striking silhouette of the three volcanoes – Masaya, Mombacho and Cerro Negro – framing the skyline, offering a lively yet relaxed atmosphere for explorers.

mgd.name: Mogadishu
mgd.text: Mogadishu, the bustling capital of Somalia, sits on the golden coastline of the Indian Ocean at the tip of the Horn of Africa. It was a major medieval port of the Somali Sultanate, famously visited by the traveller Ibn Battuta in the 14th century, and later became the administrative centre of Italian Somaliland. Today the city is a mix of old and new: colourful markets sell fragrant spices and hand-woven fabrics, the seaside promenade offers sweeping ocean views, and the rebuilt waterfront cafés buzz with friendly locals sharing tea and stories. While visitors should stay informed about safety advice, the warm Somali hospitality and vibrant street life make a trip to Mogadishu a memorable glimpse into a resilient, culturally rich city.

mhd.name: Mashhad
mhd.text: Mashhad, situated in northeastern Iran near the borders with Turkmenistan and Afghanistan, is the country’s holiest city and the capital of Razavi Khorasan Province. It grew around the shrine of Imam Reza, the eighth Shia Imam, whose burial site was established in the 9th century and has since become one of the world’s most visited pilgrimage centres. Today the city blends the reverent atmosphere of its vast, marble-clad mosque complex with bustling bazaars, modern hotels and a lively culinary scene, offering visitors a striking mix of spiritual heritage and contemporary Iranian hospitality.

mhj.name: Mahajanga
mhj.text: Mahajanga, perched on the sparkling Baie d’Ambaro on Madagascar’s north-west coast, greets visitors with a lively blend of sea breezes and colonial charm. The town grew into an important French port in the late 19th century, serving as a gateway for vanilla, cocoa and timber exported from the interior. Today, palm-lined promenades buzz with markets selling fresh fish, colourful handicrafts and fragrant spices, while nearby beaches invite sun-bathing and boat trips to the striking Tsingy de Bemaraha. Friendly locals, modest hotels and a relaxed rhythm make Mahajanga a welcoming stop for any explorer.

mia.name: Miami
mia.text: Miami is a bustling city on the southeastern tip of Florida, perched on the Atlantic shoreline where the Miami River meets Biscayne Bay and backed by the Everglades. It was formally incorporated in 1896, taking its name from the native Miami River that had long been a centre for the Tequesta people. Today the city is a lively blend of sun-kissed beaches, towering Art Deco hotels, and a vibrant multicultural scene, offering everything from Cuban-flavoured cuisine on Calle Ocho to world-class museums, nightlife and water sports, all under a perpetually warm sky.

mid.name: Merida
mid.text: Merida, the capital of Mexico’s Yucatán state, sits on the northern edge of the peninsula, about 35 km from the Gulf of Mexico and a short drive inland from the ancient Maya site of Chichén Itzá. Founded in 1542 by the Spanish conquistador Francisco de Montejo on the former Mayan town of T’Hó, the city retains a wealth of colonial buildings, wide tree-lined avenues and bustling plazas. Today visitors wander colourful markets, sample hearty Yucatecan dishes such as cochinita pibil, and enjoy a lively arts scene under a warm, sun-lit sky, all while feeling the relaxed, friendly rhythm of daily life.

mil.name: Milan
mil.text: Milan, in the north-west of Italy, sits in the fertile Po Valley between the Alps and the Adriatic Sea. First mentioned in a 6th-century Lombard document, the city became a major centre of the Renaissance, home to Leonardo da Vinci’s “The Last Supper” and the magnificent Gothic cathedral, the Duomo. Today Milan buzzes with a sleek blend of historic grandeur and modern style: you can wander its elegant arcades, sip espresso in bustling cafés, explore world-class museums, and shop the latest fashions in the vibrant Quadrilatero della Moda, all while enjoying a lively, cosmopolitan atmosphere.

mka.name: Mukalla
mka.text: Mukalla sits on Yemen’s southern coast, hugging the Arabian Sea at the mouth of the Wadi Hadhramaut in the Hadhramaut Governorate. Historically it was the capital of the Quʿaiti Sultanate and a key hub for the frankincense trade that linked the Arabian Peninsula with the wider Indian Ocean. Today the town offers a lively waterfront promenade, bustling souqs where you can haggle for spices, dates and hand-woven fabrics, and a harbour that still receives modest fishing boats. The surrounding desert scenery and nearby coral reefs make it a distinctive, if modest, stop for travellers seeking an authentic glimpse of southern Yemen.

mks.name: Makassar
mks.text: Makassar, perched on the southwestern coast of Sulawesi in Indonesia, is a bustling port city that has long served as a gateway to the spice islands. Its historic centre is dominated by Fort Rotterdam, a well-preserved 17th-century Dutch fort that once guarded the harbour and now houses museums and cultural exhibits. Today the city blends the old and the new: lively waterfront promenades line the harbor, offering fresh seafood and colourful night markets, while modern cafés and shopping arcs sit beside colonial buildings, giving visitors a vivid taste of both history and contemporary Indonesian life.

mkv.name: Moscow
mkv.text: Moscow, the capital of Russia, lies on the banks of the Moskva River in the western part of the country, roughly 530 km (330 miles) southeast of Saint Petersburg. First mentioned in chronicles in 1147, the city grew around the Kremlin, a fortified complex that became the seat of Russian rulers and still houses the president. Today Moscow buzzes with a blend of grand historic sites and modern life: you can marvel at the colourful onion domes of St Basil’s Cathedral, wander the vast Red Square, and then relax in trendy cafés or explore expansive shopping arcades, all while the city’s efficient metro shuttles you swiftly between its many neighbourhoods.

mlb.name: Malabo
mlb.text: Malabo, the capital of Equatorial Guinea, sits on the northern coast of the island of Bioko, overlooking the sparkling Atlantic Ocean. Founded by the Spanish in the early 19th century, it grew around a small fishing village and later became the administrative centre of the colony of Spanish Guinea. Today the city mixes colonial architecture—such as the striking Malabo Cathedral and the neoclassical Supreme Court—with vibrant market stalls where you can sample tropical fruit and fresh seafood. The surrounding hills offer lush rainforest walks, and the waterfront promenade provides a relaxed spot to watch colourful fishing boats bobbing in the harbor.

mle.name: Male
mle.text: Malé, the compact capital of the Maldives, sits on a tiny atoll in the central Indian Ocean, just a few kilometres from the international airport. The island has been the nation’s administrative centre since at least the 12th century, when the first sultanate established its court there, and its old Friday Mosque still bears the elegant coral stonework of that era. Today, visitors find a lively mix of colourful market stalls, sleek government buildings and the striking white-washed presidential palace, all framed by a bustling harbour from which day-trips to nearby coral reefs and sandbanks launch. The narrow streets are busy but walkable, and the scent of fresh fish and tropical flowers makes a stroll through Malé feel both historic and vibrantly contemporary.

mlt.name: Valletta
mlt.text: Valletta, the tiny capital of Malta, sits on a peninsula that juts out between the Grand Harbour and Marsamxett Creek on the central island of the Maltese archipelago. The city was founded in 1566 by the Knights of St John after their victory in the Great Siege of 1565 and was laid out on a strict grid of wide, limestone-paved streets, a design that earned it UNESCO World Heritage status in 1980. Today the fortified town feels lively yet intimate, with baroque churches, bustling cafés and open squares where you can watch colourful fishing boats drift past, while the sea breeze carries the scent of fresh pastizzi and the distant hum of ferries.

mmk.name: Murmansk
mmk.text: Murmansk sits on the Kola Bay at the entrance to the Barents Sea, far above the Arctic Circle on Russia’s north-western coast. Founded in 1916 as a supply port for the war effort, it became the only ice-free harbour in the Soviet north, playing a crucial role in both World Wars and the Cold War naval fleet. Today the city greets visitors with colourful wooden houses, a bustling waterfront promenade, and the striking Alyosha monument overlooking the sea. In summer the midnight sun brightens the streets, while winter offers chances to see the Northern Lights and sample hearty Arctic cuisine in cosy cafés.

mnc.name: Monaco
mnc.text: Monaco, perched on the French Riviera between Nice and the Italian border, is a tiny sovereign city-state covering just two square kilometres on the Mediterranean coast. First mentioned in medieval records as a fortified Genoese outpost, it later became the seat of the Grimaldi family, who have ruled continuously since the late 13th century. Today the streets are lined with luxury yachts, glittering casinos and elegant boutiques, while the famous Grand Prix snakes through its narrow boulevards each May. Despite its wealth, Monaco retains a charming blend of historic stone houses, sun-lit promenades and lush gardens that make strolling its compact centre a delightful experience.

mnl.name: Manila
mnl.text: Manila, the bustling capital of the Philippines, sits on the eastern shore of Manila Bay at the heart of Luzon Island. Founded in 1571 by Spanish conquistador Miguel López de Legazpi, the city grew around the historic Intramuros walled district, the oldest European-style settlement in the country. Today Manila is a lively mix of towering skyscrapers, colourful street markets and colonial churches, where traffic can be chaotic but the warmth of the locals is unmistakable. Visitors can savour a range of Filipino dishes, explore museums that chart the nation’s past, and enjoy vibrant nightlife beneath neon lights.

mns.name: Minsk
mns.text: Minsk, the capital of Belarus, sits in the centre of the country on the banks of the Svislach River. The settlement was first recorded in 1067 and later grew into an important trading centre before being almost completely destroyed during the Second World War, after which it was rebuilt in the distinctive Soviet style that still defines much of its skyline. Today the city feels surprisingly green and relaxed, with wide avenues, leafy parks, a clean modern metro and a lively mix of historic churches, museums and cafés where locals happily chat over a cup of strong coffee.

mor.name: Moroni
mor.text: Moroni, the capital of the Comoros, sits on the east coast of Grande Comore (Ngazidja) overlooking the Indian Ocean, its harbour framed by low, palm-lined hills. The town grew in the 19th century around a bustling port and was formalised as the capital during the French colonial period, with the historic Old Friday Mosque – dating from the 1840s – still dominating the skyline. Today visitors wander colourful markets where spices, vanilla and woven goods scent the air, sip fresh coconut water on the waterfront promenade and soak up a relaxed rhythm punctuated by friendly chatter, vibrant music and the occasional sight of traditional dhow boats drifting lazily by.

mos.name: Mosul
