mos.text: Mosul, situated on the western bank of the Tigris River in northern Iraq, lies roughly 400 km north-east of Baghdad and serves as the historic gateway to the Kurdish region. Founded in antiquity, it became a key centre of the Ottoman Empire and was known for its bustling bazaars and the famed al-Mosul University, one of the oldest modern institutions in the country. Today, visitors find a city in revival: restored mosques and markets display vibrant textiles and spices, while guided tours of the ancient citadel and the nearby archaeological sites offer a glimpse of its resilient spirit amid ongoing reconstruction.

mpl.name: Port Louis
mpl.text: Port Louis, the bustling capital of Mauritius, lies on the island’s north-west coast where the Indian Ocean meets the harbour. Founded by the French in 1735, it later became a key British naval base and a gateway for traders from Asia and Africa. Today the city blends colonial charm with vibrant street life: colourful markets spill over with spices, fresh fish and handcrafted goods, while the waterfront promenade offers views of sleek yachts and historic forts. Cafés serve fragrant tea and local delicacies, and the lively rhythm of sega music invites visitors to soak up the island’s multicultural spirit.

mpt.name: Maputo
mpt.text: Maputo, the vibrant capital of Mozambique, lies on the Indian Ocean coast at the southern tip of the country, where the Maputo River meets the sea. Founded as a Portuguese trading post in the 18th century, it became the colonial capital of Portuguese East Africa before independence in 1975. Today the city mixes art-deco architecture with bustling markets, palm-lined promenades and lively cafés serving piri-piri chicken and fresh seafood; a short walk takes you from the historic Praça da Independência to the colourful, fragrant streets of the Baixa district, offering a warm, relaxed atmosphere for visitors.

mqx.name: Mekelle
mqx.text: Mekelle, perched on the high Ethiopian plateau at about 2,500 metres, lies in the northern Tigray region near the border with Eritrea. Founded in the late 19th century, it grew into the capital of the historic Ethiopian Empire’s Tigray province and later became a centre of resistance during the 1970s and 1980s. Today the city feels vibrant and welcoming: tree-lined avenues lead to bustling markets where you can sample injera and local coffee, while the nearby ruins of ancient rock-hewn churches offer quiet glimpses of the area’s deep cultural roots. Friendly locals and a growing café scene make a visit both comfortable and memorable.

mrk.name: Marrakesh
mrk.text: Marrakesh, set at the foothills of the Atlas Mountains in western Morocco, is a bustling gateway to the desert and a former imperial capital founded in the 11th century by the Almoravid dynasty. Its historic medina, a UNESCO World Heritage site, still winds around the famous Jemaa el-Fna square where storytellers, musicians and food stalls create an ever-changing street-performance theatre. Today the city blends traditional souks selling spices, carpets and lanterns with sleek cafés, modern hotels and vibrant art galleries, offering visitors a lively mix of old-world charm and contemporary comfort.

mrv.name: Monrovia
mrv.text: Monrovia, the bustling capital perched on Liberia’s Atlantic coast, lies between the Atlantic Ocean and the lush, hilly hinterland of Montserrado County. Founded in 1822 by the American Colonisation Society as a settlement for freed African-American slaves, the city grew around a harbour that still serves as the country’s main gateway for trade and travel. Today visitors find a vibrant mix of colourful markets, colonial-era buildings and modern cafés, with the lively waterfront promenade offering fresh seafood and striking views of the Gulf of Guinea, while the warm, welcoming locals add a genuine charm to every stroll.

msp.name: Minneapolis
msp.text: Minneapolis, a vibrant city in the Upper Midwest of the United States, sits on the banks of the Mississippi River where it meets the scenic Chain of Lakes. Founded in the 1850s, it grew rapidly as a centre for flour milling, once boasting the world’s largest grain processing capacity and earning the nickname “Mill City.” Today visitors enjoy a blend of modern art, bustling food markets and extensive parkland: the Walker Art Center and its iconic Spoonbridge sculpture, the lively North Loop eateries, and miles of bike-friendly trails that wind through lush lakes and riverfront promenades, offering a fresh, lively urban experience.

msq.name: Muscat
msq.text: Muscat, the capital of Oman, sits on a sheltered inlet of the Gulf of Oman on the country’s north-eastern coast, framed by rugged hills and the sparkling sea. The city’s history stretches back to the early Islamic era, and it was a key port for traders from East Africa, India and the Persian Gulf long before European powers arrived. Today Muscat feels relaxed yet vibrant: you can wander the fragrant souks, admire the white-washed Sultan Qaboos Grand Mosque, and sip coffee on a promenade while watching traditional dhows glide past the modern waterfront.

msr.name: Misrata
msr.text: Misrata, a bustling coastal city on Libya’s central Mediterranean shore, sits about 150 km east of the capital Tripoli and is the country’s third-largest urban centre. Historically it was a key trading port in the Ottoman era, supplying grain and dates to ships crossing the sea. Today the city blends its lively market streets, where vendors sell fresh seafood and traditional sweets, with a modern waterfront promenade offering cafés, palm-shaded walkways and views of the sparkling harbour. Visitors can feel the hum of everyday Libyan life, explore the nearby ruins of ancient settlements and enjoy the warm, welcoming atmosphere of a city that’s both historic and forward-looking.

msu.name: Maseru
msu.text: Maseru, the capital of the mountainous kingdom of Lesotho, sits on the banks of the Mohokare River right on the border with South Africa, about 1 200 metres above sea level. Founded in the mid-19th century, the town grew around a mission station and later became the administrative centre when Lesotho (then Basutoland) was declared a British protectorate. Today Maseru blends modern cafés, colourful markets and colonial-era buildings, offering a friendly, laid-back vibe; you can stroll along the river promenade, sample local dishes such as pap and moroho, and feel the bustling energy of a city that’s both the gateway to Lesotho’s high-country scenery and a cultural hub in its own right.

msw.name: Massawa
msw.text: Massawa, perched on Eritrea’s Red Sea coast, is a modest port town where the sea breeze carries the scent of spices and diesel alike. Founded centuries ago, it became a key Ottoman outpost in the 16th century, later serving as a strategic harbour for Italian colonial forces before World War II. Today the town’s red-brick buildings and narrow lanes echo its layered past, while the bustling fish market, colourful coral-reef dives and the tranquil promenade offer a relaxed yet lively experience for visitors seeking both history and coastal charm.

msy.name: New Orleans
msy.text: New Orleans sits on the banks of the Mississippi River in the southeastern corner of Louisiana, United States, about 100 kilometres inland from the Gulf of Mexico. Founded in 1718 by the French, it became a key port for the Atlantic slave trade and later a melting-pot of French, Spanish, African and American cultures. Today the city bursts with life: the historic French Quarter dazzles with its pastel Creole townhouses, lively street music and fragrant beignets, while the riverfront hosts bustling markets, river cruises and festivals that showcase the city’s famous hospitality and vibrant culinary scene.

mta.name: Matadi
mta.text: Matadi, a bustling port town on the western edge of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, sits at the mouth of the Congo River about 150 km from Kinshasa and just a short distance from the Atlantic coast. Founded in the early 1880s as a key terminus for the railway that linked the interior to the sea, it grew into the country’s main gateway for imports and exports. Today visitors find a lively waterfront lined with colourful markets, colonial-era buildings and lively cafés, while the humid climate and constant river traffic give the town a vibrant, slightly chaotic charm that feels both historic and unmistakably modern.

mtp.name: Montpellier
mtp.text: Montpellier, nestled in the south-east of France on the banks of the Hérault River, lies just a short drive from the Mediterranean coast in the region of Occitanie. The city dates back to the early medieval period and is famed for its University of Montpellier, founded in 1220 and long recognised as one of the oldest medical schools in Europe. Today, Montpellier feels lively and youthful, with a mix of narrow medieval lanes, sleek modern architecture and plenty of cafés spilling onto sun-lit squares; the vibrant markets, street art and close proximity to beaches make it a delightful spot for a day or a longer stay.

mty.name: Monterrey
mty.text: Monterrey, nestled in the foothills of the Sierra Madre Oriental in north-eastern Mexico, is the bustling capital of the state of Nuevo León. Founded in 1596 by Spanish explorer Diego de Montemayor, the city grew from a modest settlement into a major industrial hub, earning a reputation as the country’s “Steel City”. Today visitors find a dynamic mix of sleek skyscrapers, lively markets and green parks framed by dramatic mountain peaks; the vibrant culinary scene serves up everything from street-side tacos to upscale Nuevo León-style grill, while museums and galleries showcase both modern art and the region’s rich heritage.

muc.name: Munich
muc.text: Munich sits in the heart of Bavaria, in southern Germany, nestled between the Alpine foothills and the River Isar. First mentioned in records from the 12th century, the city grew around a Benedictine monastery and later became the seat of the Wittelsbach dukes, giving it a rich imperial heritage visible in the grandeur of the Residenz palace. Today Munich is a lively mix of tradition and modernity: you can wander the historic Marienplatz, sip a fresh lager in a bustling beer garden, explore world-class museums, and enjoy easy access to nearby mountains for a day of hiking or skiing.

mvd.name: Montevideo
mvd.text: Montevideo, the capital of Uruguay, sits on the northern shore of the Río de la Plata opposite Buenos Ayres, forming a broad, windswept bay that feels more like an inland sea than a river. Founded by the Spanish in 1726, the city later became the site where Uruguay’s independence was declared in 1825, a pivotal moment in South-American history. Today Montevideo blends colonial charm with a relaxed, modern vibe: cobbled streets lead to colourful market stalls, the rambla stretches for kilometres alongside cafés and art galleries, and the historic Ciudad Vieja neighbourhood buzzes with live tango, fresh seafood and friendly locals eager to share a mate.

mzr.name: Mazar-i-Sharif
mzr.text: Mazar-i-Sharif sits in northern Afghanistan, on the banks of the Balkh River, about 150 km from the Uzbek border and a short drive from the historic sites of Balkh and Kunduz. Founded centuries ago, it is best known for the stunning Blue Mosque (Masjid-e-Nabawi), a shrine reputed to house the tomb of the prophet’s cousin Ali ibn-Abi-Talib and a landmark of Safavid-era architecture. Today the city feels lively and welcoming, with bustling bazaars selling colourful carpets, fresh fruit and fragrant spices, tree-lined avenues where locals enjoy tea in the shade, and a surprisingly calm ambience despite its strategic location, making it a memorable stop for travellers seeking both culture and hospitality.

nan.name: Nantes
nan.text: Nantes, situated on the banks of the Loire in western France, is a vibrant city that blends river-side charm with a rich maritime heritage. Once the historic capital of the Duchy of Brittany and a major port for Atlantic trade, its legacy is still visible in the impressive Château des Ducs de Bretagne and the preserved 18th-century shipyards of the Cité des Congrès. Today visitors can wander along the lively quays, explore the whimsical Machines of the Isle of Nantes with its giant mechanical elephant, and enjoy bustling markets, cafés and contemporary art galleries that give the city a lively, modern feel.

nap.name: Naples
nap.text: Naples, perched on the western edge of the Bay of Naples in southern Italy, is a bustling port city that has watched history unfold for over two millennia. It was a major centre of the Roman Republic and later the capital of the Kingdom of Naples, giving the region its name. Today the streets pulse with energy: you can wander past vibrant markets selling fresh mozzarella and espresso, explore the UNESCO-listed historic centre with its baroque churches and underground catacombs, and gaze across the water to the looming silhouette of Mount Vesuvius, still reminding visitors of the city’s dramatic past.

nas.name: Nassau
nas.text: Nassau, the bustling capital of the Bahamas, sits on New Providence Island just off the north-east coast of the main Bahamian archipelago, overlooking the turquoise waters of the Atlantic. Founded in the 17th century, the town became a notorious pirate haven in the early 1700s, a colourful chapter reflected in the historic Parliament Square and the famous pirate-themed museum on Bay Street. Today visitors stroll along the vibrant waterfront, browse colourful market stalls selling conch and locally-made crafts, and relax on nearby Cable Beach, while the city’s pastel colonial buildings and lively music scene give a warm, laid-back island feel.

nbo.name: Nairobi
nbo.text: Nairobi, the bustling capital of Kenya, sits in the south-central part of the country on the high-land plateau of the Great Rift Valley, at an altitude of about 1,795 metres. Founded in 1899 as a railway depot on the Uganda Railway, it quickly grew into a major administrative centre and was declared the capital of the British East Africa Protectorate in 1907. Today the city blends modern skyscrapers with lively markets, lush parks such as the Nairobi National Park where rhinos roam on the city’s edge, and a vibrant food scene that offers everything from traditional Kenyan dishes to international cuisine, making it a dynamic base for exploring East Africa.

nco.name: Nicosia
nco.text: Nicosia, the capital of Cyprus, sits in the centre of the island on the banks of the Pedieos River, straddling the dividing line between the Greek-Cypriot south and the Turkish-Cypriot north. First mentioned in medieval chronicles, the city became the island’s administrative heart in the 15th century and later served as the seat of the Ottoman governor. Today the walled old town, with its narrow stone lanes and bustling market, invites visitors to wander past historic churches, the 16th-century Leventis Municipal Museum and lively cafés, while the modern streets outside offer sleek shops, lively tavernas and a vibrant cultural scene.

ndi.name: Nadi
ndi.text: Nadi lies on the western side of Viti Levu, Fiji’s main island, just a short drive from the country’s international airport. Founded in the late 1800s as a sugar-cane settlement, the town grew around the railway that once linked the plantations to the port, a reminder of its colonial past. Today Nadi bustles with colourful markets, friendly cafés and the famous Garden of the Sleeping Giant, while the nearby beaches offer calm waters perfect for a first splash in the South Pacific. Its warm, laid-back atmosphere makes it an easy base for exploring the islands beyond.

ndj.name: N'Djamena
ndj.text: N'Djamena, the capital of Chad, lies on the banks of the Chari River in the far-southwest of the country, close to the border with Cameroon. Founded as Fort-Lamy by the French in 1900, it became the administrative centre of French Equatorial Africa and was renamed N'Djamena after independence in 1960. Today the city bustles with a lively market where you can haggle for textiles, spices and handcrafted jewellery, while cafés serve strong coffee and local millet beer. Though traffic can be chaotic and the heat intense, friendly locals are eager to share stories of the Sahel’s rich cultural tapestry.

ngo.name: Nagoya
ngo.text: Nagoya, situated in the heart of Japan’s Chūbu region on the island of Honshū, lies between Osaka and Tokyo along the fertile Nōbi Plain and the coast of Ise Bay. The city grew around Nagoya Castle, erected in 1612 by Tokugawa Ieyasu’s son Tokugawa Yoshinao as a strategic stronghold of the Owari branch of the shogunate. Today Nagoya blends its rich heritage with a vibrant, modern vibe: sleek skyscrapers tower over bustling shopping arcades, the famed miso-katsu and tebasaki chicken tempt food lovers, and easy access to museums, gardens and the nearby historic post towns makes it a welcoming base for exploring central Japan.

nhv.name: Newhaven
nhv.text: Newhaven is a small coastal town in East Sussex, perched on the mouth of the River Ouse where it meets the English Channel, just a short drive east of Brighton. It grew around a medieval fishing harbour that later became an important packet-boat terminal for cross-Channel services in the 19th century, and the town’s historic harbour walls still echo that maritime past. Today visitors can stroll along the lively promenade, watch the ferries to Dieppe, enjoy fresh seafood in cosy pubs, and take in sweeping sea views from the nearby cliffs, all in a relaxed, friendly atmosphere.

nia.name: Niamey
nia.text: Niamey, the capital of Niger, sits on the banks of the winding Niger River in the country's far-southwest, close to the border with Burkina Faso. It grew from a modest French colonial outpost founded in the early 1900s and was officially made the capital of French Upper Volta in 1926, a status it retained after independence. Today the city buzzes with colourful markets where traders sell everything from woven fabrics to fresh mangoes, while the National Museum offers insight into the region’s rich cultural heritage. Strolling along the riverfront at sunset, you’ll feel the warm hospitality of a town that blends traditional life with the energy of a growing West African hub.

nic.name: Nice
nic.text: Nice, perched on the sun-kissed French Riviera between the Mediterranean Sea and the foothills of the Alps, is a vibrant coastal city in the southeast of France. It grew from a small fishing settlement into a fashionable resort after the railway arrived in 1864, attracting artists and aristocrats alike. Today the promenade along the famous Baie des Anges is lined with palm trees, cafés and the iconic pebble beach, while the narrow streets of the old town reveal colourful baroque houses, bustling markets and the scent of socca. Visitors can stroll the promenade, explore museums such as the Musée Matisse, and enjoy the blend of French and Italian influences that give Nice its distinct charm.

nkc.name: Nouakchott
nkc.text: Nouakchott, the capital of Mauritania, lies on the edge of the Atlantic Ocean in the far west of the Sahara, where the desert meets the sea. Founded in 1958 as the new administrative centre after French colonial rule, it quickly grew into the country’s main port and political hub. Today the city feels relaxed yet bustling: wide, palm-lined avenues lead to a lively fish market where fresh catches are sold, the freshly painted Museum of Black Africa showcases local heritage, and the nearby beaches offer gentle waves against a backdrop of low-rise modernist buildings and expansive dunes.

nkg.name: Nanjing
nkg.text: Nanjing, situated on the lower reaches of the Yangtze River in eastern China, was the capital of several Chinese dynasties and the seat of the early Republic of China, famously hosting the 1912 provisional government. Today the city blends its deep history with a lively modern vibe: you can wander along the historic city wall, explore the solemn Memorial Hall of the Nanjing Massacre, and then relax in bustling pedestrian streets lined with cafés, boutique shops and neon-lit skyscrapers. The surrounding Qinhuai River area offers charming lantern-lit night walks, while nearby Purple Mountain provides peaceful trails and spectacular views over the urban landscape.

nnc.name: Nancy
nnc.text: Nancy, situated in the Grand Est region of north-eastern France near the borders of Luxembourg and Germany, is a historic city that grew around the medieval duchy of Lorraine. It is famous for Place Stanislas, the grand 18th-century square commissioned by Stanisław Leszczyński, former king of Poland and Duke of Lorraine, whose harmonious classical architecture earned UNESCO World Heritage status. Today the city blends that regal past with a lively cultural scene: cafés spill onto cobbled streets, museums showcase Art Nouveau treasures, and the nearby Parc de la Pépinière offers a pleasant green escape for walkers and families alike.

nng.name: Nanning
nng.text: Nanning, the capital of Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region in southern China, sits on the banks of the Nan River a few hundred kilometres from the Vietnamese border. Historically it served as a regional administrative centre during the Tang dynasty and later became the seat of the provincial government after the establishment of the People’s Republic. Today the city is celebrated for its lush, tree-lined streets and plentiful parks, earning it the nickname “Green City”. Visitors can wander the lively Qingxiu Mountain, sample the spicy Zhuang cuisine in bustling night markets, and enjoy a relaxed blend of modern malls and traditional riverfront scenery.

nou.name: Nouadhibou
nou.text: Nouadhibou, Mauritania’s second-largest city, sits on the Atlantic coast at the western tip of the Sahara, just north of the border with Western Sahara. It began life as the French colonial settlement of Port-Étienne in the early 1900s, growing around a modest fishing harbour that later became a hub for exporting the country’s iron ore. Today the town bustles with colourful markets, bustling fish stalls and the striking “ship graveyard” where rusting hulls line the shoreline. Visitors can enjoy fresh seafood, watch lively dhow crews at work and feel the quiet expanse of the desert meeting the sea.

noum.name: Noumea
noum.text: Nouméa, the capital of New Caledonia, sits on the southern coast of the island’s main landmass, facing the warm waters of the Pacific’s Grande Terre. Founded as a French penal colony in 1854, the city still bears the imprint of its colonial past in the elegant Haussmann-style avenues and the historic Musée de Nouvelle-Calédonie. Today Nouméa is a lively blend of French cafés, bustling markets and sun-kissed beaches; you can sip a café au lait on a palm-shaded promenade, wander the colourful bayside promenade, or explore nearby reefs, all while enjoying a relaxed, tropical atmosphere tinged with European charm.

npr.name: Napier
npr.text: Napier lies on the eastern coast of New Zealand’s North Island, facing Hawke’s Bay and the Pacific Ocean. The town was virtually rebuilt in the 1930s after a devastating earthquake in 1931, which gave it its distinctive Art Deco architecture and earned it a reputation as the world’s finest example of the style. Today visitors can stroll along the sunny waterfront, explore the colourful streets lined with cafes, galleries and boutique shops, and sample the region’s famed wines on nearby vineyards, all while enjoying a relaxed, sunny climate and warm hospitality.

nuk.name: Nukus
nuk.text: Nukus lies in the far west of Uzbekistan, perched on the edge of the Kyzylkum Desert near the border with Kazakhstan. Founded in the 19th century as a small fortress, it became the capital of the autonomous Karakalpakstan region in the Soviet era and today houses the world-renowned Savitsky Museum, which safeguards an extraordinary collection of avant-garde art saved from Soviet censorship. Visiting now feels like stepping into a quiet, sun-baked city where wide streets are lined with Soviet-era apartment blocks, bustling bazaars sell fresh melons and carpet-weaving workshops, and the desert backdrop offers striking sunsets that colour the sky in vivid pinks and golds.

nyc.name: New York
nyc.text: New York, United States – perched on the east coast where the Hudson River meets the Atlantic, this bustling metropolis is the most populous city in America. Founded by the Dutch in the early 17th century, it was later renamed after the English Duke of York and grew into a gateway for millions of immigrants arriving through Ellis Island. Today the city dazzles visitors with its iconic skyline, from the soaring Freedom Tower to the historic Empire State Building, while neighbourhoods buzz with diverse food, world-class museums, vibrant street art and endless theatres, making every stroll feel like a fresh adventure.

nyt.name: Naypyidaw
nyt.text: Naypyidaw, the modern capital of Myanmar, lies in the heart of the country on the banks of the Irrawaddy River, about 320 km north of the former capital Yangon. The city was deliberately built in the early 2000s and officially became the nation’s seat of government in 2005, when the capital was shifted from Yangon. Today visitors find a surprisingly spacious metropolis with wide avenues, orderly parks and impressive government buildings, alongside curious attractions such as the massive Uppatasanti Pagoda and a surprisingly quiet zoo; the city feels quiet, orderly and a little surreal compared with Myanmar’s bustling historic towns.

oax.name: Oaxaca
oax.text: Oaxaca, nestled in the fertile Valley of Oaxaca in southern Mexico and framed by the Sierra Madre del Sur mountains, is the colourful capital of the state of the same name. The city grew on the site of the pre-Hispanic Zapotec centre of Monte Albán and was formally founded by the Spanish in 1532, later becoming a centre of colonial administration and art. Today it is a lively UNESCO World Heritage site, famous for its bustling markets, centuries-old stone streets, vibrant festivals and world-renowned cuisine such as mole and tlayudas, making a visit feel like stepping into a living museum of colour and tradition.

ods.name: Odesa
ods.text: Odesa, a bustling port city on the north-western coast of the Black Sea in southern Ukraine, sits where the Dniester River meets the water. Founded in 1794 by the Russian Empire, it quickly became a major trading hub and is famous for its 19th-century architecture, including the grand Potemkin Stairs that lead down to the harbour. Today Odesa charms visitors with its lively promenade, sunny beaches and a vibrant café culture where locals chat over coffee and fresh fish. The city’s multicultural vibe is evident in its lively markets, street art and the melodic echo of sea shanties that drift from the waterfront taverns.

oka.name: Naha
oka.text: Naha, the capital city of Okinawa Prefecture, sits on the southern coast of Okinawa Island and faces the East China Sea. It grew around Shuri Castle, the historic seat of the Ryukyu Kingdom, which was destroyed in World War II and later reconstructed as a UNESCO World Heritage site. Today Naha blends tradition and modernity: narrow, colourful streets of Kokusai Dori offer bustling markets, tasty Okinawan dishes and souvenir stalls, while the waterfront promenade provides a relaxed place to watch ferries and enjoy tropical sunsets. The city’s warm climate, friendly locals and mix of heritage sites make it a lively gateway to Japan’s southern islands.

okc.name: Oklahoma City
okc.text: Oklahoma City lies in the heart of the American Midwest, perched on the banks of the North Fork of the Canadian River in the state of Oklahoma. Founded during the Land Run of 1889, the city grew rapidly as a centre for cattle trading and later for oil production, shaping its rugged frontier character. Today it offers a lively blend of modern culture and historic charm: the vibrant Bricktown entertainment district buzzes with restaurants and river-front walks, the impressive National Cowboy & Western Heritage Museum showcases Western art, and spacious parks provide a welcoming atmosphere for visitors of all ages.

oma.name: Omaha
oma.text: Omaha, Nebraska, sits on the western bank of the Missouri River at the heart of the Midwestern United States, roughly three-hundred miles north of Kansas City. Founded in 1854 as a frontier outpost, it quickly became a key stop on the Oregon Trail and later the eastern terminus of the first transcontinental railroad, cementing its role in westward expansion. Today the city blends river-front charm with a lively cultural scene: the historic Old Market district offers cobbled streets, independent shops and cafés, while the Henry Doorly Zoo, modern museums and a bustling riverwalk give visitors a pleasant mix of nature, history and contemporary Midwestern hospitality.

oms.name: Omsk
oms.text: Omsk, a large city in southwestern Siberia, sits on the banks of the Irtysh River near the junction with the Om River, about 2 500 km east of Moscow. Founded in 1716 as a fortress on the Russian frontier, it later became an important trading hub on the Siberian route and served as a temporary capital of the anti-Bolshevik White movement during the Russian Civil War. Today Omsk offers a blend of wide, tree-lined avenues, striking Soviet-era architecture and lively riverfront promenades; visitors can explore the ornate wooden cathedral of St. Nicholas, the regional museum of fine arts, and enjoy the bustling cafés and markets that give the city a warm, modern feel despite its remote location.

opo.name: Porto
opo.text: Porto, Portugal, sits on the north-west coast where the Douro River meets the Atlantic, its historic centre spilling up the steep hillsides that frame the riverbanks. The city’s medieval roots are evident in the 12th-century São Francisco Church and the iconic Ribeira district, a UNESCO World Heritage site that has been a bustling port since the age of discovery. Today Porto is a lively blend of old and new: you can wander past pastel-coloured stone facades, sip world-renowned port wine in cosy cellars, and enjoy vibrant cafés, street art and a lively waterfront promenade that buzzes with locals and visitors alike.

osa.name: Osaka
osa.text: Osaka, situated on the main island of Honshu where the Yodo River meets Osaka Bay, is Japan’s vibrant commercial hub and the capital of Osaka Prefecture. Historically it flourished as the “kitchen of Japan” during the Edo period, supplying rice and other staples to the rest of the country, and it was the site of Osaka Castle, rebuilt after a 1615 siege. Today the city buzzes with neon-lit streets, bustling food markets such as Kuromon, and modern attractions like the Osaka Aquarium Kaiyukan; you can wander from historic temples to ultra-modern skyscrapers, all while sampling the famous takoyaki and okonomiyaki that give the city its delicious reputation.

osh.name: Osh
osh.text: Osh sits in the fertile Ferghana Valley of southern Kyrgyzstan, cradled by the foothills of the Alai Range and close to the borders with Uzbekistan and Tajikistan. It is one of the country’s oldest settlements, with a history that stretches back over three millennia and a long-standing role as a bustling stop on the Silk Road. Today the town buzzes with lively bazaars where traders sell everything from fresh apricots to hand-woven felt, while the nearby Sulayman Mountain, a UNESCO-listed sacred site, offers panoramic views and a glimpse of the region’s layered past.

osl.name: Oslo
osl.text: Oslo, Norway’s capital, sits at the head of the Oslofjord, framed by forested hills and islands that spill into the sea. First mentioned in medieval sagas, the city grew around the royal estate of Oslo founded in the 11th century and later became the seat of Norway’s government. Today it feels refreshingly compact and modern, with a lively waterfront lined with museums, cafés and sleek architecture such as the opera house’s sloping marble roof. You can stroll through Vigeland’s sculpture park, explore the historic Akershus Fortress or take a short ferry ride to the scenic islands for a taste of Nordic charm.

oua.name: Ouagadougou
oua.text: Ouagadougou, the vibrant capital of Burkina Faso, sits in the centre of the country on the gently rolling savannah of the Upper Volta basin. Founded as a modest settlement in the 15th century, it became the seat of the Mossi kingdom of Ouagadougou in the 19th century and later the administrative centre of French Upper Volta. Today the city hums with colour: bustling markets overflow with woven textiles, fresh mangoes and handcrafted jewellery, while wide avenues lead to lively cafés and the modern National Museum of Art and History. Visitors enjoy a warm, welcoming atmosphere, with the scent of grilled fish and the rhythm of traditional drumming echoing through the streets.

ovb.name: Novosibirsk
ovb.text: Novosibirsk, the bustling heart of Siberia, lies on the banks of the Ob River about 3,300 km east of Moscow and 2,800 km west of the Russian-Chinese border. Founded in 1893 as the railway settlement Novonikolayevsk, it quickly grew into a key industrial and scientific centre, later becoming the capital of the Siberian Soviet Republic. Today the city blends Soviet-era architecture with modern cafés, lively riverfront promenades and a vibrant arts scene; visitors can explore the impressive Novosibirsk State Academic Theatre, sample hearty Siberian cuisine, and stroll through the leafy Central Park while the Trans-Siberian Railway whistles past.

oxf.name: Oxford
oxf.text: Oxford, set in the heart of southern England on the River Thames, lies about 60 miles northwest of London. The city grew around the University of Oxford, founded in the 12th century and renowned as the oldest English-speaking university in the world. Today visitors can wander its historic cobbled streets, admire the dreaming spires of colleges such as Christ Church and Magdalen, and enjoy bustling market squares, independent bookshops and riverside punts. With a lively mix of academia, museums and cosy cafés, Oxford feels both timeless and vibrantly modern.

pap.name: Port-au-Prince
pap.text: Port-au-Prince sits on the Gulf of Caribbean on Haiti’s western coast, nestled between the sprawling hills of the Château de Mona and the bustling harbour that has long been the island’s gateway to the sea. Founded by French colonists in the 18th century, it became Haiti’s capital after independence in 1804 and later endured a devastating earthquake in 2010 that reshaped much of the city. Today the streets buzz with colourful market stalls, lively music and resilient locals; you can explore vibrant art galleries, sample hearty Haitian cuisine and feel the warm, welcoming spirit that pulses through the rebuilt neighbourhoods.

par.name: Paris
par.text: Paris, the capital of France, sits on the banks of the River Seine in the north-central part of the country. Founded by the Celtic Parisii tribe, it became an imperial centre when the Romans built Lutetia on the island now known as Île de la Cité, and it later grew into a hub of art, fashion and cuisine. Today the city dazzles visitors with its iconic skyline of Haussmannian boulevards, world-renowned museums such as the Louvre, and lively cafés spilling onto cobbled streets. A stroll along the Seine offers a mix of historic monuments, modern shops and the unmistakable buzz of a metropolis that still feels romantic and vibrant.

pat.name: Patras
pat.text: Patras sits on the north-west coast of the Peloponnese, perched on the Gulf of Patras and serving as a key gateway between Greece and Italy via its busy ferry terminal. It grew from an ancient Roman colony that became the chief port of the region of Achaea, and it is traditionally linked to Saint Andrew, who is said to have been martyred on a nearby hill in the first century. Today the city hums with a lively mix of historic stone façades, bustling markets and vibrant cafés, while the promenade along the waterfront offers striking sunset views and easy access to lively nightlife and cultural festivals.

pbm.name: Paramaribo
pbm.text: Paramaribo, the capital of Suriname, lies on the banks of the Suriname River just a few kilometres inland from the Atlantic coast. Founded by the Dutch in the early 17th century, the city’s historic centre – a UNESCO World Heritage site – still shows the distinctive wooden colonial architecture that survived the 1821 fire. Today the streets buzz with a relaxed, multicultural vibe; you can wander past colourful market stalls selling fresh tropical fruit, sample a blend of Creole, Indian and Javanese flavours in cosy cafés, and cruise on the river to watch sunset-lit mangroves framing a laid-back, yet lively, Caribbean atmosphere.

pct.name: Picton
pct.text: Picton is a small coastal town perched at the head of Queen Charlotte Sound on the northern edge of New Zealand’s South Island, where the Marlborough Sounds meet Cook Strait. The settlement was formally established in the 1850s and took its name from Sir Thomas Picton, a British general, after an earlier Māori village occupied the site. Today Picton is a lively gateway for ferries to the North Island and a hub for exploring the surrounding waterways, with scenic walks, wildlife-rich marine reserves and a reputation for fresh seafood served in its harbour-front cafés, all set against spectacular mountain and sea views.

pdl.name: Ponta Delgada
pdl.text: Ponta Delgada, the capital of São Miguel in the Azores, sits on the southern coast of the island facing the Atlantic and is framed by volcanic hills and lush green pastures. Founded in the 15th century, it became an important stop for ships crossing between Europe and the Americas, and its historic Forte de São Brás still guards the harbour. Today the town blends old-world charm with a lively waterfront promenade, pastel-coloured stone houses and bustling cafés where you can savour fresh fish and pineapple rum while watching ferries glide past and the distant sea breezes rustle the bougainvillea.

pdx.name: Portland
pdx.text: Portland, Oregon, lies in the Pacific Northwest of the United States where the Willamette and Columbia rivers meet, about 70 miles east of the Pacific coast. Founded in 1845 and incorporated in 1851, the city grew around timber and river trade and later became known for its progressive urban planning. Today visitors find a vibrant mix of lush parks, bike-friendly streets and a thriving food scene, with famous coffee roasters, food-truck pods and a bustling Saturday market by the waterfront. The surrounding mountains and nearby vineyards add outdoor adventure and wine-tasting to the city’s laid-back, eco-conscious charm.

pee.name: Perm
pee.text: Perm lies on the banks of the wide, winding Kama River at the western foothills of the Ural Mountains, marking the traditional divide between European and Asian Russia. It was founded in 1723 as a modest settlement serving the salt-mining industry and grew into a key industrial hub during the 19th-century railway boom. Today the city offers a lively mix of cultural attractions – the striking Perm Opera and Ballet Theatre, the contemporary art-filled Perm Museum of Contemporary Art, and the open-air Koltushi Park – alongside cosy cafés and bustling markets, making a pleasant base for exploring both river scenery and the surrounding forested hills.

pen.name: Penang
pen.text: Penang, an island state on the northwest coast of Malaysia, sits just across the Strait of Malacca from the mainland town of Butterworth. Its capital, George Town, was founded by the British East India Company in 1786 and later became a bustling entrepôt of trade, earning a UNESCO World Heritage listing for its well-preserved colonial architecture and vibrant street life. Today, visitors wander pastel-coloured shophouses, sample famous street food at hawker stalls, and enjoy the mix of Malay, Chinese, Indian and European influences that give the island its uniquely eclectic, laid-back charm.

per.name: Perth
per.text: Perth sits on the southwestern coast of Western Australia, cradled by the Indian Ocean and the Swan River, about 3,300 km west of Sydney. Established as the Swan River Colony in 1829, it was one of the first British settlements on the continent and retains a distinctive colonial charm. Today the city blends a relaxed, sun-kissed lifestyle with a vibrant cultural scene: you can stroll along the riverfront cafés, explore the modern art galleries of the Art Gallery of Western Australia, or catch a sunset on the golden sands of Cottesloe Beach, all under a generally mild climate and friendly local vibe.

pew.name: Peshawar
pew.text: Peshawar, the bustling capital of Pakistan’s Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, lies at the eastern edge of the historic Khyber Pass, a gateway between South Asia and Central Asia. Founded over two millennia ago, it was an important centre of the ancient Gandhara civilisation and later thrived as a key trading hub on the Silk Road. Today the city greets visitors with a vibrant mix of colonial architecture, lively bazaars brimming with spices, hand-woven textiles and fragrant street food, while the towering Mahabat Khan Mosque and the bustling Saddar Market offer a colourful glimpse into its rich past and lively present.

pfo.name: Paphos
pfo.text: Paphos sits on the southwestern coast of Cyprus, overlooking a sparkling bay that has welcomed sailors since antiquity. The town is famed for its UNESCO-listed archaeological park, where the well-preserved Roman mosaics at the House of Dionysos depict scenes from mythology and confirm Paphos’ status as a historic centre of worship to the goddess Aphrodite. Today the waterfront promenade buzzes with cafés, boutique shops and colourful market stalls, while the golden beaches and clear Mediterranean waters make it easy to relax after a stroll through the charming old town streets lined with stone houses and fragrant orange trees.

pgn.name: Perpignan
pgn.text: Perpignan is a lively city in the far south of France, perched on the banks of the River Têt just a few kilometres from the Spanish border and the Mediterranean Sea. It was once the capital of the Kingdom of Majorca, and the 13th-century Palais des Rois de Majorque still dominates the historic centre with its red-brick towers. Today the town blends French and Catalan influences, offering sun-filled streets lined with cafés, colourful markets and a network of canals that give it a charming, almost Venetian feel. Visitors can enjoy tapas-style cuisine, explore Romanesque churches and soak up a relaxed, Mediterranean atmosphere.

phc.name: Port Harcourt
phc.text: Port Harcourt, the bustling capital of Rivers State in southern Nigeria, sits on the banks of the Bonny River near the Niger Delta. Founded in 1912 by the British colonial administration, it was named after Lewis Vernon Harcourt, the then Secretary of State for the Colonies, and later grew into a major hub for Nigeria’s oil industry. Today the city blends modern high-rise office blocks with lively markets, waterfront promenades and a vibrant music scene; visitors can sample spicy river-fish dishes, explore the nearby mangrove forests and feel the energetic pulse of a town that is both a commercial powerhouse and a cultural gateway to the Delta.

phl.name: Philadelphia
phl.text: Philadelphia, nestled in the southeastern corner of Pennsylvania along the Delaware and Schuylkill rivers, is a city steeped in American history; it was the meeting place for the Continental Congress where the Declaration of Independence was debated and the Constitution signed. Today the streets buzz with a lively mix of historic cobblestones and modern skyscrapers, inviting visitors to stroll past the iconic Liberty Bell, explore world-class museums on the “Museum Mile,” and savour diverse food markets ranging from classic cheesesteaks to global street fare, all set against a backdrop of vibrant neighbourhoods and green riverfront parks.

phx.name: Phoenix
phx.text: Phoenix, Arizona, lies in the heart of the Sonoran Desert about 350 miles southeast of Las Vegas and 200 miles north of the Mexican border, cradled by the Salt River and surrounded by low mountains. Founded in 1867 as a farming community near the Hohokam canals, it grew into the capital of the territory and later the state in 1912. Today the city blends modern skyline and sprawling suburbs with desert-cactus scenery, offering vibrant arts districts, world-class museums and easy access to hiking in nearby Camelback Mountain, making it a warm, lively base for exploring the Southwest.

pia.name: Praia
pia.text: Praia, the bustling capital of Cape Verde, sits on the southern coast of Santiago island where the Atlantic sweeps up against a palm-fringed harbour. Established by the Portuguese in the 1500s, it became the colony’s administrative centre in 1770, replacing the older town of Ribeira Grande. Today the city is a lively mix of pastel-coloured houses, lively market stalls and wide, tree-lined avenues that lead to a pleasant waterfront promenade. Visitors can explore the historic Plateau with its colonial buildings, sample fresh fish at local eateries, and enjoy the warm, welcoming atmosphere that blends African rhythm with Portuguese heritage.

pit.name: Pittsburgh
pit.text: Pittsburgh, situated at the confluence of the Allegheny, Monongahela and Ohio rivers in western Pennsylvania, grew from a frontier fort into a powerhouse of industry in the 19th century, famously known for its steel production that earned the city the nickname “Steel City”. Today the skyline is a blend of historic brick warehouses and sleek glass towers, while the river valleys provide scenic bridges and bustling waterfront parks. Visitors can explore vibrant neighbourhoods such as the Strip District’s food markets, the cultural riches of the Carnegie museums, and enjoy a lively craft-beer scene against a backdrop of rolling hills.

plm.name: Palembang
plm.text: Palembang lies on the east bank of the mighty Musi River in South Sumatra, Indonesia, and is the province’s bustling capital. It was the heart of the powerful Srivijaya maritime empire that dominated regional trade from the 7th to the 13th century, leaving a legacy of impressive stone stelae and temple ruins nearby. Today the city blends old and new: you can stroll along riverfront promenades, admire the striking red-painted arches of the Ampera Bridge, and sample famous local dishes such as pempek while the lively night markets buzz with colour and the scent of fresh seafood.

ply.name: Plymouth
ply.text: Plymouth sits on the southern coast of Devon, where the River Plym meets the English Channel, and its natural harbour has been a gateway to the world for centuries. It is famously the departure point of the Mayflower in 1620, when the first group of Pilgrims set sail for North America. Today the city blends maritime heritage with a lively waterfront: you can wander along the historic Barbican, explore the National Marine Aquarium, and enjoy fresh seafood in bustling cafés while the modern shopping precincts and the iconic Smeaton’s Tower lighthouse remind you that Plymouth is both a historic port and a vibrant, contemporary destination.

pme.name: Portland, Maine
pme.text: Portland, Maine sits on a sheltered inlet of the Atlantic called Casco Bay, at the mouth of the Presumpscot River in the far north-east of the United States. Founded in 1632, the city grew as a major shipbuilding and fishing port and was an important base for the Union Navy during the Civil War. Today the waterfront is a lively mix of colourful lobster shacks, boutique shops and craft breweries, while the historic Old Port cobbles echo with the clatter of tram-trolley tours. Visitors can stroll along the scenic Eastern Promenade, explore art galleries and enjoy fresh seafood with a view of the harbor.

pna.name: Patna
pna.text: Patna, the capital of Bihar in eastern India, sits on the south bank of the wide Ganges River and has been a centre of Indian life for millennia. Known in ancient times as Pataliputra, it was the capital of the Mauryan Empire under Emperor Ashoka, who built a famous stone pillar that still stands in the city. Today Patna blends its historic aura with lively street life: bustling bazaars sell everything from silk saris to spicy snacks, the Bihar Museum showcases artefacts spanning pre-historic to modern times, and the expansive Gandhi Maidan offers a green respite where locals gather for concerts, fairs and evening walks.

pnh.name: Phnom Penh
pnh.text: Phnom Penh, the bustling capital of Cambodia, lies on the banks of the Mekong River where it meets the Tonlé Sap, about 150 km inland from the South-China Sea. Founded in the 14th century, it became the royal seat of the Khmer Empire in the 19th century after King Norodom moved the court there, and it later served as the centre of French colonial administration. Today the city is a lively mix of historic temples, sleek riverside cafés and vibrant night markets; tuk-tuks weave through traffic while the scent of lemongrass and grilled satay drifts from street stalls, offering visitors a colourful glimpse of Cambodia’s past and its energetic present.

pnp.name: Pohnpei
pnp.text: Pohnpei, the main island of the Federated States of Micronesia, lies in the heart of the western Pacific, about 2,400 km east of the Philippines and roughly 1,600 km north of Papua New Guinea. It is famed for the ancient stone city of Nan Madol, built on a network of artificial islets between the 13th and 17th centuries and once the ceremonial centre of the Saudeleur dynasty. Today the island is a lush, tropical paradise with towering rainforest, sparkling waterfalls and friendly villages where visitors can snorkel vibrant reefs, trek scenic trails and sample fresh seafood in relaxed beachfront cafés.

pnq.name: Pune
pnq.text: Pune, a bustling city in the western state of Maharashtra, lies on the Deccan Plateau about 150 km southeast of Mumbai. It grew from the 17th-century Maratha stronghold of Shivaji’s son, who established the city as a centre of administration and learning. Today Pune mixes old and new: leafy avenues are lined with historic forts, colonial-era buildings and lively markets, while modern cafés, tech parks and universities give it a youthful, cosmopolitan vibe. Visitors can explore the tranquil Osho Garden, sample street-food delicacies such as misal pav, and enjoy the pleasant climate that makes strolling through its streets pleasant year-round.

pnr.name: Pointe-Noire
pnr.text: Pointe-Noire, perched on the Atlantic coast of the Republic of Congo, is the country’s principal seaport and commercial hub, lying about 350 km south-west of the capital Brazzaville. The town grew around the terminus of the Congo-Ocean Railway, which was finally completed in 1934, linking the interior to the sea and spurring rapid development. Today visitors find a lively mixture of modern hotels, bustling markets and palm-fringed beaches; the waterfront promenade is dotted with cafés where you can watch cargo ships and local fishermen alike, while the warm, humid climate makes it pleasant to explore the city’s lively streets and nearby nature reserves.

poa.name: Porto Alegre
poa.text: Porto Alegre lies on the eastern bank of the Guaíba estuary in southern Brazil, at the foothills of the Serra Gaúcha. Founded in 1769 as a Portuguese military outpost, it later became the capital of the state of Rio Grande do Sul and a key centre for the gaucho culture that blends European, Indigenous and African influences. Today the city feels lively and cosmopolitan, with tree-lined avenues, bustling cafés and a vibrant arts scene; the historic centre offers colonial architecture, while the waterfront parks provide relaxed views of the water and a chance to sample the region’s famous barbecues and wine.

pom.name: Port Moresby
pom.text: Port Moresby, the bustling capital of Papua New Guinea, sits on the southern coast of the island at the edge of the Gulf of Papua, framed by low hills and a harbour that once sheltered colonial steamers. It was first charted by the British naval officer Captain John Moresby in 1873, after whom the town is named, and later became the administrative centre of the Australian-administered Territory of New Guinea. Today the city offers a warm, humid climate, colourful markets where you can haggle for hand-woven bilums, the National Museum and Art Gallery showcasing indigenous art, and a leafy nature park where parrots and tree kangaroos roam, all set against a lively waterfront that blends modern cafés with traditional island hospitality.

por.name: Portsmouth
por.text: Portsmouth is a bustling coastal city on the southern coast of England, set on a natural harbour at the tip of the Langstone Peninsula in Hampshire. It has a rich naval heritage; the world-famous HMS Victory, Admiral Nelson’s flagship at the Battle of Trafalgar, still lies in the historic dockyard. Today the city blends maritime history with a lively waterfront: you can wander the historic streets, explore museums and the modern shopping precinct, enjoy fresh seafood by the sea, and catch ferries to the Isle of Wight, all under a backdrop of striking Victorian architecture and vibrant waterfront parks.

pos.name: Port of Spain
pos.text: Port of Spain sits on the western coast of Trinidad, tucked against the sheltered Gulf of Paria and framed by the lush Northern Range. The town was founded by the Spanish in 1592 and later fell under British control in 1797, becoming the island’s administrative centre. Today it buzzes with a lively mix of cultures: colourful market stalls sell fresh fruit and handmade crafts, the waterfront promenade offers panoramic sea views, and the streets come alive with music and dance during the world-famous Carnival. Visitors enjoy a blend of historic colonial architecture, modern cafés and a warm, welcoming atmosphere.

ppt.name: Pontianak
ppt.text: Pontianak sits on the banks of the Kapuas River in West Kalimantan, on the island of Borneo, and is famous for straddling the equator, marked by a modest monument where visitors can stand with one foot in each hemisphere. Founded in 1771 by Sultan Syarif Abdurrahman, the city grew as a trading hub for pepper and other spices during the Dutch colonial era. Today, Pontianak blends quiet riverside promenades with bustling night markets; you can sample fresh river fish, explore colourful Chinese temples, and enjoy a relaxed pace while the humid, tropical air carries the scent of incense and street food.

pra.name: Prague
pra.text: Prague, the capital of Czechia, sits on the Vltava River in the heart of Central Europe, roughly halfway between Berlin and Vienna. First recorded as a fortified settlement in the 9th century, it became the seat of Holy Roman Emperors in the 14th century, a period that left the city awash with Gothic and Baroque splendour. Today, wandering its cobbled streets feels like stepping into a living museum: the historic Old Town Square bustles with cafés, the Charles Bridge offers sunrise views over red-brick rooftops, and the vibrant mix of museums, street music and lively pubs makes every corner feel both timeless and lively.

pri.name: Pristina
pri.text: Pristina, the capital of Kosovo, sits in the eastern part of the country at the foot of the Çezare hills and is crossed by the river Prishtevica. The city’s roots stretch back to Roman times, and it later became an important Ottoman centre, evident in the striking architecture of the Imperial Mosque built in the late-16th century. Today Pristina buzzes with a youthful energy: cafés spill onto sidewalks, vibrant street art decorates old stone walls, and the bustling Mother Teresa Square hosts markets, concerts and lively conversations, offering visitors a warm blend of history and modern Balkan hospitality.

psd.name: Port Sudan
psd.text: Port Sudan is a bustling port city on Sudan’s far-eastern Red Sea coast, just a short drive from the border with Eritrea. Founded in 1905 to replace the older harbour of Suakin, it quickly grew into the country’s main gateway for maritime trade and for the export of oil and livestock. Today the city blends modern high-rise apartments with colourful fish markets, and the waterfront promenade offers fresh seafood, lively cafés and easy boat trips to nearby coral reefs. The warm, salty breeze and the sight of dhow-sailing boats give visitors a vivid sense of life on the Red Sea.

pse.name: Port Said
pse.text: Port Said sits at the northern entrance of the Suez Canal on the Mediterranean coast of Egypt, a bustling gateway where the sea meets the canal’s busy waterway. Founded in 1859 to serve the canal’s construction, it quickly grew into an international port and was a key base for the Allied forces during the 1948 Arab-Israeli conflict. Today the city blends historic charm with modern energy: you can wander the wide promenade lined with cafés, explore the lively souk for spices and crafts, and watch massive container ships glide past, while the sea breezes carry a sense of maritime adventure.

pty.name: Panama City
pty.text: Panama City, the bustling capital of Panama, sits on the Pacific coast at the southern end of the isthmus that links Central America with South America. Founded by the Spanish in 1519, it grew around the Pacific entrance to the Panama Canal, a marvel of engineering completed in 1914 that still shapes the city’s rhythm. Today visitors find a lively mix of sleek skyscrapers, colourful colonial districts such as Casco Viejo, and bustling markets where the scent of fresh seafood mingles with the hum of traffic. The waterfront promenade offers striking views of ships transiting the canal, while cafes and museums showcase the city’s multicultural heritage.

pus.name: Busan
pus.text: Busan, South Korea’s second-largest city, sits on the southeastern tip of the Korean Peninsula, hugging a natural harbour between rugged mountains and the Sea of Japan (East Sea). Historically, it was the site of the 1592 Battle of Busan where Japanese forces first landed during the Imjin War, marking a pivotal moment in the region’s defence. Today the city buzzes with a lively mix of modern skyscrapers, bustling fish markets and relaxed beachside promenades; you can savour fresh seafood at Jagalchi Market, stroll along the colourful streets of Gamcheon Culture Village, or watch the sunrise from Haeundae Beach while the city’s vibrant night life hums in the background.

pyg.name: Pyongyang
pyg.text: Pyongyang, the capital city of North Korea, lies on the Taedong River in the west-central part of the Korean Peninsula, roughly 190 km north of the demilitarised zone. Founded over a thousand years ago, it became the political centre of the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea in 1948 and was heavily rebuilt after the Korean War, giving it a distinctive mix of monumental socialist architecture and wide, tree-lined boulevards. Today visitors find a city of impressive monuments, orderly streets and strict security; guided tours allow glimpses of grand squares, museums and the vibrant local markets, though movement is closely monitored and photography of certain sites is restricted.

qta.name: Quetta
qta.text: Quetta, perched on a plateau in the south-western province of Balochistan, lies about 30 kilometres east of the Afghan border and 1,680 metres above sea level, giving it a surprisingly cool climate for the region. The city grew around a British Indian Army garrison and was severely damaged by the great earthquake of 1935, an event that led to extensive rebuilding and the distinctive colonial-era architecture that still dots its streets. Today visitors find a bustling market famous for fresh fruit and dry fruits, colourful bazaars selling traditional crafts, and easy access to striking limestone hills such as the Hazarganji-Chiltan National Park, making Quetta a rewarding mix of history, culture and natural beauty.

rak.name: Marrakech
rak.text: Marrakech, perched in the foothills of the Atlas Mountains in southern Morocco, is a vibrant crossroads of culture and history. Founded in the 11th century by the Almoravid dynasty, its red sandstone walls earned it the nickname “the Red City,” and its medina still buzzes with the same energy that once attracted caravans from across the Sahara. Today visitors wander the lively souks of Djemaa el-Fna square, sample fragrant tagines, and explore beautifully restored riads, while the scent of jasmine and the call to prayer create an unforgettable, sensory-rich atmosphere.

ram.name: Ramallah
ram.text: Ramallah, perched on a gentle hill about twelve kilometres north of Jerusalem in the central West Bank, is the administrative centre of the Palestinian Authority and a lively hub of modern Palestinian culture. Historically, it grew from a small Ottoman village into a prominent town and was declared the capital of the Palestinian National Authority in 1994, marking its political significance. Today visitors find a bustling mix of cafés, art galleries and bustling markets alongside leafy streets and panoramic views of the surrounding hills; the city’s friendly atmosphere, lively street art and a calendar full of festivals make it a rewarding stop for anyone exploring the region.

rec.name: Recife
rec.text: Recife, the capital of Pernambuco on Brazil’s northeastern coast, sits on a narrow strip of land between the Atlantic Ocean and a network of rivers and lagoons, giving it the nickname “the Venice of Brazil.” Founded by the Portuguese in the 16th century, the city grew around a strategic harbour that once protected the lucrative sugar-cane trade. Today visitors wander its colourful colonial quarter of Recife Antigo, explore vibrant markets and sample spicy seafood, while the bustling beaches of Boa Viagem and the lively rhythm of frevo music showcase a lively mix of history, culture and tropical sunshine.

rep.name: Siem Reap
rep.text: Siem Reap, nestled in north-western Cambodia about 320 km north of Phnom Penh, sits on the edge of the expansive floodplain of the Tonlé Sap lake. It is the gateway to the world-famous Angkor temple complex, which was the capital of the Khmer Empire from the early 9th to the 15th century and includes the iconic Angkor Wat, begun in the early 12th century. Today the town hums with a relaxed yet lively atmosphere: bustling night markets offer street food and handicrafts, cosy cafés line the riverfront, and the ruins are easily explored on bike or tuk-tuk, making Siem Reap a welcoming blend of ancient wonder and modern charm.

rig.name: Riga
rig.text: Riga, the capital of Latvia, sits on the banks of the Daugava River where it meets the Gulf of Riga in the Baltic Sea, about halfway between Tallinn and Tallinn. First mentioned in 1210, it grew into a prosperous Hanseatic trading hub, and its well-preserved medieval centre, the Old Town, still displays the ornate Art Nouveau façades that earned the city a UNESCO World Heritage listing. Today visitors wander cobbled streets lined with cafés and markets, climb the spire of St Peter’s Church for sweeping city views, and enjoy a lively mix of historic charm, modern design and a bustling riverside promenade.

rio.name: Rio de Janeiro
rio.text: Rio de Janeiro lies on Brazil’s southeastern coast, nestled between the Atlantic Ocean, the towering Sugarloaf Mountain and the expansive Guanabara Bay. Founded by the Portuguese in 1565, the city grew around a natural harbour that later became a key port for the empire’s gold shipments. Today Rio buzzes with a vibrant mix of beach culture, samba rhythms and striking street art; you can stroll along Copacabana’s golden sands, take a cable-car up to the iconic Christ the Redeemer statue for panoramic views, or explore bustling markets where the scent of grilled meat mingles with the salty sea breeze.

rkv.name: Reykjavik
rkv.text: Reykjavik, the capital of Iceland, lies on the southwestern coast at the mouth of the Faxaflói Bay, framed by gentle hills and the striking sea. Founded in the late 9th century, it grew from the settlement of Ingólfur Arnarson, the island’s first permanent Norse inhabitant, and later became the centre of Iceland’s medieval parliament, the Althing. Today the city feels compact yet vibrant, with colourful wooden houses, a lively café culture and easy walks to geothermal pools, museums and the striking Hallgrímskirkja church; the ever-present backdrop of mountains and ocean gives every visit a fresh, almost otherworldly feel.

rnd.name: Rostov-on-Don
rnd.text: Rostov-on-Don sits on the western bank of the Don River in southern Russia, a gateway to the vast steppe and the Black Sea coast. Founded in the mid-18th century as a fortress to protect the empire’s southern frontier, it grew into a bustling trade hub and today it buzzes with a lively mix of history and modernity. Visitors can wander the wide embankment lined with cafés, explore the striking Rostov Kremlin and its golden domes, and soak up the vibrant atmosphere of markets selling everything from fresh fish to traditional crafts, all under a warm, sun-lit sky.

rom.name: Rome
rom.text: Rome, the bustling capital of Italy, sits in the central part of the country on the banks of the Tiber River. It was the heart of the ancient Roman Empire, famed for landmarks such as the Colosseum, an arena built in the first century AD where gladiators once fought. Today the city blends its rich past with modern life: cobbled streets lead past bustling cafés, vibrant markets and stunning baroque churches, while locals and visitors alike enjoy leisurely walks past ruins, gelato in sunny piazzas and the lively hum of trams threading through centuries-old neighbourhoods.

ror.name: Koror
ror.text: Koror, the bustling centre of Palau, sits on a cluster of islands in the western Pacific just south of the Philippines and east of Indonesia, with the main town spread across Koror Island and nearby Ngerekebesang. It was the national capital until 2006, when the government relocated to Ngerulmud on Babeldaob, and during World War II it served as a Japanese naval base. Today the town blends colourful market stalls, friendly cafés and quiet beaches, while the iconic Rock Islands lie a short boat ride away, offering snorkellers crystal-clear lagoons and striking limestone karsts that feel both relaxed and adventure-filled.

ros.name: Roscoff
ros.text: Roscoff is a charming fishing port on the north-west coast of Brittany, France, facing the English Channel and just a short ferry ride from Plymouth. Founded in the Middle Ages, the town became famous in the 19th century as the departure point for the first regular trans-Channel steamship service, linking France and Britain. Today Roscoff delights visitors with its colourful harbour, slate-roofed houses and a bustling market where fresh seafood and the celebrated “Roscoff pink” seaweed are sold. Stroll along the promenade, explore the historic granite church and sample the local cider for a quintessential Breton experience.

rot.name: Rotterdam
rot.text: Rotterdam sits on the banks of the Nieuwe Maas in the western Netherlands, just a short train ride from The Hague and a half-hour from the North Sea coast. The city rose from the ashes after World War II when its historic centre was heavily bombed, prompting a bold rebuild that gave Rotterdam its striking modern skyline. Today, visitors can wander along the bustling waterfront, admire daring architecture such as the cube houses and Erasmus Bridge, and enjoy a lively mix of multicultural cafés, bustling markets and world-class museums, all set against the backdrop of the busy port that is the heart of Europe's shipping trade.

rou.name: Rouen
rou.text: Rouen, perched on the River Seine in north-western France, is the historic capital of Normandy, roughly an hour and a half by train from Paris. It was here in 1419 that Joan of Arc was tried and later executed, a moment that still haunts the city’s medieval streets. Today the town blends cobbled alleys and half-timbered houses with bustling cafés, a vibrant arts scene and impressive Gothic architecture such as the towering Notre-Dame Cathedral that famously inspired Monet’s series of paintings. A stroll through its markets, museums and riverfront promenades feels both timeless and lively.

rsl.name: Rosslare
rsl.text: Rosslare, perched on the south-eastern tip of County Wexford, looks out over the Atlantic and the narrow St Gillian’s Strait that separates Ireland from Wales. The town grew around Rosslare Harbour, which was opened in 1906 to serve the new steam-packet service to Fishguard and still handles daily ferries to Pembroke Dock. Today the harbour area is a bustling gateway for travelers, while the adjoining sandy beach and flat promenade invite leisurely strolls, and a handful of cosy cafés and traditional pubs offer a relaxed taste of coastal life.

rsu.name: Roseau
rsu.text: Roseau, the capital of Dominica, sits on the island’s western coast at the mouth of the Roseau River, framed by lush hills and the Caribbean Sea. The town began as a modest French fishing village in the 1760s and was designated the island’s administrative centre after the British took control later that decade. Today Roseau is a bustling yet relaxed hub, with colourful market stalls selling fresh produce and crafts, well-preserved colonial buildings, and a vibrant waterfront promenade that leads into the surrounding rainforest, offering visitors a warm welcome and easy access to hiking, waterfalls and the island’s famous natural beauty.

rtr.name: Rotorua
rtr.text: Rotorua, situated on the North Island’s Bay of Plenty about 230 km southeast of Auckland, is famous for its steaming geothermal parks and Māori cultural heritage. The town grew around the famous geyser that erupted in 1887, a landmark that helped put Rotorua on the map as a tourist destination in the late 19th century. Today visitors can wander through sulphur-smelling valleys, soak in mineral-rich hot pools, and enjoy performances of traditional haka and carving. With a lively lakeside promenade, a variety of cafés and adventure activities such as mountain-bike trails, Rotorua feels both a living museum and a vibrant playground for nature lovers.

ryd.name: Riyadh
ryd.text: Riyadh, the capital of Saudi Arabia, sits in the heart of the Arabian Peninsula on a plateau surrounded by desert and the rugged foothills of the Najd region. Historically it became the seat of the Saudi state in the early 20th century under Abdul-Aziz ibn Saud, who unified the kingdom from this modest town. Today the city dazzles visitors with sleek skyscrapers such as the Kingdom Centre, bustling souqs where spices and gold sparkle, and wide, palm-lined avenues that lead to modern museums showcasing the nation’s heritage. Despite its rapid growth, the warm hospitality and a touch of old-world charm remain ever present.

sal.name: Salisbury
sal.text: Salisbury is a historic market city set on the River Avon in the heart of Wiltshire, about 80 miles west of London and a short drive south from the stone circles of Stonehenge. Founded in Saxon times, it became famous in the 13th century for its magnificent cathedral, which boasts the tallest spire in England and houses the original Magna Carta. Today the city feels relaxed yet lively, with its medieval streets lined with independent shops, cozy cafés and a bustling market hall; the cathedral’s clock tower offers sweeping views of the surrounding countryside, making a visit both scenic and steeped in history.

san.name: Santander
san.text: Santander, perched on the northern coast of Spain in the autonomous community of Cantabria, is a lively seaside town overlooking the Bay of Biscay. Founded by the Romans as Portus Victoriae, it later became an important port for the Spanish crown, and its historic centre still shows the influence of 19th-century expansion under Queen María de las Mercedes. Today the city mixes elegant Art-Deco architecture with a bustling promenade, golden beaches and a vibrant culinary scene centred on fresh anchovies and local cheeses. Visitors can stroll along the Magdalena Peninsula, explore the maritime museum and enjoy the relaxed, salty air of this charming coastal gem.

sao.name: Sao Paulo
sao.text: Sao Paulo, Brazil’s sprawling southern-central metropolis, sits on a plateau about 70 km inland from the Atlantic coast, at the confluence of the Tietê and Pinheiros rivers. Founded by Jesuit priests in 1554, it grew from a modest village into the country’s industrial heart during the early 20th century, driving Brazil’s coffee boom and later its manufacturing might. Today the city dazzles with soaring skyscrapers, bustling markets and a vibrant street-art scene; you can wander the leafy Avenida Paulista, sample diverse cuisine from sushi to feijoada, and feel the energetic mix of cultures that makes Sao Paulo a dynamic, modern gateway to Brazil.

sbh.name: Sabha
sbh.text: Sabha is a bustling oasis town in southwestern Libya, set amid the vast Sahara and serving as the administrative centre of the Sabha District in the historic region of Fezzan. It grew to prominence as a key caravan hub on trans-Saharan trade routes, linking coastal ports with the interior and was later an important base for the Senussi movement in the early 20th century. Today visitors find a mix of modern life and traditional architecture, with palm-lined streets, a lively market where dates and textiles are sold, and nearby dunes that invite desert excursions under clear, bright skies.

scl.name: Santiago
scl.text: Santiago, Chile, lies in the fertile central valley of the country, cradled by the towering Andes to the east and the coastal range to the west, and it serves as the nation’s bustling capital. Founded in 1541 by the Spanish conquistador Pedro de Valdivia, the city grew from a modest colonial outpost into a major South-American metropolis. Today visitors find a lively mix of sleek skyscrapers, historic neighbourhoods such as Bellavista with its colourful murals, and expansive parks like the sprawling Cerro San Cristóbal, while the nearby vineyards and mountain passes offer easy escapes for wine-tasting and outdoor adventure.

scu.name: Santiago de Cuba
scu.text: Santiago de Cuba, perched on the southeastern coast of the island at the mouth of the Bay of Santiago, is Cuba’s second-largest city and a lively gateway to the island’s Afro-Cuban heritage. Founded in 1515, it later became the cradle of the Cuban Revolution, with the iconic Castillo del Morro watching over the harbour where Fidel Castro’s forces entered the city in 1959. Today the streets pulse with the rhythms of son and salsa, colourful colonial façades line bustling markets, and the surrounding hills offer spectacular views, making a visit feel like stepping into a vibrant, living history book.

sdg.name: San Diego
sdg.text: San Diego lies on the southern coast of California, bordering the Pacific Ocean and just a short drive from the Mexican border. Founded as a Spanish mission in 1769, the city grew around the historic Presidio and became a key naval base in the 20th century. Today it feels relaxed yet vibrant, with sun-kissed beaches, a bustling waterfront at the Embarcadero, and a mix of cultural attractions from the lively Gaslamp Quarter to the world-class museums of Balboa Park. Warm weather, friendly locals and endless outdoor activities make it a pleasant stop for any traveller.

sdq.name: Santo Domingo
sdq.text: Santo Domingo sits on the southern coast of the Dominican Republic, overlooking the Caribbean Sea where the Ozama River meets the harbour. Founded in 1496, it is the oldest continuously inhabited European settlement in the Americas and its historic Zona Colonial is a UNESCO World Heritage site full of cobbled streets, colourful façades and the first cathedral of the New World. Today the city blends the old with the new: lively plazas buzz with street musicians, modern cafés line the Paseo de los Trinitarios, and rooftop bars offer sweeping views of the sparkling sea and bustling port.

sea.name: Seattle
sea.text: Seattle, perched on the north-western edge of the United States where the Puget Sound meets Lake Washington, is a vibrant coastal city surrounded by water, mountains and evergreen forests. Founded in the 1850s, it grew quickly after the 1889 Great Seattle Fire and later became the gateway for the Klondike Gold Rush, which brought a surge of prospectors and wealth. Today visitors find a lively mix of modern skylines – highlighted by the iconic Space Needle – and historic neighbourhoods, bustling markets, coffee culture and ferry rides that showcase stunning views of the Olympic and Cascade ranges.

sel.name: Seoul
sel.text: Seoul, the capital of South Korea, sits on the Han River in the north-west part of the Korean Peninsula, surrounded by low mountains and modern high-rise districts. Founded over six centuries ago, it became the Joseon dynasty’s capital in 1394, and the ancient palace of Gyeongbokgung still marks that era. Today the city buzzes with a mix of sleek skyscrapers, bustling street markets and tranquil temples; you can sip coffee in a high-tech café, wander the neon-lit streets of Myeong-dong, or stroll along the riverbanks for a view of both historic rooftops and the futuristic skyline.

sev.name: Seville
sev.text: Seville, in the south-west of Spain, lies on the fertile banks of the Guadalquivir River and serves as the capital of the Andalusia region. It was the historic capital of the Islamic Emirate of al-Ándalus and later the seat of the powerful Spanish Inquisition. Today the city buzzes with a lively mix of tradition and modernity: you can wander the fragrant orange-tree-lined streets of the old Barrio Santa Cruz, marvel at the soaring arches of the Gothic cathedral and the ornate tiles of the Alcázar, and unwind in bustling tapas bars where the scent of jamón and sherry fills the air.

sey.name: Seydisfjordur
sey.text: Seydisfjörður is a colourful little town tucked into a deep fjord on the east coast of Iceland, where the mountains plunge straight into the sea. It grew up around a busy trading post in the 19th century and later became the terminus of the country’s first railway line, opened in 1949, which still runs from the harbour up to the highlands. Today the town is a haven for artists and hikers: its brightly painted wooden houses line cobbled streets, cafés spill onto the waterfront, and the surrounding hills and waterfalls offer spectacular walks, all under a backdrop of dramatic, ever-changing light.

sfo.name: San Francisco
sfo.text: San Francisco, a bustling city on the west coast of the United States, lies on a peninsula between the Pacific Ocean and San Francisco Bay in northern California. Founded in 1776 as a Spanish mission and later a key gateway for the Gold Rush of 1849, it grew into a centre of trade, innovation and culture. Today the city is famed for its iconic skyline crowned by the Golden Gate Bridge, its steep, cable-car-laden streets, and vibrant neighbourhoods such as the Mission and Chinatown. Visitors can savour world-class cuisine, explore museums and parks, and enjoy stunning sea-level views from every corner.

sgn.name: Ho Chi Minh City
sgn.text: Ho Chi Minh City, formerly Saigon, lies in southern Vietnam at the mouth of the Saigon River, about 60 km from the Cambodian border. Founded by the Khmer Empire and later taken by the French in the mid-19th century, it became the capital of South Vietnam until 1975.
