Today the city hums with a blend of sleek skyscrapers, bustling markets and colonial-era cafés; motorbikes swarm the streets while the scent of fresh pho and coffee drifts from street stalls. Visitors can explore historic landmarks such as the Reunification Palace, wander the lively Ben Thanh Market, and enjoy the vibrant night life along Bùi Viện.

sha.name: Shanghai
sha.text: Shanghai, perched on the east coast of China at the mouth of the Yangtze River, is a bustling metropolis where the past and future collide. Once a modest fishing village, it became an international treaty port in the mid-19th century, opening its doors to foreign trade and architecture that still lines the historic Bund. Today the city dazzles visitors with soaring skyscrapers like the Shanghai Tower, vibrant night markets, and tranquil gardens such as Yuyuan. Efficient metro lines whisk you between sleek shopping districts, art galleries and centuries-old temples, making Shanghai a lively, easy-to-explore gateway to modern China.

shz.name: Shiraz
shz.text: Shiraz, nestled in the south-western part of Iran, lies on the fertile plains near the Zāyanderud River, about 800 km south-east of Tehran. Renowned as the birthplace of the great poet Hafez, the city has long been a centre of Persian literature and art; its historic gardens and the remains of the ancient Persepolis complex just a short drive away testify to its storied past. Today Shiraz welcomes visitors with a relaxed, fragrant atmosphere, where the scent of orange blossoms drifts through tree-lined avenues, traditional tea houses sit beside sleek cafés, and the striking pink tiles of the Nasir al-Mulk mosque sparkle in the sunlight, offering a vivid blend of old-world charm and modern hospitality.

sin.name: Singapore
sin.text: Singapore, a bustling city-state at the southern tip of the Malay Peninsula, sits where the Singapore Strait meets the South China Sea. Founded as a British trading post in 1819, it grew from a modest port into a global hub of finance, technology and cuisine. Today the island offers a seamless blend of ultra-modern skyscrapers, lush gardens and vibrant neighbourhoods; you can stroll through the futuristic Marina Bay skyline, wander the heritage lanes of Chinatown and Little India, or relax in the tropical oasis of the Gardens by the Bay. Efficient public transport and a safe, multicultural atmosphere make it easy to explore the many flavours and sights this dynamic destination has to offer.

sjj.name: Sarajevo
sjj.text: Sarajevo, the capital of Bosnia and Herzegovina, sits in a verdant valley where the Miljacka River cuts between the Dinaric Alps and the surrounding hills of the Balkans. It was the site of the 1914 assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand that triggered the First World War, a pivotal moment in modern history. Today the city blends Ottoman bazaars, Austro-Hungarian architecture and vibrant street art, offering cosy cafés, lively markets and museums that trace its multicultural past. Walking the cobbled streets you feel a warm hospitality and a lively, resilient spirit that makes a visit both fascinating and welcoming.

sjn.name: St John's
sjn.text: St John’s, the bustling capital of Antigua and Barbuda, sits on the north-eastern coast of Antigua overlooking a natural harbour that has welcomed ships since the island was first settled in the 1600s. The town grew around the historic St John’s Cathedral, whose impressive stone tower dates from the mid-19th century, and it became the island’s commercial hub during the sugar-plantation era. Today the streets are a lively mix of pastel-coloured buildings, a vibrant market selling Caribbean spices and crafts, and a promenade where cruise-ship passengers mingle with locals, while the nearby beaches and clear waters provide a relaxed, tropical backdrop.

sjo.name: San Jose
sjo.text: San José lies in the heart of Costa Rica’s lush Central Valley, cradled by volcanic peaks such as Poás and Irazú and a short bus ride from both Pacific beaches and rainforest highlands. Founded in 1738 as a modest settlement, it was officially designated the nation’s capital in 1823 after independence from Spain and quickly grew into the country’s political and cultural hub. Today the city buzzes with a friendly, laid-back rhythm: colourful markets sell fresh fruit and artisan crafts, historic buildings house museums and cafés, and a network of green parks offers shade for strolling locals and curious travellers alike.

sju.name: San Juan
sju.text: San Juan, the capital of Puerto Rico, sits on the northeastern tip of the island, cradling a natural harbour between the Atlantic Ocean and the San Juan Bay. Founded in 1521, it is the oldest European settlement under United States jurisdiction and its walled Old Town still showcases forts such as El Morro, built to guard against 17th-century pirates. Today the city blends colourful Spanish colonial streets with modern cafés, vibrant street art and lively music venues; you can stroll beneath pastel façades, sip a cold Medalla beer on a rooftop terrace, and watch the sunset paint the sea while the rhythm of salsa drifts from nearby plazas.

skp.name: Skopje
skp.text: Skopje, the capital of North Macedonia, sits where the Vardar River cuts through a valley between the Šar and Kozjak mountains, about 240 km south-west of Belgrade. The city’s roots stretch back to antiquity; it was refounded as Scupi by the Romans after the original settlement was destroyed in the 4th-century earthquake, and later became an important Ottoman centre, evident in the 6th-century Stone Bridge that still spans the river. Today Skopje bustles with a mix of modern cafés, colourful street art and historic bazaars, offering visitors a lively blend of East-West culture beneath a backdrop of striking, newly rebuilt façades.

slc.name: Salt Lake City
slc.text: Salt Lake City lies in the north-western corner of the United States, nestled at the foot of the Wasatch Mountains and alongside the great Great Salt Lake in Utah. Founded in 1847 by Mormon pioneers led by Brigham Young, it quickly grew into a hub for westward settlers and the trans-continental railroad. Today the city blends modern skyscrapers with historic temples, offering easy access to outdoor adventures such as skiing, hiking and lake-side cycling, while its lively downtown boasts museums, a vibrant food scene and a welcoming, laid-back atmosphere.

sli.name: Saint-Louis
sli.text: Saint-Louis lies on the north-west coast of Senegal, perched on the left bank of the River Senegal just a short ferry ride from the capital Dakar. Founded in the 17th century as a French trading post, it became the capital of French West Africa in the 19th century before the seat moved to Dakar. Today the town is a charming blend of colonial architecture and lively markets: pastel-coloured houses line narrow streets, the historic Island of Saint-Louis offers cobbled lanes, museums and cafés, and the Atlantic breezes make evening walks along the waterfront especially pleasant.

sll.name: Salalah
sll.text: Salalah, nestled on the southern coast of Oman in the Dhofar Governorate, is a lush oasis framed by the Arabian Sea and dramatic mountains. Historically it was a key port on the ancient frankincense trade route, exporting the prized resin that once perfumed the courts of Egypt and Rome. Today the town dazzles visitors with its year-round greenery, especially during the khareef season when cool mist transforms the landscape into a tropical-like paradise. Stroll along the palm-lined waterfront, explore the ruins of the 17th-century Al-Baleed archaeological site, and savour fresh seafood in a relaxed, welcoming atmosphere.

sma.name: San Marino
sma.text: San Marino, the capital of the Republic of San Marino, sits on a hilltop in the Apennine foothills of central Italy, just a short drive north of Rimini on the Adriatic coast. It is famously the world’s oldest surviving republic, founded in 301 AD by a Christian stonemason named Marinus, and it has retained its independence through centuries of regional conflict. Today the town is a charming blend of medieval stone walls, narrow cobbled streets and bustling cafés, where visitors can wander the historic piazza, explore the three towering fortresses and enjoy panoramic views of the surrounding countryside while sipping an espresso.

smf.name: Sacramento
smf.text: Sacramento, the capital city of California, sits where the Sacramento and American Rivers meet in the heart of the state's fertile Central Valley. It grew rapidly during the Gold Rush, becoming the state capital in 1854 and preserving much of its 19th-century charm in the cobbled streets of Old Sacramento. Today the city offers a pleasant mix of history and modernity: riverfront parks invite picnics and kayaking, a lively farm-to-table restaurant scene showcases local produce, and museums such as the California State Railroad Museum and the Crocker Art Museum provide engaging cultural stops, all set against a backdrop of sunny skies and friendly locals.

smk.name: Samarkand
smk.text: Samarkand, nestled in the fertile valley of the Zarafshan River in southern Uzbekistan, was a key stop on the ancient Silk Road where merchants, scholars and caravans met for centuries. The city is famed for the breathtaking Registan Square, a trio of 15th-century madrasas whose intricate tilework and soaring arches showcase Timurid architecture at its finest. Today, Samarkand buzzes with a lively mix of bustling bazaars, fragrant tea houses and well-preserved monuments, making it easy to wander from the historic core to modern cafés while feeling the echo of its storied past.

sna.name: Sanaa
sna.text: Sanaa, the capital of Yemen, sits high in the western highlands at around 2,300 metres above sea level, overlooking the Wadi al-Sah. Its Old City, a UNESCO World Heritage site, is famed for towering mud-brick houses and intricately carved wooden windows that have been inhabited for centuries, making it one of the world’s oldest continuously lived-in settlements. Today, visitors wander bustling souks fragrant with coffee and spices, hear the call to prayer echo from ancient mosques, and experience a vibrant mix of tradition and resilience despite the challenges the city faces, offering a uniquely authentic glimpse of Yemeni culture.

sof.name: Sofia
sof.text: Sofia, the capital of Bulgaria, lies in the western part of the country at the foot of Vitosha Mountain, where the Iskar River winds through a broad valley. It has been inhabited since antiquity, and the city’s name first appears in Roman records as Serdica, a key centre of the empire in the fourth century. Today Sofia blends leafy boulevards, lively cafés and impressive Orthodox churches with the modern buzz of museums, galleries and a growing tech scene; a short funicular ride takes you up Vitosha for panoramic views and fresh mountain air, making a visit feel both historic and contemporary.

sou.name: Southampton
sou.text: Southampton, a port city on England’s south-coast, lies on the northern shore of the Solent where the River Itchen meets the sea. It is famous as the departure point for the RMS Titanic in 1912, a historic moment that still echoes in the city's maritime museums. Today the waterfront buzzes with a mix of modern waterfront bars, historic dockside warehouses and the vibrant cultural quarter around the old medieval walls. Visitors can wander the bustling market, explore the SeaCity Museum, enjoy a stroll along the historic Ocean Village marina, and take a short ferry ride to the Isle of Wight, all set against a backdrop of lively cafés and a friendly, bustling atmosphere.

spb.name: St Petersburg
spb.text: St Petersburg sits on the banks of the Neva River at the head of the Gulf of Finland, in north-western Russia, about 650 km west of Moscow. Founded by Peter the Great in 1703, it quickly became the imperial capital and a showcase of European architecture, exemplified by the Winter Palace and the network of canals that earned it the nickname “the Venice of the North”. Today the city dazzles visitors with its golden-dome cathedrals, world-class museums such as the Hermitage, bustling Nevsky Prospect and lively riverfront cafés, offering a blend of grand history and vibrant modern life.

spk.name: Sapporo
spk.text: Sapporo, the capital of Hokkaido in northern Japan, lies on a broad plain flanked by the Ishikari River and the surrounding mountains. Established as a centre for agricultural development in the late 19th century, the city grew rapidly after the 1871 land-grant policy that encouraged settlers from the mainland, and it later hosted the first Winter Olympics in 1972. Today Sapporo dazzles visitors with its tidy streets, fragrant ramen stalls, expansive parks and the famous snow festival, where towering ice sculptures light up the winter evenings, while summer offers cool breezes and easy access to nearby ski resorts.

spl.name: Split
spl.text: Split sits on the sparkling Adriatic coast of Croatia, roughly halfway between the Istrian peninsula and the island of Hvar, and it is the country’s second-largest city. Its heart is the massive Diocletian’s Palace, a 4th-century Roman imperial complex that still forms the bustling old town, a UNESCO World Heritage site that still houses shops, homes and cafés within its ancient walls. Today visitors wander the marble streets, enjoy fresh seafood on the Riva promenade, and can easily hop on ferries to nearby islands, while the Mediterranean climate, lively markets and striking sea views give the city a vibrant, relaxed atmosphere.

sps.name: San Pedro Sula
sps.text: San Pedro Sula sits in the north-western part of Honduras, on the banks of the Río Ulúa and just a short drive from the Caribbean coast. Founded in the 16th century, it grew into a major trading hub for bananas and coffee, helping to shape the country’s export economy. Today the city buzzes with a lively mix of modern malls, bustling markets and street-side eateries serving hearty baleadas and fresh seafood. Visitors can explore vibrant murals, sample the local nightlife in the lively downtown area, and use the city as a convenient base for trips to the nearby beaches and rainforest reserves.

srg.name: Sorong
srg.text: Sorong is a bustling port town on the north-west tip of West Papua, Indonesia, perched on the edge of the spectacular Raja Ampat archipelago. It grew out of a Dutch colonial outpost in the early 20th century, serving as a gateway for traders and missionaries travelling between the mainland and the surrounding islands. Today the town hums with motorbikes and market stalls, offering fresh seafood, colourful textiles and easy ferry links to the world-renowned diving spots of Raja Ampat. Visitors can explore lively waterfront cafés, sample local cuisine and soak up a lively, multicultural atmosphere framed by tropical hills and sea.

ssa.name: Salvador
ssa.text: Salvador, perched on the Atlantic coast of Brazil in the state of Bahia, is the country’s oldest colonial capital, founded in 1549 as the first seat of Portuguese administration in the New World. Its historic centre, the Pelourinho, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site where pastel-coloured baroque churches and cobbled streets echo the city’s Afro-Brazilian heritage. Today the city bursts with music, street art and bustling markets; you can savour spicy Bahian cuisine, dance to samba and axé in lively squares, and relax on sun-kissed beaches just a short tram ride from the colourful old town.

ssv.name: San Salvador
ssv.text: San Salvador, the bustling capital of El Salvador, sits in a wide valley surrounded by volcanic peaks such as the towering San Salvador Volcano to the north and the imposing San Miguel and Ilopango craters nearby. Founded in the early 16th century, it became the seat of the Spanish colonial administration after the conquest of the region. Today the city mixes colourful colonial architecture, lively markets and modern cafés; you can wander the historic centre, admire murals that celebrate its revolutionary past, and enjoy the cool, pleasant evenings that drift in from the surrounding highlands, making it a vibrant yet relaxed stop for travellers.

stg.name: St George's
stg.text: St George’s, the capital of Grenada, nestles on the island’s sheltered south-west coast, its harbour ringed by pastel-coloured buildings and the looming silhouette of Fort George, which was erected in the early 1800s to protect the town from sea-borne attack. Founded by the French in the mid-17th century and later becoming a British possession, the town retains a charming blend of Caribbean and colonial architecture. Today visitors wander the bustling market square, sip fresh coconut water on the waterfront promenade, and set off on day trips to nearby spice-plantation trails, all under a warm, breezy sky that makes St George’s feel both historic and vibrantly alive.

sth.name: Stockholm
sth.text: Stockholm, the capital of Sweden, spreads across 14 islands where the Baltic Sea meets Lake Mälaren in the eastern part of the country. First mentioned in a 13th-century charter, the city grew around the medieval Gamla Stan, its cobbled old town centred on the 13th-century St Nicholas Church and the Royal Palace. Today Stockholm feels clean and relaxed yet vibrant, with sleek waterfront promenades, leafy parks and a thriving café culture; you can wander from historic alleys to cutting-edge museums such as the Fotografiska, hop on a ferry to explore the archipelago, and enjoy long summer evenings illuminated by countless lanterns.

stj.name: Santiago
stj.text: Santiago de los Caballeros, nestled in the fertile Cibao valley of the Dominican Republic’s north-central plateau, is the island’s second-largest city and a hub of coffee and cacao production. Founded in the late-15th century, it later became the centre of the 19th-century Restoration War, a fact commemorated by the towering Monument to the Heroes of the Restoration that dominates the skyline. Today the city blends colonial charm with modern vibrancy: colourful market stalls line the bustling streets, lively cafés serve strong coffee, and the surrounding mountains offer scenic drives and opportunities to taste the region’s renowned rum and fresh tropical fruit.

stl.name: St Louis
stl.text: St Louis lies on the western bank of the Mississippi River in the heart of the American Midwest, about 300 miles west of the Illinois border. Founded in 1764 by French fur traders, the city grew around the historic Gateway Arch, a 630-foot stainless-steel monument that commemorates the westward expansion of the United States. Today visitors can stroll along the vibrant Riverfront, explore world-class museums such as the St Louis Art Museum and the Science Centre, and savour famous barbecue in the bustling downtown districts, all while enjoying the city’s blend of historic brick warehouses and modern skyline.

sto.name: Sao Tome
sto.text: São Tomé, the bustling capital of São Tomé and Príncipe, sits on the north-eastern coast of the island of São Tomé, midway between the west coast of Africa and the equator in the Gulf of Guinea. The town grew around a 16th-century Portuguese fort, São Sebastião, established when the islands became a key sugar-cane colony and later a centre of cocoa production. Today the streets are lined with pastel-coloured houses, lively markets and cafés serving fresh fish and tropical fruit, while the nearby volcanic hills offer gentle hikes and panoramic views of the sparkling Atlantic, making it a relaxed yet vibrant stop for curious travellers.

str.name: Strasbourg
str.text: Strasbourg, perched on the banks of the River Ill where France meets Germany, is the capital of the Alsace region in north-eastern France. Founded as a Roman settlement, it later became an Imperial Free City of the Holy Roman Empire and was a key centre of the Reformation, hosting the famous 1529 Diet of Augsburg delegates. Today the city charms visitors with its UNESCO-listed Grande Île, where the timber-framed “half-timber” houses line cobbled streets and the stunning Gothic cathedral towers above the bustling markets. A blend of French and German cuisine, lively cafés and modern European institutions makes Strasbourg a vibrant, walkable destination.

sub.name: Surabaya
sub.text: Surabaya, Indonesia’s bustling port city on the north-eastern coast of Java, lies where the Mahakam River meets the sea. It earned a place in history as the centre of the 1945 Battle of Surabaya, a pivotal fight for independence that left a legacy of pride still visible in its monuments and museums. Today the city blends colonial architecture with modern skyscrapers, offering lively markets, delicious street food such as satay and rawon, and a vibrant waterfront promenade where you can watch ships drift by and feel the energetic rhythm of everyday life.

suv.name: Suva
suv.text: Suva, the capital of Fiji, sits on the southeastern coast of Viti Levu, the country’s largest island, nestled between the deep blue harbour and the lush slopes of the surrounding hills. Established as a colonial administration centre in the late 19th century, it became the official capital in 1877 and retains many heritage buildings such as the old Parliament House. Today the city bustles with a friendly mix of markets, cafés and museums; you can stroll along the waterfront promenade, sample fresh seafood at the night market, and feel the laid-back island rhythm alongside the hum of a modern Pacific hub.

svc.name: Victoria
svc.text: Victoria, the tiny but lively capital of the Seychelles, sits on the north-west coast of Mahé, the archipelago’s largest island. The settlement began in 1778 under French control and was renamed Victoria in 1841 to honour Queen Victoria, becoming the administrative heart of the colony. Today the town is a pleasant blend of pastel-coloured Creole houses, a bustling market where spices, fresh fish and handmade crafts are hawked, and the iconic clock tower that watches over the harbour. Strolling along the waterfront, you can watch yachts bobbing beside colourful fishing boats and feel the relaxed rhythm of island life.

svx.name: Yekaterinburg
svx.text: Yekaterinburg, a sprawling city perched on the eastern side of the Ural Mountains, marks the traditional boundary between Europe and Asia. Founded in 1723 by the Russian tsar Peter the Great’s decree to develop the region’s mineral wealth, it later became infamous as the site where the last Russian tsar, Nicholas II, and his family were executed in 1918. Today the city blends Soviet-era grandeur with a vibrant contemporary scene: wide boulevards lead to stylish cafés, the historic Plotnitsa River walks are lined with art galleries, and the panoramic view from the nearby Ilmensky Plateau offers striking vistas of the city’s red-brick skyline against the rugged Urals.

syd.name: Sydney
syd.text: Sydney, Australia, sits on the eastern coast where the sparkling waters of Port Jackson meet the Pacific Ocean, framed by the iconic Harbour Bridge and the soaring sails of the Opera House. Founded in 1788 as a penal colony, it grew into a vibrant, multicultural metropolis. Today the city buzzes with outdoor cafés, bustling markets and sun-lit beaches such as Bondi and Manly, while the harbour offers stunning walks and ferry rides. With its mix of historic sandstone buildings, leafy parks and a lively arts scene, Sydney feels both relaxed and cosmopolitan, inviting visitors to explore its natural beauty and cultural flair.

syx.name: Shenyang
syx.text: Shenyang, the capital of Liaoning province in northeast China, sits on the Hun River about 300 km inland from the Yellow Sea. Historically it was the imperial capital of the early Qing dynasty, where the grand Mukden Palace was built in the early 17th century before the court moved to Beijing. Today the city blends modern skyscrapers with wide, tree-lined avenues, and visitors can wander the restored palace grounds, explore the bustling Zhongjie shopping street, and sample hearty local cuisine such as dumplings and braised pork, all against a backdrop of crisp, clean air and friendly hospitality.

szx.name: Shenzhen
szx.text: Shenzhen, a bustling metropolis in southern China, sits on the eastern shore of the Pearl River Delta, just north of Hong Kong. It was a modest fishing village until 1980, when it was designated as China’s first Special Economic Zone, sparking rapid development and turning it into a global technology hub. Today the city dazzles visitors with its soaring skyscrapers, vibrant street markets and world-class museums, while its parks and coastline offer quieter spots to relax. Efficient public transport makes it easy to explore the mix of cutting-edge innovation and colourful local culture.

tam.name: Toamasina
tam.text: Toamasina, often still called Tamatave, sits on the eastern coast of Madagascar where the Indian Ocean laps against a broad, low-lying harbour, making it the island’s principal seaport. The town grew in the early-19th century as a French trading post and later became a key hub for the export of coffee, sugar and vanilla. Today the streets are a lively mix of bustling markets, modest colonial-era buildings and colourful street food stalls, while the waterfront promenade offers relaxed cafés and views of fishing boats returning with their catch, giving visitors a genuine taste of coastal Malagasy life.

tao.name: Qingdao
tao.text: Qingdao, a coastal city in Shandong province on China’s Yellow Sea, is famed for its blend of German colonial heritage and modern seaside charm. Founded as a fishing village, it became a German concession in 1898, which left the striking red-tiled roofs of the former Governor’s Hall and the historic Badaguan neighbourhood. Today visitors can stroll along the bustling waterfront promenade, sip locally brewed Tsingtao beer in lively pubs, wander the fragrant jasmine-lined streets, and enjoy fresh seafood while taking in the backdrop of gentle hills and crystal-clear bays.

tar.name: Tartu
tar.text: Tartu, Estonia’s second-largest city, lies on the banks of the Emajõgi River in the south-eastern part of the country, about 180 km southeast of Tallinn. Founded in the 13th century, it became a centre of learning when the University of Tartu was established in 1632 and has retained a lively student atmosphere ever since. Today the city blends historic charm with modern vibrancy: cobbled streets lead to colourful wooden houses, the bustling market square hosts cafés and art stalls, and the riverfront offers pleasant walks, making Tartu a welcoming stop for culture lovers and curious travellers alike.

tbk.name: Timbuktu
tbk.text: Timbuktu, perched on the southern edge of the Sahara in northern Mali, lies where the Niger River bends and the desert begins. In the 14th-15th centuries it thrived as a centre of trade and scholarship, its famous Sankore University attracting scholars from across the Muslim world. Today the town is a quiet, sun-baked settlement of mud-brick buildings, bustling markets and the occasional tourist caravan. Visitors can wander the historic mosques, see ancient manuscript collections in guarded rooms, and feel the stark beauty of endless sand meeting the slow-flowing river, all while experiencing the warm hospitality of the local Tuareg and Songhai peoples.

tbs.name: Tbilisi
tbs.text: Tbilisi, the capital of Georgia, lies in the South-Caucasus where the Kura River meets the foothills of the Greater Caucasus mountains, about 400 km south-west of the Black Sea. Founded in the 5th century, it became a key crossroads on the ancient Silk Road, trading silk, spices and ideas between East and West. Today the city bursts with colour: narrow, winding streets in the historic Old Town sit alongside modern glass towers, while sulphur-smelling bathhouses, vibrant cafés and lively street art give a warm, welcoming feel that blends centuries of history with a lively contemporary spirit.

tbu.name: Nukualofa
tbu.text: Nukuʻalofa, the bustling capital of Tonga, sits on the western coast of the main island Tongatapu, its harbour framed by low hills and swaying palm trees. The town became the kingdom’s political centre in the mid-1800s, and the Royal Palace, erected in 1867, still overlooks the sea as a reminder of that era. Today the streets are a cheerful mix of colourful market stalls, friendly cafés and modest hotels, while the waterfront promenade offers easy walks, fresh fish on the barbie and a relaxed pace that lets visitors soak up the warm Pacific charm.

tbz.name: Tabriz
tbz.text: Tabriz, a bustling city in north-western Iran, lies in the fertile valley of the Qafqaz River near the foothills of the mighty Zagros range. It was the historic capital of the Safavid dynasty and the site of the famous 1909 constitutional revolution that helped shape modern Iranian politics. Today the city mixes ancient charm with modern energy: the UNESCO-listed Bazaar of Tabriz teems with colourful stalls selling carpets, spices and hand-crafted wares, while sleek cafés and art galleries line its lively streets. Visitors can wander its stone-paved alleys, savour local dishes such as ash e doogh, and enjoy panoramic views of the surrounding mountains.

teh.name: Tehran
teh.text: Tehran, Iran’s bustling capital, lies in a wide basin at the foot of the Alborz mountains, roughly 1,200 metres above sea-level in the north-central part of the country. Founded in the 18th century, it became the capital under the Qajar dynasty in 1796 and has since grown into a vibrant metropolis. Today the city blends towering glass skyscrapers with historic bazaars and lush parks; you can wander the bustling Grand Bazaar, admire the turquoise tiles of the Golestan Palace, and ride the scenic Tehran Metro up to the foothills for panoramic views. The mix of modern cafés, street food stalls and cultural museums makes a visit feel both contemporary and steeped in history.

tfs.name: Santa Cruz de Tenerife
tfs.text: Santa Cruz de Tenerife sits on the north-eastern coast of Tenerife, the largest of Spain’s Canary Islands, facing the Atlantic just off the African mainland. The city grew from a modest settlement established shortly after the Spanish conquest of the island in the late 15th century and became the island’s administrative centre in the 19th century. Today it is a lively, cosmopolitan port with palm-lined boulevards, modern art museums and bustling markets, while its nearby black-sand beaches and the famous Carnival add a festive, relaxed atmosphere that makes a stroll along the waterfront feel both contemporary and distinctly island-touched.

tgd.name: Podgorica
tgd.text: Podgorica, the capital of Montenegro, lies at the confluence of the Ribnica and Morača rivers in the country’s central plain, only a short drive from the Adriatic coast and the rugged mountains of the interior. First mentioned in Ottoman records in the 15th century, the city grew around a historic bridge that still spans the Morača, a reminder of its long role as a crossroads of trade and empire. Today Podgorica mixes modern cafés, leafy parks and vibrant street art with remnants of its past, offering visitors a relaxed yet lively base from which to explore Montenegro’s beaches, medieval towns and spectacular national parks.

tgu.name: Tegucigalpa
tgu.text: Tegucigalpa, the bustling capital of Honduras, sits high in a valley surrounded by the rugged mountains of the Central American interior at about 1,000 metres above sea level. Founded by Spanish settlers in the late 16th century, it became the nation’s official capital in the late 19th century, replacing the older city of Comayagua. Today the city mixes colonial charm with modern energy: colourful markets spill onto narrow streets, the historic cathedral watches over lively plazas, and cafés serve strong coffee while the surrounding hills offer striking views and opportunities for day-trips into lush national parks.

ths.name: Thessaloniki
ths.text: Thessaloniki, Greece’s vibrant second-city, sits on the north-eastern edge of the Thermaic Gulf at the foot of Mount Horti, where the Aegean Sea meets the inland plains of Central Macedonia. Founded in 315 BC by Cassander, it soon became a crucial Roman and Byzantine port and later the capital of the short-lived Kingdom of Thessalonica. Today the city buzzes with a lively waterfront promenade, bustling markets and a mix of Ottoman, Byzantine and modernist architecture; cafés spill onto the streets, the scent of fresh seafood drifts from tavernas, and the annual film festival adds a cosmopolitan sparkle to its historic charm.

tia.name: Tirana
tia.text: Tirana, the bustling capital of Albania, lies in the heart of the country where the River Lana meets the hills of Dajti National Park. Founded in the early 17th century, it grew around the historic Sulejman Pasha Mosque, a reminder of its Ottoman past. Today the city is a colourful mix of wide, tree-lined boulevards, striking modern architecture and lively cafés spilling onto the sidewalks. Visitors can wander through the vibrant Pazari i Ri market, admire the colourful façades of Skanderbeg Square, and take a short funicular ride up to Dajti for panoramic views over the lively streets below.

tij.name: Tijuana
tij.text: Tijuana, a bustling border city in north-western Mexico, sits just south of San Diego, California, straddling the Pacific coast and the US-Mexico frontier. Founded in 1889, it grew rapidly after the opening of the railway to the United States in the early 1900s, becoming a key gateway for trade and migration. Today the city hums with a vibrant mix of colourful street art, lively mercados and world-renowned street food, especially its famous tacos al pastor, while the waterfront promenade offers sweeping views of the ocean and the distant skyline of San Diego.

tim.name: Thimphu
tim.text: Thimphu, the capital of Bhutan, lies in the western Himalayas on a broad valley at about 2,300 metres above sea level, bordered by the Wang Chhu river and the towering peaks of the Himalaya range. It became the administrative centre in 1961, replacing Punakha, and the historic Tashichho Dzong still houses the king’s offices and the throne room. Today the town blends traditional Bhutanese architecture with modern cafés, colourful markets and lively festivals, offering visitors gentle walks through narrow streets, stunning mountain vistas and a warm welcome from locals who proudly preserve their unique culture.

tip.name: Tripoli
tip.text: Tripoli, the capital of Libya, lies on the central Mediterranean coast where the ancient Phoenician harbour merges with the modern cityscape. Founded in the 7th century BC, it later became the bustling centre of the Ottoman province of Tripolitania and still retains parts of the historic Medina with its narrow alleys and Ottoman-era forts. Today visitors find a blend of sandy beaches, vibrant souks selling spices and textiles, and a waterfront promenade lined with cafés offering fresh seafood. The city’s lively markets, colonial-style cafés and nearby ruins give a vivid glimpse of its layered past while providing a welcoming, cosmopolitan atmosphere.

tkb.name: Turkmenbashi
tkb.text: Turkmenbashi is a seaside town on the eastern shore of the Caspian Sea in western Turkmenistan, about 200 km west of the capital Ashgabat. It began life in 1869 as the Russian naval outpost of Krasnovodsk, a strategic port for ships crossing the Caspian. Renamed after the first president of independent Turkmenistan, the town now offers a relaxed waterfront promenade, a bustling fish market where you can sample freshly grilled sturgeon, and the chance to catch a ferry to Azerbaijan. The modern marina is lined with cafés and hotels, and the wide, sandy beaches provide a pleasant escape for walkers and sun-seekers alike.

tkd.name: Takoradi
tkd.text: Takoradi, a bustling coastal town in the Western Region of Ghana, lies on the Atlantic shoreline about 220 km west of Accra and forms part of the twin city Sekondi-Takoradi. Founded in the 19th century as a harbour for the export of cocoa and timber, it later became a key naval base during World War II, a role that still echoes in its historic fort and museum. Today the town buzzes with colourful markets, lively street food stalls serving grilled fish and jollof rice, and a laid-back waterfront where palm-shaded promenades invite visitors to watch ferries and fishing boats glide by, offering a warm mix of commerce, culture and seaside charm.

tku.name: Turku
tku.text: Turku lies on the southwest coast of Finland, at the mouth of the Aura River where it meets the Archipelago Sea, making it a natural gateway between mainland Finland and the islands. Founded in the 13th century, it served as the country’s first capital and retains the medieval Turku Castle, a sturdy stone fortress that has watched over the city since the 1280s. Today the town buzzes with a relaxed, creative atmosphere: cobbled streets lead to lively cafés, museums and the vibrant riverbank promenade, while festivals, art galleries and a thriving food scene give visitors plenty to explore in a compact, walkable setting.

tll.name: Tallinn
tll.text: Tallinn, the capital of Estonia, sits on the northern coast of the country overlooking the Gulf of Finland. Its medieval Old Town, a UNESCO World Heritage site, still retains the original city walls and cobblestone streets that were first fortified in the 13th century when the Danes founded the settlement. Today the city blends history with a lively modern vibe: you can wander the pastel-coloured houses, enjoy innovative cuisine in stylish cafés, and explore tech-forward museums and galleries, all while the Baltic Sea breezes give the town a fresh, welcoming feel.

tlr.name: Toliara
tlr.text: Toliara, on Madagascar’s southwestern coast, sits beside the Baie des Baly and faces the vast Indian Ocean, with the arid spiny forest of the Antsokay Reserve just inland. Founded in the mid-19th century as a French trading post, the town grew around its natural harbour, which once handled ivory and spices. Today visitors find a relaxed seaside atmosphere, colourful market stalls selling fresh seafood and zebu meat, and easy access to striking limestone cliffs and the famous “Shipwreck Beach” where the wreck of the MV Mimosa rests. The warm climate and friendly locals make it a rewarding off-the-beaten-path stop.

tls.name: Toulouse
tls.text: Toulouse, in southwestern France, lies on the banks of the Garonne River about 150 km east of the Atlantic coast. Known as “La Ville Rose” for its distinctive pink-hued bricks, the city was a centre of medieval commerce and later became a hub of the aerospace industry, home to the headquarters of Airbus. Visitors today can wander its historic centre, admire the towering Saint-Sernin basilica, and relax in lively cafés lining the riverfront, while the modern university atmosphere adds a youthful buzz to the charming, sun-lit streets.

tlv.name: Tel Aviv
tlv.text: Tel Aviv, Israel’s vibrant Mediterranean coastline city, lies just north of the ancient port of Jaffa and stretches along a sun-kissed shoreline. Founded in 1909 by Jewish families breaking away from Jaffa, it quickly grew into a modern, cosmopolitan hub and was the temporary seat of Israel’s government after independence in 1948. Today the city buzzes with lively markets, Bauhaus-style white-washed buildings, bustling cafés and a famed nightlife, while its wide promenades and golden beaches invite relaxed strolls or a dip in the sea; the mix of history, culture and seaside leisure makes it a compelling stop for any traveller.

tng.name: Tangier
tng.text: Tangier, perched on the north-western tip of Morocco where the Mediterranean meets the Atlantic, has long been a gateway between Europe and Africa. Historically it was a key port for Phoenician traders and later became famous in the 20th century as an international zone that attracted artists, writers and spies. Today the town bustles with colourful souks, sleek cafés overlooking the Strait and a mix of modern hotels beside restored medina streets; you can wander the Kasbah for sweeping sea views, sample fresh seafood in the harbour, and feel the relaxed, multicultural rhythm that still defines this historic crossroads.

tnr.name: Antananarivo
tnr.text: Antananarivo, the bustling capital of Madagascar, sits on a high plateau in the island’s central highlands, about 1,200 metres above sea level and surrounded by rolling hills and volcanic craters. Founded in the early 17th century as the royal city of the Merina kingdom, it became the administrative centre of the French colony in the late 1800s. Today the city blends historic wooden palaces and vibrant markets with colourful street art and lively cafés; visitors can wander the bustling Analakely market, explore the former royal palace on the hilltop, and enjoy sweeping views of the surrounding countryside while sampling Malagasy coffee and cuisine.

tof.name: Tomsk
tof.text: Tomsk lies in western Siberia, on the banks of the Tom River about 650 km east of the Ural Mountains and roughly 2 000 km northeast of Moscow. Founded in 1604 as a fort on the Siberian trade route, it is one of the oldest towns in the region and today hosts Russia’s first university, established in 1888. Visitors find a lively mix of historic wooden houses, leafy avenues and modern cafés, while the riverfront offers pleasant walks and occasional boat trips. Museums, theatres and a vibrant student community give the city a youthful, cultural buzz that contrasts pleasantly with its frontier heritage.

tol.name: Toledo
tol.text: Toledo, perched on a high plateau above the Tagus River in the heart of Castilla-La Mancha, lies about 70 kilometres south-west of Madrid. The city was the capital of the Visigothic Kingdom in the 6th century and later became a celebrated centre where Christian, Muslim and Jewish communities lived side by side, a legacy still visible in its winding medieval streets and the impressive cathedral that dominates the skyline. Today visitors can wander the cobbled alleys, explore the Alcázar fortress, sample the famous marzipan and enjoy sweeping river views from the ancient walls, all amidst a vibrant mix of history and lively cafés.

tou.name: Tours
tou.text: Tours, set on the gentle bend of the River Loire in the heart of France’s historic Centre-Val de Loire, is a lively gateway to the country’s famed châteaux. Its medieval old town grew around the impressive Saint-Gatien cathedral, which dates back to the 12th century and bears the marks of the Hundred Years’ War. Today the city blends that rich heritage with a bustling, contemporary vibe: cobbled streets are lined with cafés and boutique shops, the vibrant market on Place Plumereau hums with locals, and river cruises offer relaxed views of the surrounding vineyards. Tours feels both comfortably historic and refreshingly modern, making it a pleasant stop for any traveller.

tpa.name: Tampa
tpa.text: Tampa sits on the western edge of Florida, straddling the Hillsborough River where it meets the Gulf of Mexico, and is the largest city in the Tampa Bay area. The settlement began as Fort Brooke in 1824, later growing into a bustling port and, in the late-19th century, becoming famous for its thriving cigar factories in Ybor City, a neighbourhood founded by Cuban and Spanish immigrants. Today the city offers a lively mix of modern skyline, waterfront parks and a lively historic quarter, while nearby sandy beaches, Busch Gardens and a diverse food scene make a visit both relaxed and exciting.

tpe.name: Taipei
tpe.text: Taipei, the bustling capital of Taiwan, sits in the northern part of the island at the edge of the Tamsui River and is framed by the surrounding hills of Yangmingshan. It was designated the provincial capital in 1887 during Qing rule and later grew under Japanese administration before becoming the island’s political and cultural centre. Today the city blends skyscrapers such as Taipei 101 with lively night markets, fragrant street-food stalls and tranquil temples; an efficient MRT network makes it easy to wander from modern malls to historic neighbourhoods, offering a friendly, energetic experience for any visitor.

trp.name: Tripoli
trp.text: Tripoli, Lebanon, sits on the Mediterranean coast about 85 km north of Beirut, nestled between the sea and the rugged hills of the Nahr al-Kebir valley. Founded in the 2nd century BC, it became a thriving centre of the Crusader Kingdom of Jerusalem and still bears the imprint of that era in its well-preserved medieval citadel and winding souk. Today the town bustles with colour-filled markets selling olives, spices and hand-woven textiles, while cafés spill onto sun-drenched streets and the nearby beaches offer a relaxed escape, making Tripoli a lively blend of history and everyday Lebanese hospitality.

tsh.name: Tashkent
tsh.text: Tashkent, the bustling capital of Uzbekistan, lies in the east-central part of the country on the fertile banks of the ancient Syr Darya river. Once a key stop on the Silk Road, the city was famously rebuilt after a powerful earthquake in 1966, which gave it a striking mix of Soviet-era apartment blocks and sleek modern skyscrapers. Today visitors can wander through colourful bazaars selling spices, silk and ceramics, relax in leafy parks shaded by plane trees, and ride the clean, efficient metro that threads through the historic centre, feeling both the weight of history and the pulse of contemporary life.

tsn.name: Tianjin
tsn.text: Tianjin, a bustling port city in northern China, sits on the banks of the Hai River about 120 kilometres southeast of Beijing. It grew into a major treaty port after the Opium Wars, when foreign concessions were established in the 19th century, leaving a distinctive mix of European-style architecture and traditional Chinese streets. Today the city blends sleek skyscrapers with historic districts such as the Italian-style St Leonardo’s Avenue, offering lively food markets, river cruises, and modern art galleries. Visitors can savour fresh seafood, wander the colourful hutongs and enjoy a vibrant nightlife that reflects both its rich past and its fast-moving present.

tun.name: Tunis
tun.text: Tunis, the bustling capital of Tunisia, sits on the north-eastern edge of the country where the Mediterranean Sea meets the fertile plain of the Gulf of Tunis. Founded by the Phoenicians and later becoming a major centre of the Roman province of Africa, its medina still contains the impressive 9th-century Great Mosque of Al-Zaytuna. Today the city blends ancient winding alleys with modern cafés, lively souks and a vibrant waterfront promenade; you can wander past Ottoman-era palaces, sample fragrant harissa-spiced dishes, and enjoy sweeping sea views from the nearby Carthage ruins.

tur.name: Turin
tur.text: Turin, nestled in the north-west of Italy at the foot of the Alps and straddling the Po River, was the first capital of a unified Italy in 1861 and retains grand boulevards reminiscent of its regal past. Today the city blends elegant baroque architecture with a lively café culture; you can sip an espresso beside the Mole Antonelliana, explore the sleek museums of contemporary art, and wander the leafy Valentino Park. Its bustling markets, Michelin-starred chocolate shops and vibrant university atmosphere make Turin a warm, cosmopolitan stop for any traveller.

tus.name: Tucson
tus.text: Tucson, nestled in the southern part of Arizona about 60 miles north of the Mexican border, lies at the edge of the Sonoran Desert and is framed by the Santa Catalina, Rincon and Tucson Mountains. The town began as a Spanish presidio in 1775, making it one of the oldest European-settled communities in the American Southwest. Today the city blends desert scenery with a lively cultural scene: you can wander historic Fourth Avenue, explore the University of Arizona’s museums, admire towering saguaro cacti in Saguaro National Park, and enjoy a thriving food and arts scene that feels both relaxed and surprisingly cosmopolitan.

tvn.name: Torshavn
tvn.text: Tórshavn, the capital of the Faroe Islands, lies on the southern tip of Streymoy island where the narrow inlet of the harbour meets the North Atlantic, and it is linked by bridges to the neighbouring island of Hestur. Founded in the 9th century, it received its town charter from King Christian III in 1583, making it one of the oldest continuously inhabited settlements in the North Atlantic. Today the town feels surprisingly intimate: colourful timber houses line cobbled streets, cosy cafés serve fresh fish and rye bread, and the harbour is a lively meeting point for sailors, cyclists and anyone keen to soak up rugged coastal charm.

tws.name: Tarawa
tws.text: Tarawa, the bustling strip of villages that make up South Tarawa, sits on a narrow coral atoll in the central Pacific and serves as the capital of Kiribati, about 4,500 km south-west of Honolulu. It was the scene of the fierce Battle of Tarawa in February 1943, when United States forces captured the Japanese-held island of Betio during World War II. Today the capital feels like a lively, low-lying town of pastel-coloured homes, bustling markets and friendly locals, with a modest but welcoming tourism scene – you can explore mangrove-fringed lagoons, sample fresh tuna and enjoy relaxed evenings watching the sunrise over the endless Pacific.

tyo.name: Tokyo
tyo.text: Tokyo, Japan’s bustling capital, sits on the eastern coast of the island of Honshu where the Sumida River meets Tokyo Bay. Once a small fishing village called Edo, it became the seat of the Tokugawa shogunate in the early 1600s and was renamed Tokyo, meaning “Eastern Capital”, when the emperor moved there in 1868. Today the city blends towering skyscrapers, neon-lit districts such as Shibuya and historic sites like the Meiji Shrine, offering a seamless mix of ultra-modern technology, vibrant street food and tranquil gardens that make every stroll feel both exciting and surprisingly calm.

tzx.name: Trabzon
tzx.text: Trabzon sits on the northeastern coast of Turkey, perched on the Black Sea’s rugged shoreline and framed by the Pontic Mountains. Historically it was the capital of the ancient kingdom of Pontus and later an important Byzantine port, famously the terminus of the Silk Road’s maritime leg. Today the city blends seaside charm with lively bazaars, fresh seafood cafés and the striking Sumela Monastery clinging to a cliff above the forested valley. Visitors can stroll along the promenade, explore the vibrant market of the old town and enjoy panoramic views from the hilltop parks that overlook the sparkling sea.

ufa.name: Ufa
ufa.text: Ufa, the capital of Bashkortostan in the western foothills of the Ural Mountains, sits on the banks of the Belaya River about 1,200 km east of Moscow. Founded in 1574 as a Russian fortress, it later became an important centre for oil production in the early 20th century, shaping its industrial heritage. Today the city blends Soviet-era architecture with vibrant cultural life: you can stroll along the river promenade, explore the colourful Bashkir State Museum, and sample hearty Tatar and Bashkir cuisine in bustling cafés, while the surrounding hills offer easy hikes and a refreshing contrast to the urban bustle.

uio.name: Quito
uio.text: Quito, the capital of Ecuador, sits high in the Andes at an altitude of about 2,850 metres, making it one of the world’s highest capital cities. Founded by the Spanish in 1534, it preserves a remarkably intact colonial centre that was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1978, with churches, plazas and narrow cobbled streets that echo the city’s 16th-century past. Today visitors find a vibrant mix of old and new: bustling markets selling fresh fruit and handmade crafts, modern cafés perched on sun-lit terraces, and a backdrop of snow-capped volcanoes that frame the city’s lively streets and friendly atmosphere.

ulb.name: Ulaanbaatar
ulb.text: Ulaanbaatar sits in north-central Mongolia, perched at about 1,350 metres on the banks of the Tuul River and surrounded by the vast steppe and forested hills of the country's heartland. The city began life in 1639 as a mobile Buddhist monastery and, after a nomadic wander, was established permanently and later declared the national capital in 1911. Today the capital is a lively blend of Soviet-era apartment blocks, gleaming glass towers and traditional ger neighbourhoods, with bustling markets, museums and cafés offering a warm welcome despite the crisp, often snowy, climate.

ule.name: Ulan-Ude
ule.text: Ulan-Ude, perched on the western bank of the mighty Selenga River where it meets Lake Baikal, is the capital of the Republic of Buryatia in eastern Siberia, just a few hours’ train ride east of Irkutsk. Founded as a Russian fort in the mid-17th century, the town later became an important stop on the Trans-Siberian Railway, a fact still evident in its bustling station and historic wooden houses. Today visitors find a vibrant blend of Russian and Buryat cultures: colourful Buddhist monasteries sit alongside Soviet-era buildings, street markets overflow with traditional crafts and fresh fish, and the nearby lake offers crisp, clean air and stunning sunrise reflections that make Ulan-Ude a uniquely refreshing gateway to Siberia.

urc.name: Urumqi
urc.text: Urumqi, the capital of Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region in north-west China, sits at the foot of the Tianshan Mountains where the ancient Silk Road once linked China with Central Asia. Founded more than two millennia ago, the city became a key trading hub in the 13th-century Mongol Empire, a fact reflected in the historic Grand Bazaar where spices, carpets and dried fruit still change hands. Today visitors find a modern metropolis framed by snow-capped peaks, with wide boulevards, vibrant night markets, and museums that showcase the diverse cultures of the region, all set against a backdrop of clear, high-altitude air.

ush.name: Ushuaia
ush.text: Ushuaia, the southernmost city in the world, sits on the edge of the Beagle Channel at the tip of Argentina’s Tierra del Fuego island, framed by snow-capped mountains and windswept seas. It was founded in 1884 as a penal colony, and later grew into a gateway for Antarctic expeditions. Today the town feels lively yet relaxed, with colourful wooden houses, bustling marinas and cosy cafés serving hearty Patagonian fare. Visitors can wander the waterfront, take a cable-car up to the Martial Glacier for stunning views, or set off on boat trips to explore the surrounding national park and its abundant wildlife.

utr.name: Utrecht
utr.text: Utrecht, situated in the heart of the Netherlands about 35 kilometres southeast of Amsterdam, is a historic city built around the winding canals that radiate from its medieval centre. It grew around the 7th-century cathedral that became the seat of the powerful Bishopric of Utrecht, and the iconic Dom Tower, the tallest church tower in the country, still dominates the skyline. Today the city feels relaxed yet vibrant: you can wander the shaded Oudegracht wharf, sip coffee in a cosy café tucked beneath the canal arches, explore quirky museums and enjoy a lively market scene, all within easy reach of the surrounding Dutch countryside.

vad.name: Vatican City
vad.text: Vatican City, a tiny independent enclave nestled within Rome, Italy, sits on the western bank of the Tiber River and covers just 44 hectares. It became a sovereign state in 1929 with the signing of the Lateran Treaty, establishing the Holy See’s temporal independence after centuries of papal rule. Today the city feels like an open-air museum: you can wander past the soaring dome of St Peter’s Basilica, admire Michelangelo’s frescoes in the Sistine Chapel, stroll through tranquil gardens, and savour the quiet reverence that lingers alongside bustling pilgrim crowds.

val.name: Valencia
val.text: Valencia, Spain, sits on the eastern Mediterranean coast where the Turia River meets the sea, about three hours by train south of Barcelona. Founded as a Roman colony in the second century BC, the city later flourished under Moorish rule and retained its medieval walls, parts of which you can still see strolling through the historic centre. Today Valencia feels vibrant and laid-back: you can wander the futuristic City of Arts and Sciences, sip a chilled horchata in a sun-dappled plaza, or wander the bustling Central Market, all while the scent of paella drifting from seaside restaurants reminds you why this port city is a favourite stop for travellers.

van.name: Vancouver
van.text: Vancouver, a coastal city on the mainland of British Columbia, sits on the Pacific shoreline between the North Shore mountains and a bustling harbour, with the spectacular backdrop of the Pacific Ocean. Established in 1886 as a terminus for the Canadian Pacific Railway, it grew rapidly and later hosted the 2010 Winter Olympics, showcasing its world-class facilities and stunning natural scenery. Today the city feels lively and welcoming, offering a blend of towering skyscrapers, lush parks such as Stanley Park, vibrant multicultural neighbourhoods, and a renowned food scene that ranges from fresh seafood to Asian street-style markets, all within easy reach of mountains and sea.

vap.name: Valparaiso
vap.text: Valparaiso, perched on the steep hillsides of central Chile overlooking the Pacific, is a bustling port city about 120 km northwest of Santiago. Founded in the 16th century, it grew into one of the world’s most important harbours in the 19th century, famously becoming a key stop for ships travelling between Europe and the Americas. Today the city dazzles visitors with its colourful, maze-like neighbourhoods, historic funiculars and vibrant street art that climbs the cliffs, while the bustling waterfront offers fresh seafood, lively markets and a lively café culture that captures the city’s eclectic, bohemian spirit.

vdz.name: Vaduz
vdz.text: Vaduz, the capital of the tiny Alpine principality of Liechtenstein, sits on the eastern bank of the Rhine, tucked between Switzerland and Austria. The town grew around a medieval fortress that was first mentioned in the 12th century and later became the residence of the Liechtenstein princely family. Today Vaduz feels both regal and relaxed: you can wander past the pastel-coloured buildings to the striking Vaduz Castle perched above the town, explore the modern art museum, and enjoy cafés with views of the surrounding mountains, all within a compact, pedestrian-friendly centre.

ven.name: Venice
ven.text: Venice, a city of islands in the north-east of Italy, sits in the shallow lagoon of the Adriatic Sea and is linked by more than 400 bridges and narrow canals. It was a powerful maritime republic from the Middle Ages, dominating trade between Europe and the East and famed for its elaborate glassmaking on the island of Murano. Today, visitors wander past bustling markets and quiet back-streets, glide beneath elegant arched bridges in a vapour-rising gondola, and enjoy coffee in historic squares where the scent of fresh seafood mixes with the echo of centuries-old bells.

ver.name: Veracruz
ver.text: Veracruz, a bustling port city on the Gulf of Mexico, sits on a broad, palm-lined bay about 400 km southeast of Mexico City. Founded by Hernán Cortés in 1519, it quickly became the principal gateway for Spanish treasure ships and still bears the imposing 16th-century fortress of San Juan de Ulúa, a reminder of its pirate-filled past. Today the city hums with Afro-Caribbean rhythm; the lively Malecón offers fresh seafood, colourful markets and the scent of coffee, while the historic centre showcases colonial churches and lively plazas where locals dance to son jarocho, making a visit feel both vibrant and steeped in history.

vie.name: Vienna
vie.text: Vienna, the capital of Austria, lies in the country’s eastern corner along the Danube River, framed by the Alpine foothills. It was the imperial seat of the Habsburg dynasty for centuries, and its historic centre still bears the grandeur of that era with baroque palaces such as the Hofburg and the stunning State Opera House. Today the city blends this regal past with a lively, modern vibe: coffee houses hum with conversation, museums showcase works from Klimt to contemporary artists, and the streets are lined with markets, parks and efficient tram lines that make exploring a pleasure for any visitor.

vli.name: Port Vila
vli.text: Port Vila, the capital of Vanuatu, sits on the sheltered harbour of Efate Island in the South Pacific, framed by volcanic hills and turquoise waters. Founded as the French colonial settlement of Port du Saint-Esprit in the early 20th century, it later became the joint administrative centre of the British-French Condominium before Vanuatu’s independence in 1980. Today the town is a vibrant blend of colourful market stalls, cosy cafés and modern boutiques, with friendly locals eager to share their Melanesian culture; the surrounding reefs and nearby islands make it a popular base for snorkeling, sailing and relaxed island exploration.

vln.name: Vilnius
vln.text: Vilnius, the capital of Lithuania, sits on the banks of the Neris River in the country’s southeastern corner, close to the borders of Belarus and Poland. First mentioned in written sources in 1323, the city grew around the medieval Old Town, which today is a UNESCO World Heritage site famed for its cobbled streets, Baroque churches and the striking Gediminas Tower. Visitors can wander the lively market square, enjoy coffee in cosy cafés, and explore museums that trace Lithuania’s rich past, while the surrounding hills and parks offer a peaceful escape from the bustling city centre.

vns.name: Varanasi
vns.text: Varanasi, perched on the banks of the Ganges in the Indian state of Uttar Pradesh, is one of the world’s oldest continuously inhabited cities. It has been a centre of Hindu worship for millennia, and the ghats where pilgrims bathe were already described by the Greek traveller Fa-Hien in the early 5th century CE. Today the city hums with a lively mix of ancient rituals and modern bustle: sunrise sees devotees performing rites on the steps of the river, while narrow lanes overflow with colourful market stalls, fragrant street food and the echo of temple bells, offering visitors a truly immersive cultural experience.

vte.name: Vientiane
vte.text: Vientiane, the capital of Laos, sits on the banks of the Mekong River opposite Thailand, at the country’s north-western edge. Founded centuries ago as a modest settlement, it became the royal seat in the 14th-century Lan Xang kingdom and later a French colonial outpost, leaving a quiet blend of Buddhist temples and colonial architecture. Today the city feels relaxed and walkable, with the gilded stupa of Pha That Luang dominating the skyline, riverside cafés serving fresh coffee, and night markets offering fragrant street food. Its laid-back pace, friendly locals and modest riverfront charm make Vientiane a pleasant stop for any traveller.

vvi.name: Santa Cruz
vvi.text: Santa Cruz de la Sierra sits in the eastern lowlands of Bolivia, about 400 km east of the Andes and close to the border with Brazil, forming the capital of the Santa Cruz department. It was founded in 1561 by the Spanish explorer Ñuflo de Chaves as a modest settlement on the banks of the Piraí River. Today the city bursts with colour and energy: wide, tree-lined avenues lead to lively plazas, modern cafés sit alongside bustling mercados, and the surrounding tropical countryside offers easy trips to wildlife reserves and waterfalls, making a visit both contemporary and full of natural charm.

vvo.name: Vladivostok
vvo.text: Vladivostok, perched on the rugged coast where the Pacific Ocean meets the Sea of Japan, is the far-eastern gateway of Russia, just a stone’s throw from the borders of China and North Korea. Founded in 1860 as a military outpost, it grew into a bustling port and the headquarters of the Russian Pacific Fleet. Today the city blends Soviet architecture with modern cafés, offering a lively waterfront promenade, fresh seafood markets and the iconic Russky Bridge spanning the strait. Visitors can ride the cable car up to Eagle’s Nest for sweeping city views, explore the historic railway museum, and enjoy a relaxed atmosphere that feels both distinctly Russian and surprisingly cosmopolitan.

war.name: Warsaw
war.text: Warsaw, the capital of Poland, sits on the banks of the Vistula River in the east-central part of the country. The city’s Old Town, with its colourful townhouses and cobbled squares, was painstakingly rebuilt after being razed during the Second World War and is now a UNESCO World Heritage site. Today Warsaw buzzes with a lively mix of history and modernity: sleek skyscrapers rise beside grand palaces, world-class museums sit alongside bustling cafés, and the numerous parks and river promenades make it a pleasant place to wander and soak up both Polish culture and contemporary European flair.

wdh.name: Windhoek
wdh.text: Windhoek, the capital of Namibia, sits in the central highlands at an altitude of about 1 700 metres, framed by the rugged Dâures and Khomas mountains. Founded in 1840 as a small settlement of the Herero people, it later became a German colonial outpost, and many red-brick buildings from that era still line its streets. Today the city blends colonial charm with modern African energy: lively cafés serve local coffee, the bustling craft market offers woven blankets and jewellery, and the surrounding semi-desert scenery makes a striking backdrop for relaxed strolls through tree-lined avenues and historic plazas.

wlg.name: Wellington
wlg.text: Wellington, the capital city perched at the southern tip of New Zealand’s North Island, sits where Cook Strait meets a rugged harbour and is framed by hills that spill down to a vibrant waterfront. Founded in 1840, it became the nation’s political centre in 1865 and has since grown into a cultural hub known for its museums, live music and thriving café scene. Today visitors can ride the iconic cable car for panoramic views, stroll along the lively waterfront promenade, explore the quirky art installations at Te Papa Museum, and enjoy the city’s famously windy but welcoming atmosphere, all within easy walking distance of shops, restaurants and stunning natural scenery.

wuh.name: Wuhan
wuh.text: Wuhan, the bustling capital of Hubei province in central China, sits where the Yangtze and Han rivers meet, giving the city a striking waterfront and easy river crossings. It was the site of the 1911 Wuchang Uprising, which sparked the fall of the Qing dynasty and the birth of modern China. Today Wuhan blends historic charm with modern energy: you can wander the leafy East Lake, explore the striking Yellow Crane Tower, and sample famous hot-dry noodles at lively street stalls, while the skyline glitters with towering skyscrapers and a vibrant nightlife scene.

xia.name: Xi'an
xia.text: Xi’an, nestled in the heart of Shaanxi province in north-western China, sits on the fertile plains of the Wei River and marks the eastern end of the historic Silk Road. It was the capital of several great dynasties, most famously the Qin, whose first emperor commissioned the Terracotta Army that was unearthed nearby in 1974. Today the city blends old and new: you can stroll along the well-preserved city wall, wander the bustling Muslim Quarter with its fragrant street food, and still catch sight of sleek skyscrapers rising behind the ancient pagodas, offering a lively glimpse of modern Chinese life.

xmn.name: Xiamen
xmn.text: Xiamen, a bustling coastal city in Fujian province on China’s southeast seaboard, sits opposite the Taiwan Strait and is linked to the historic Gulangyu Island by a short ferry ride. It became a treaty port in the mid-19th century after the First Opium War, which sparked its development as a centre of overseas trade. Today the city charms visitors with palm-shaded promenades, a lively pedestrian street full of street food stalls, well-preserved temples and modern cafés, and a pleasant subtropical climate that makes exploring its harbourside parks and colourful neighbourhoods a relaxed delight.

xnn.name: Xining
xnn.text: Xining, the capital of Qinghai province on the eastern edge of the Tibetan plateau, lies where the Huangshui River meets the high-altitude grasslands of north-west China. For centuries it served as a key trading post on the ancient Silk Road, linking Chinese markets with Tibetan caravans. Today the city blends modern amenities with a distinctive cultural flavour: wide boulevards host bustling street markets selling yak cheese and hand-spun tea, while nearby Qinghai Lake offers stunning vistas and easy day-trips. Visitors enjoy a relaxed pace, colourful temples and the crisp, clean air of the highlands.

yae.name: Yaounde
yae.text: Yaoundé, the capital of Cameroon, sits on a series of hills in the central part of the country, about 750 km east of the Atlantic coast. Founded in 1888 as a German outpost, it became the administrative centre of French Cameroon after World War I and was declared the national capital in 1960. Today the city buzzes with a mix of modern cafés, bustling markets and leafy avenues shaded by jacaranda trees; you can wander the lively neighbourhood of Mfoundi, sample local dishes such as ndolé, and enjoy panoramic views of the surrounding plateau from the hilltop park near the presidential palace.

yar.name: Yaren
yar.text: Yaren, the de facto capital district of the tiny island nation of Nauru, sits on the western coast of the central plateau and faces the warm Pacific. Though Nauru gained independence in 1968 after decades of phosphate mining under Australian administration, Yaren today is modest, with the parliament building, a handful of government offices and a small waterfront promenade. Visitors find a quiet, friendly atmosphere, palm-shaded streets and easy access to the island’s famed white-sand beaches and World War II wrecks that lure snorkellers and divers. Facilities are limited but the laid-back charm and the sense of being on one of the world’s most remote islands make a stop in Yaren a memorable glimpse of Pacific life.

yeg.name: Edmonton
yeg.text: Edmonton, the capital of Alberta, sits in western Canada where the North Saskatchewan River winds through a broad prairie valley, roughly 300 km east of the Rocky Mountains. Founded in 1795 as a Hudson’s Bay Company trading post, the city grew around the historic Fort Edmonton, which later became a centre of the fur trade and early settlement. Today the city is known for its vibrant arts scene, a lively river valley park system and the world-renowned West Eddie Festival of Jazz, while its modern skyline is dotted with sleek towers and friendly cafés, making it a welcoming stop for explorers seeking both culture and outdoor adventure.

yfc.name: Fredericton
yfc.text: Fredericton, the capital city of New Brunswick, lies on the banks of the Saint John River in the heart of the province’s western valley. Founded in 1785 and named after Prince Frederick, the town grew around a Loyalist settlement and later became a centre for the province’s timber trade, a heritage still hinted at in its historic wooden warehouses. Today visitors can stroll along the riverfront promenade, explore the striking Legislative Assembly building and vibrant downtown filled with galleries, cafés and the University of New Brunswick campus, all set against a backdrop of leafy parks and gentle river views.

ygn.name: Yangon
ygn.text: Yangon, the largest city in Myanmar, sits on the banks of the Yangon River in the country’s southern coastal plain. Founded as a small fishing village, it became the colonial capital of British Burma in the 19th century and retains a mix of teak-wood colonial architecture and towering golden pagodas, the most famous being Shwedagon, which has been a place of worship for over two millennia. Today the city hums with bustling markets, street-food stalls and friendly locals; you can wander beneath leafy bougainvillaea-lined avenues, sip tea in a colonial café and watch the sunset glow over the river’s shimmering waters.

yks.name: Yakutsk
yks.text: Yakutsk, perched on the banks of the Lena River in the heart of Siberia, is the capital of the Sakha Republic and one of the world’s coldest cities, where winter temperatures regularly plunge below –40 °C. Founded in 1632 as a Russian outpost, it grew into a centre for the fur trade and later for diamond mining, which still fuels the local economy. Today the town is a surprising blend of modernity and tradition: colourful wooden houses line lively streets, museums showcase indigenous Yakut culture, and a hearty cuisine of reindeer and fish warms visitors after a crisp, clear-air stroll beneath snow-capped hills.

ymq.name: Montreal
ymq.text: Montreal, nestled on the Island of Montreal at the meeting point of the Saint Lawrence and Ottawa rivers in the province of Quebec, is a lively, bilingual city where French and English coexist amid a rich cultural tapestry. Founded in 1642 as the French settlement of Ville-Marie, it grew from a fur-trading outpost into Canada’s second-largest metropolis. Today visitors wander cobbled streets lined with historic stone buildings in Old Montreal, savour world-class cuisine ranging from poutine to fine-dining, and soak up the buzz of festivals, street art and bustling markets, all set against a backdrop of modern skyscrapers and leafy parks.

yok.name: Yokohama
yok.text: Yokohama, Japan’s vibrant port city, lies on the western shore of Tokyo Bay, about a half-hour’s train ride south of the capital. It first opened to foreign trade in 1859, becoming one of the first Japanese ports to welcome Western ships after centuries of isolation. Today the city blends sleek skyscrapers with historic neighbourhoods; you can stroll along the bustling Minato Mirai waterfront, explore the retro charm of the Red Brick Warehouse, and savour fresh sushi in the lively fish market, all while enjoying sweeping bay views and a relaxed, cosmopolitan atmosphere.

yor.name: York
yor.text: York, a historic city in North Yorkshire, lies at the confluence of the Rivers Ouse and Foss, about 30 miles north-east of Leeds and 190 miles north of London. Founded by the Romans as Eboracum, it later became a key Viking-era centre and the site of the famous medieval York Minster. Today the walled city feels compact and lively: you can wander the cobbled Shambles, explore the National Railway Museum, and enjoy the vibrant cafés and independent shops that spill onto the ancient streets, while the impressive city walls offer pleasant walks with views over the modern town below.

yow.name: Ottawa
yow.text: Ottawa, the capital city of Canada, sits on the southern banks of the Ottawa River at the junction of Ontario and Quebec, about 200 km west of Montreal. Founded in 1826 and chosen as the seat of government by Queen Victoria in 1857, it grew around the historic Rideau Canal, a UNESCO World Heritage Site built in the early 19th century to protect the city from naval attack. Today the city blends grand stone parliament buildings and bustling markets with leafy waterfront trails, vibrant festivals and a lively food scene, offering visitors a friendly mix of history, culture and outdoor leisure.

yqb.name: Quebec City
yqb.text: Quebec City, perched on the north-bank of the St Lawrence River in eastern Canada, is the capital of the province of Quebec and one of North America’s oldest European settlements. Founded in 1608 by French explorer Samuel de Champlain, its fortified Old Town (Vieux-Québec) is a UNESCO World Heritage site, with cobbled streets, stone-clad houses and the iconic Château Frontenac looming above. Today the city buzzes with a lively mix of historic charm and modern culture: you can wander the bustling market on Rue du Petit-Champlain, sample poutine and maple-sweetened treats, and enjoy festivals, galleries and riverside promenades that showcase both its French heritage and vibrant contemporary spirit.

yqr.name: Regina
yqr.text: Regina, the capital of Saskatchewan in Canada, sits on the flat, golden prairie plain about 190 kilometres south of the province’s northern border and 250 kilometres north of the United States. The city grew from a railway settlement founded in 1882 and was promptly chosen as the provincial capital, a status it retains today. Its most striking landmark is the grand sandstone Legislative Building, whose copper dome can be seen from many points in town. Modern visitors find a friendly, laid-back atmosphere, with excellent museums, a vibrant culinary scene and wide-open riverfront parks that showcase the sweeping skies and endless horizons of the Canadian West.

yqt.name: Thunder Bay
yqt.text: Thunder Bay sits on the north-western shore of Lake Superior in Ontario, Canada, where the Kaministiquia River meets the lake’s vast waters. The city grew from the historic fur-trading outpost of Fort William, a key Hudson’s Bay Company centre in the early 1800s that helped open the interior to European trade. Today the town blends rugged natural beauty with a relaxed, welcoming vibe: you can stroll along the waterfront boardwalk, explore the striking rock formations of the nearby Sleeping Giant, enjoy Indigenous art galleries and sample fresh lake fish in cosy cafés, all under a backdrop of striking shoreline and pine-clad hills.

ywg.name: Winnipeg
ywg.text: Winnipeg lies in the heart of Canada’s prairies, at the confluence of the Red and Assiniboine rivers in the province of Manitoba. It grew from the Red River Settlement founded by the Hudson’s Bay Company in the early 19th century and became the centre of the Canadian railway network, earning its nickname “Gateway to the West”. Today the city is a vibrant mix of cultural districts, with the historic Exchange District’s brick warehouses now housing cafés, galleries and boutique shops, while the sprawling Assiniboine Park offers riverside walks, a zoo and a striking sculpture garden, making Winnipeg a welcoming stop for any traveller.

yxe.name: Saskatoon
yxe.text: Saskatoon sits on the east bank of the South Saskatchewan River in the central part of the Canadian province of Saskatchewan, roughly midway between Calgary and Winnipeg. Founded in the late 19th century, the town grew around a North West Company trading post and was officially incorporated in 1906, becoming a key hub for grain and railway traffic on the Canadian Prairies. Today visitors find a vibrant mix of modern cafés, art galleries and riverside parks, with the striking skyline reflected in the river’s waters and a lively cultural scene that celebrates both its Indigenous heritage and its pioneering past.

yxy.name: Whitehorse
yxy.text: Whitehorse, the capital of Yukon in north-west Canada, sits on the banks of the mighty Yukon River about 30 kilometres south of the Alaska border. It grew from a modest river-crossing called “the White Horse Rapids” into a bustling supply hub during the Klondike Gold Rush of the late 1890s, when prospectors streamed through on their way to the goldfields. Today the town blends frontier charm with modern comforts: colourful storefronts line Main Street, the Yukon Beringia Interpretive Centre showcases ancient fossils, and the surrounding mountains and river offer spectacular hiking, wildlife spotting and, in winter, brilliant aurora borealis displays.

yyc.name: Calgary
yyc.text: Calgary, nestled in the foothills of the Canadian Rockies in southern Alberta, sits where the Bow and Elbow rivers meet and is the province’s largest city.
