It began in 1875 as Fort Calgary, a North-West Mounted Police outpost, and grew into a bustling centre of the western cattle and oil industries, famously hosting the 1988 Winter Olympics. Today visitors find a lively mix of modern skyscrapers and historic brick streets, world-class museums, and a thriving food scene, while the nearby parks and the annual Calgary Stampede give a vivid taste of the city’s rugged, friendly spirit.

yyg.name: Charlottetown
yyg.text: Charlottetown, the capital of Prince Edward Island, sits on the southern shore of the island at the head of Charlottetown Harbour, where the Northumberland Strait meets the Gulf of St Lawrence. In 1864 the town hosted the Charlottetown Conference, the first meeting that set the foundations for Canadian Confederation, earning it the nickname “Birthplace of Confederation”. Today the city blends historic charm with a lively modern vibe: colourful Victorian houses line the waterfront, boutique shops and cafés spill onto pedestrian streets, and the bustling summer festivals fill the air with music and the scent of fresh seafood, making a visit both relaxed and culturally rich.

yyj.name: Victoria
yyj.text: Victoria, British Columbia, sits on the southern tip of Vancouver Island opposite the mainland’s bustling city of Vancouver, and serves as the province’s capital. Established in 1843 as Fort Victoria by the Hudson’s Bay Company, the settlement grew around a deep natural harbour that once sheltered the fur-trade fleet. Today the city charms visitors with its colourful pastel-painted buildings, fragrant gardens and a relaxed waterfront promenade where you can watch historic double-decker buses trundle past the Parliament Buildings and the iconic Empress Hotel, while cafés and craft markets spill onto the streets, offering a gentle blend of colonial heritage and vibrant Pacific-coast culture.

yyt.name: St. John's
yyt.text: St. John’s, the capital of Newfoundland and Labrador on Canada’s east coast, sits on the eastern edge of the Avalon Peninsula where the Atlantic Ocean meets colourful, tightly packed houses that climb the cliffs of Signal Hill. The city was the site of the first permanent English settlement in North America, founded in 1610, and its historic harbour still echoes with the clatter of fishing boats. Today visitors wander the bustling waterfront, sip locally roasted coffee in cozy cafés, explore museums that tell the story of early trans-atlantic voyages, and enjoy vibrant music festivals against a backdrop of dramatic seascapes and friendly locals.

yyz.name: Toronto
yyz.text: Toronto, Canada’s largest city, sits on the north-western shore of Lake Ontario where the lake meets the River Don and the Humber, about 250 km west of the U.S. border. Founded as the town of York in 1793, it was renamed Toronto when it became a city in 1834 and later the capital of the province of Ontario. Today the city buzzes with a multicultural vibe, offering towering skyscrapers such as the iconic CN Tower, vibrant neighbourhoods like Kensington Market, extensive waterfront parks, and a thriving food scene that reflects its many cultures, making it a lively destination for any traveller.

yzd.name: Yazd
yzd.text: Yazd, situated in the heart of central Iran on the edge of the great desert plateau, is famed for its ancient mud-brick architecture and its status as a historic centre of Zoroastrian culture; the city’s fire temple, dating back to the 5th-century AD, still houses a sacred flame that has supposedly never been extinguished. Today the narrow, wind-towered alleys are a pleasant maze of quiet courtyards, fragrant bazaars and cool, shaded tea houses, while the striking skyline of towering domes and the UNESCO-listed historic centre invite leisurely exploration under a clear, sun-lit sky.

yzf.name: Yellowknife
yzf.text: Yellowknife, the capital of Canada’s Northwest Territories, sits on the northern shore of Great Slave Lake, just below the Arctic Circle. Founded in the 1930s during the region’s gold-rush, the town was named after the Yellowknife Dene, whose traditional lands include the area. Today the city is a vibrant mix of modern amenities and wilderness adventure, offering museums that showcase Indigenous culture and mining history, colourful waterfront promenades, and easy access to spectacular northern lights, dog-sledding and canoe trips on the lake, all set against a backdrop of boreal forest and crisp, clean air.

zag.name: Zagreb
zag.text: Zagreb, the capital of Croatia, sits in the north-west of the country where the Sava and Medveščak rivers meet, a short drive from the Slovenian border and the Adriatic coast. First mentioned in a 1093 charter, the city grew around the medieval Kaptol cathedral district and later became a key Habsburg administrative centre. Today Zagreb buzzes with a relaxed yet lively atmosphere: its pedestrian-only Ban Jelačić Square hosts cafés, street musicians and markets, while the Upper Town offers cobbled lanes, museums and stunning views of the red-tiled roofs that stretch beneath the surrounding hills.

zar.name: Zaragoza
zar.text: Zaragoza, nestled in the north-east of Spain on the banks of the Ebro River, lies roughly halfway between Madrid and Barcelona and serves as the capital of the autonomous community of Aragon. The city’s most famous landmark, the Basilica of Our Lady of the Pillar, has been a major pilgrimage site since the early medieval period, when legend says the Virgin Mary appeared to the apostle James here. Today Zaragoza buzzes with a lively mix of historic charm and modern energy: you can stroll through bustling tapas bars, explore the Roman-era Aljafería Palace, and enjoy riverside walks while the city’s vibrant cultural calendar offers festivals, music and art throughout the year.

zns.name: Zanzibar
zns.text: Zanzibar town, perched on the western coast of the Tanzanian archipelago, lies on the island of Unguja at the mouth of the historic Stone Town harbour. This UNESCO World Heritage site was once the thriving centre of the 19th-century spice trade and the capital of the Sultanate of Oman, famous for its bustling markets and Arab-influenced architecture. Today visitors wander narrow, winding alleys lined with richly carved wooden doors, explore bustling bazaars selling fragrant cloves and fresh seafood, and relax on nearby white-sand beaches while the gentle Indian Ocean breeze carries the scent of spices and sea.

zqn.name: Queenstown
zqn.text: Queenstown lies on the shores of Lake Wakatipu in the South Island of New Zealand, framed by the towering Remarkables and surrounded by rugged alpine scenery. Founded during the 1860s gold-rush era, the town grew from a modest mining settlement into a bustling hub for adventurers. Today it pulses with energy: you can glide down the slopes in winter, zip-line over forested valleys in summer, and savour world-class wines at nearby vineyards, all while enjoying a relaxed café culture and spectacular sunset reflections on the lake’s glassy surface.

zrh.name: Zurich
zrh.text: Zurich lies in the north-east of Switzerland, nestled at the tip of Lake Zürich and framed by the Limmat River and the Swiss Alps. First mentioned in a document of 846 AD, the city grew around a Benedictine abbey that became a centre of trade and later a hub of the Reformation. Today Zurich blends historic charm with modern vitality: you can wander the well-preserved medieval Altstadt, admire art at the Kunsthaus, and savour coffee in stylish cafés while the efficient trams whisk you past gleaming banks, bustling markets and tranquil lakeside promenades.
